In the context of trust and prayer (especially in the Psalms), "help" becomes almost synonymous with "salvation" or "deliverance" — it is the call that believers send out to their God.
H5828.portee: This word reminds the believer that he is not alone in facing the difficulties of life. God does not ask man to bear everything alone: He created the human community (the woman for the man) so that each one supports the other. Even more, God Himself commits as a faithful help for His people. It is a word of comfort: those who fear the Lord can place their trust in Him, for God is a help always present and capable.

sens: Man of the tribe of Judah, son of Hur
Father of Hushah
H5829G.detail:
1. Ezer is a man of the tribe of Judah, living during the time of Egypt and the desert. He is the son of Hur, who was himself the firstborn of Ephrath and the father of Bethlehem. Ezer thus belongs to an important lineage in the history of Israel, as shown by his mention in 1 Chronicles 4:4.
2. Ezer is known as the father of Hushah. His name appears in the genealogy of Judah to mark the transmission of this family lineage through the generations.
H5829G.origine: The name Ezer means "treasure" in Hebrew. It expresses the idea of something precious and carefully kept. It is a name that suggests value and importance, which suits a man from a prominent family in the tribe of Judah.
H5829G.emploi: Ezer appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 4:4. He is listed in the genealogy of Judah, among the descendants of Hur. This genealogical context is typical of how the Bible preserves the memory of important families in Israel, even for characters who play only a minor role in the narrative.

sens: Gadite chief during the time of King David
H5829H.detail: Ezer is a military leader of the tribe of Gad who joined David during his battles. He is mentioned in 1 Chronicles 12:9 as one of the warriors of Gad who rallied to David at Ziklag, before he became king of Israel.
H5829H.origine: The name Ezer means "treasure" in Hebrew. It is a common theophoric name (expressing a relationship to God) in the Old Testament, notably borne by other characters in the history of Israel.
H5829H.emploi: Ezer appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 12:9, where he is presented as a Gadite war chief. This mention occurs in the context of David's flight from Saul, before his accession to the throne. His inclusion in the list of leaders who supported him shows the importance of these warriors in the formation of his future royal army.

sens: Man of the tribe of Judah living during the time of the Exile and return
H5829I.detail: Ezer is a biblical character mentioned only once in the book of Nehemiah. He is a man of Judah, son of Joshua, who was chief of Mizpah. He participated in the reconstruction of the wall of Jerusalem after the return from exile in Babylon (Nehemiah 3:19).
H5829I.origine: The name Ezer means "treasure" in Hebrew. It comes from a root that expresses the idea of wealth or something precious. This name was borne by several characters in the history of Israel: notably a father named Hushah among the sons of Hur, a Gadite chief who fought alongside David, and this Levite during the time of Nehemiah.
H5829I.emploi: Ezer appears only once in the Bible, in Nehemiah 3:19. He is mentioned in the context of the reconstruction of the wall of Jerusalem after the return from exile. He held the title of chief of Mizpah and was responsible for repairing a section of the wall, near the ascent to the arsenal and a strategic corner of the city. His involvement shows that local authorities in the cities of Judah actively participated in this great restoration project.

sens: Levite who participated in the consecration of the wall of Jerusalem under Nehemiah
H5829J.detail: 1. Ezer is a Levite who is among the singers during the ceremony of consecration of the wall of Jerusalem, at the time of Nehemiah. He is mentioned alongside other musicians such as Maaseiah and Jonathan (Nehemiah 12:42).
H5829J.origine: The name Ezer means "treasure" in Hebrew. It derives from a root evoking wealth and value. It is a traditional name borne by several men in the history of Israel, including warriors and servants of worship.
H5829J.emploi: Ezer appears only once in the Bible, in Nehemiah 12:42. He is presented as one of the Levite singers who participated in the solemn consecration of the wall of Jerusalem after the Babylonian exile, at the time of Nehemiah. This passage celebrates the restoration of the temple and the Jewish community, and Ezer is among the musicians tasked with praising God during this important feast.

sens: Man of the tribe of Ephraim during the time of Egypt and the desert
Father of Hushah among the sons of Hur
Gadite chief who fought with David
Levite who helped repair the wall of Jerusalem during Nehemiah's time
H5829K.detail: The biblical text directly mentions only one Ezer: a man of the tribe of Ephraim, son of Ephraim himself, living during the time of Egypt and the desert (1 Chronicles 7:21). He is the brother of Shuthelah, Becher, Tahan, Elad, and Beriah. The Bible reports that with his brother Elad, he went down to take livestock, but the men of Gath, born in the land, killed them. Rabbinic tradition identifies other bearers of this name — a father of Hushah among the builders, a Gadite chief alongside David, and a Levite who participated in the repairs of the wall of Jerusalem — but they are not attested in this specific passage.
H5829K.origine: The name Ezer means "treasure" in Hebrew, derived from a root expressing the idea of wealth or precious value. It is a symbolic name that evokes value and blessing, frequently given in the genealogies of the Old Testament.
H5829K.emploi: Ezer primarily appears in the genealogies of the tribe of Ephraim (1 Chronicles 7:21), where he is presented as the son of Ephraim and brother of Elad. The only detailed account concerning him reports his death, killed by the men of Gath with his brother when they attempted to seize livestock. This name reappears in other contexts in the history of Israel — notably with characters bearing the same name involved in the reconstruction of Jerusalem — illustrating how the same name could be borne by multiple people at different periods in biblical history.

sens: Jewish priest and scribe of the time of the return from exile
The one who led the religious reforms in Jerusalem after the return from Babylon
Spiritual leader and educator of the people of Israel
H5830G.detail:
1. Ezra is a priest and a scribe, meaning a man educated in the law of God, who lived during the time of the Babylonian captivity and the return to the Holy Land (Ezra 7:1). He is the son of Seraiah and a descendant of the priestly lineage of the Levites.

2. Ezra is the great religious reformer who led the Israelites returning from exile to turn away from their sins, particularly from mixed marriages (Ezra 10:5). He rises with spiritual authority to remind the people of their obedience to the law of the Lord.

3. Ezra is also an educator: he teaches the law and commandments of God to the assembled people (Nehemiah 8:4, 8:9). In Jerusalem, he reads and explains the words of the law to the crowds who weep as they become aware of their faults and of divine grace.
H5830G.origine: The name "Ezra" comes from the Hebrew "Ezra," which means "help" or "one who helps." This meaning well reflects Ezra's role in the history of Israel: he comes to aid the people by bringing them back to faithfulness to God and His law after the terrible years of exile in Babylon.
H5830G.emploi: Ezra appears 19 times in the Bible, mainly in the books of Ezra and Nehemiah, which recount the return of the Jews from captivity in the 5th century B.C. First introduced as a priest and scribe in Ezra 7:1, he is sent by the king of Persia to restore religious order in Jerusalem. The book of Ezra shows him leading decisive reforms: he intervenes so that the Israelites renounce their unions with foreign women, which would threaten the purity of worship. In Nehemiah, Ezra appears as the colleague of Nehemiah, the governor: together, they solemnly read and interpret the law to the assembled people at the Water Gate.
H5830G.portee: Ezra embodies for the Christian the role of spiritual teacher and faithful reformer. His life shows how a man can fully dedicate himself to the study and teaching of the Word of God, and how this knowledge bears fruit by bringing an entire people to repentance and obedience. His commitment to the purity of worship and the transmission of the law invites the believer to take the Word of God seriously in their own life.

sens: priest and scribe who led the reforms of the exiles returned to Jerusalem
priest companion of Zerubbabel at the return from exile
another Jew of the post-exilic period
H5830H.detail:
1. Ezra is primarily the high priest and scribe who played a major role in the religious and moral restoration of Jerusalem after the return from exile in Babylon. He worked alongside Nehemiah to reorganize the life of the people according to the Law. He appears in the book that bears his name (Ezra) and in Nehemiah, notably at the time he returned with Zerubbabel, son of Shealtiel (Nehemiah 12:1).
2. Ezra was also a priest among those who returned with Zerubbabel during the first wave of return (Nehemiah 12:1, 12:13).
3. The name Ezra also refers to other characters of the post-exilic period, as indicated by its mention in the lists of Nehemiah 12:33, where he is among those who participated in public ceremonies.
H5830H.origine: The name Ezra comes from the Hebrew עֶזְרָא (Ezra), which literally means "help" or "assistance." This name reflects the image of a helper, a liberator. It corresponds to the Greek name Ἔσδρας (Ezra) in ancient translations. The book of Ezra recounts how this character became indeed a help for his people by bringing them back to the Law of God.
H5830H.emploi: Ezra is mentioned three times in the book of Nehemiah, always in connection with the return from exile and the restoration of Jerusalem in the 5th century B.C. In Nehemiah 12:1, he is listed among the priests and Levites who returned with Zerubbabel. In Nehemiah 12:13, he is again cited in a genealogy of priests, while his name follows that of Ezra from another lineage. In Nehemiah 12:33, Ezra appears during the dedication ceremonies of the walls of Jerusalem. The main character of Ezra the priest and scribe is primarily developed in the book of Ezra itself, where he is described as a spiritual leader and a major reformer.
H5830H.portee: Ezra illustrates the crucial role of spiritual leaders in the restoration of a people. His commitment to the Law of God and his courage to lead religious reforms show that the material restoration of a nation is inseparable from its spiritual restoration. For today's believer, Ezra reminds us that knowing and teaching the Word of God requires dedication and perseverance.

sens: Jewish priest and scribe of the time of exile and return
Leader of the religious reforms of the exiles returned to Jerusalem
Collaborator of Nehemiah in the restoration of the Jewish community
H5831.detail: Ezra is a priest and scribe of the tribe of Levi who played a decisive role in the return from exile to Jerusalem. His name means "help" or "assistance." The Persian king Artaxerxes recognizes him as a major religious and legal authority: he entrusts him with the power to establish judges and magistrates to apply the law of God among the Jews returned beyond the River (Ezra 7:25). Ezra unites in himself the two essential roles of Jewish leadership: priest (he can offer sacrifices) and scribe (he knows and teaches the Law). His authority rests on his deep knowledge of divine law and on the support of the Persian power, which allows him to gather the necessary resources for the temple (Ezra 7:21).
H5831.origine: The name Ezra comes from Hebrew and Aramaic with the meaning of "help" or "assistance." It derives from a root expressing the idea of assistance. Ezra is the son of Seraiah and the brother of Jehozadak. His ministry is part of the continuity of the great restorers of the Jewish people after the Babylonian exile.
H5831.emploi: Ezra appears three times in the book that bears his name, all in the context of the royal decree of King Artaxerxes (Ezra 7). It is through this edict that the king recognizes Ezra as a priest and scribe well-versed in the law of the God of heaven, and grants him the authority to reform the Jewish community. The text emphasizes his legal and religious competence ("according to the wisdom of God that you possess"). Ezra is presented not only as an expert but as God's representative before the Persian power and as the restorer of religious and moral order among the returned exiles.
H5831.portee: The figure of Ezra teaches that God can place His servants in positions of authority in complex political contexts, and that a solid knowledge of His Word is the true foundation of spiritual leadership. It also shows how faith can be realized in just and lasting reforms, and how the study of the Law of God is inseparable from its practical application to communal life.

sens: Korahite warrior who joined David at Ziklag
H5832G.detail: Azareel is a warrior from the priestly tribe of the Korahites who joined David when he had taken refuge at Ziklag, before becoming king of Israel (1 Chronicles 12:6). He belonged to those valiant and faithful men who supported David during his difficult years.
H5832G.origine: The name means "God has helped": it combines two Hebrew elements, one evoking help or assistance, the other designating God. It is a theophoric name, meaning it carries the divine name, expressing trust in God's help — a common form of personal name among the Hebrews.
H5832G.emploi: Azareel is mentioned only once in the entire Bible, in 1 Chronicles 12:6. This passage lists the Korahite warriors who left Saul to join David at Ziklag when he was still being pursued by the reigning king. Azareel is included among these quality fighters.

sens: man of the tribe of Dan during the time of David
prince of the tribe of Dan
son of Jeroham
H5832H.detail: Azareel is a man from the tribe of Dan mentioned only once in the Bible, during the census of the tribes of Israel ordered by King David. He is designated as prince or chief of his tribe (1 Chronicles 27:22), which means he held recognized authority among the Danites. His father's name was Jeroham, a name borne by several men in Israel's history.
H5832H.origine: The name Azareel means "God has helped": it is formed from two Hebrew elements: "azar" (to help) and "el" (God). It is a theophoric name, meaning it confesses divinity and celebrates its aid. Several men bore this name during different periods of Israel's history: warriors of David, Levitical musicians, and priests from the time of the return from exile.
H5832H.emploi: Azareel is mentioned only once in 1 Chronicles 27:22, in the context of the census of the twelve tribes of Israel undertaken by King David. He is listed as the prince or chief of the tribe of Dan at that time. The Segond translates his name as "Azareel" (French spelling of the Hebrew transliteration). This brief mention is part of a genealogical and administrative list, without particular details about his exploits or personal life.

sens: Man from the period of exile and return to Jerusalem
one of the sons of Bani who had married a foreign woman
H5832I.detail:
1. Azareel is a name borne by several men in Israel's history, particularly during the time of the return from exile after the Babylonian captivity. The name means "God has helped" in Hebrew, reminding that God supported the people in their trials.
2. In the specific context of the book of Ezra, Azareel is one of the sons of Bani who had taken a foreign woman as his wife (Ezra 10:41). Ezra asked these men to send away their foreign wives in order to restore the purity of the Jewish community returning from captivity. Azareel, like the others, had turned away from Israel's marital laws.
H5832I.origine: The name Azareel comes from Hebrew and literally means "God has helped" or "God has rescued". It is composed of "azar" (to help, to rescue) and "El" (God). This theophoric name expresses trust in divine help. According to the full definition, several men bore this name: a Korahite warrior of David, a Levitical musician, a Danite prince, and others. The biblical text preserved in Ezra 10:41 reports the specific case of Azareel son of Bani.
H5832I.emploi: Azareel appears only once in the Bible, in Ezra 10:41. He is listed among the men who, upon returning from exile under the leadership of Ezra and Nehemiah, had contracted marriages with non-Jewish women. This practice was considered a serious transgression due to the biblical prohibition of mixed marriages and the risk of idolatry it entailed. The list in Ezra 10 represents a decisive moment of religious and national purification for the Jewish community returned from Babylon.
H5832I.portee: The case of Azareel shows that the return from exile was not just a political and architectural restoration, but primarily a moral and spiritual restoration. Even men who acknowledged God could fall into compromises with the surrounding pagan world. His story invites the reader to be vigilant against influences that lead away from obedience to God, and to the grace of repentance offered to those who recognize their waywardness.

sens: Levitical musician during the time of Nehemiah
H5832J.detail: Azareel is a Levitical musician who participates in the festivities of the dedication of the wall of Jerusalem upon the return from exile (Nehemiah 12:36). He belongs to a family of musicians and priests, and is mentioned alongside his brothers who play together with the instruments of David.
H5832J.origine: The name Azareel means "God has helped" in Hebrew, composed of two elements: "azar" (to help, to rescue) and "El" (God). It is a classic theophoric name in ancient Israel, expressing trust in divine help. Several characters bear this name at different periods in Israel's history.
H5832J.emploi: Azareel appears only once in the Bible, in Nehemiah 12:36. He is presented as a Levitical musician belonging to a complete brotherhood of priests and musicians during the time of Nehemiah. He is among those who celebrate the dedication of the wall of Jerusalem after the return from exile, playing with the traditional instruments associated with temple worship.

sens: Levitical priest in Jerusalem after the exile
priest from the family of Immer
H5832K.detail:
1. Azareel is a Levitical priest living in Jerusalem after the return from exile in Babylon. His name means "God has helped" in Hebrew. He is the father of Amaschsaï (or Amashaï), who is among the priests returned to Jerusalem and who dwells in the holy city (Nehemiah 11:13).
2. Azareel belongs to the priestly family of Immer, one of the major priestly families in Israel. He represents the continuity of liturgical service after the exile, when the Jews were able to return from captivity and restore temple worship.
H5832K.origine: The name Azareel (עֲזַרְאֵל) is composed of two Hebrew elements: "azar" (עָזַר), which means "to help" or "to rescue", and "El" (אֵל), which designates God. The name thus expresses trust in divine help. It is a theophoric name, meaning a name that proclaims a relationship with God, typical of the Israelite tradition.
H5832K.emploi: Azareel appears only once in the Bible, in Nehemiah 11:13, in the list of priests and Levites returned from exile to Jerusalem. This passage enumerates the heads of the paternal houses and the priestly families who rebuilt religious life in the city. Azareel is presented there as the father of Amaschsaï, a renowned priest, and as the son of Achzaï and grandson of Meschillémoth, all from the family of Immer.
H5832K.portee: The name Azareel, "God has helped", reminds the reader that the return from exile was a manifestation of God's help and faithfulness to His people. The mention of these priestly families in Nehemiah emphasizes that the restoration of the temple and worship was only possible through divine grace. For the Christian, this passage testifies to God's constancy in history and His commitment to uplift His people.

sens: Levitical musician from the family of Heman during the time of King David
H5832L.detail: Azareel is a Levite from the tribe of Levi who lived during the time of King David. He belongs to the musical family of Heman, one of the great musicians of the temple. In the register of temple musicians (1 Chronicles 25), Azareel is classified as "the eleventh" among the sons of Heman with his brothers (1 Chronicles 25:18), which means he held the eleventh rank in the musical service of the sanctuary, with his own sons and brothers to assist him. It was an honor to be counted among the Levitical musicians of the temple in Jerusalem.
H5832L.origine: The name Azareel comes from Hebrew and means "God has helped". It is formed from two elements: "azar" (to help) and "El" (God). It is a classic theophoric name in Israel, expressing the faith that God helps His people. The same character is also referred to elsewhere by the similar name Uzziel (H5816J), another name for the same person with a comparable meaning.
H5832L.emploi: Azareel appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 25:18, in the official list of Levitical musicians of the temple during the time of David. He is mentioned as the eleventh son of Heman, who himself was one of the three great choir leaders of the temple (the others being Asaph and Jeduthun). This mention in a precise genealogical register shows the importance of sacred music in Israel's worship and the specific role that the Levites from Heman's family held.
H5832L.portee: Azareel reminds the reader that serving God involved many unknown faithful, all contributing to praise and worship in the temple. His name, "God has helped", reflects the faith that these Levitical musicians placed in the Lord to fulfill their ministry. It is an invitation to see every service rendered to the Lord, even if unnoticed, as an honorable participation in the worship of God's people.

sens: Material or military aid provided to someone
Divine intervention for deliverance or salvation
The one who comes to help
H5833.detail:
1. The word primarily refers to concrete help, often military: a reinforcement, troops sent to support. Thus, in Judges 5:23, Meroz is cursed for not coming to the "help" during a battle, meaning for not lending a hand to the fighters of Israel.
2. Very often, the word expresses God's salvific intervention. This is what the psalmist cries: "Come quickly to my help" (Psalms 40:14). He pleads with the Lord to come down to pull him from danger, death, or distress — as in Psalms 94:17, where the author acknowledges that without God's "help," his soul would be lost.
3. The word can also refer to the person or power that provides this help: the one who comes to assist, God Himself conceived as protector and savior.
H5833.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that evokes the idea of supporting, propping up, coming alongside someone to lift them up. It is a notion of active help, support in need. In Aramaic and Hebrew, the same family of words speaks of one who "helps," one who "supports." The word fundamentally expresses a helpful presence alongside the one who is weak.
H5833.emploi: The word appears 25 times in the Old Testament, mostly in the Psalms (half of the occurrences) and in the prophets. The psalmists constantly cry out to God: it is the cry of the weak to the Almighty. The context varies: sometimes it is about military help that nations seek from other powers (Isaiah 31:1, where the Egyptians seek help in horses and chariots), sometimes it is about divine help implored by the faithful in distress. In Psalms 60:13 and Psalms 108:13, the psalmist asserts that "the help of man is only vanity" and therefore asks God for His help: this is the heart of the message. God alone is reliable, unlike human alliances.
H5833.portee: This word reminds the believer that he should not seek his salvation in human resources — money, power, political alliances — but in God's intervention. Crying out "Lord, come to my help!" is the admission of weakness and the trust that only God can truly lift us up. This is why the Psalms are filled with it: they teach the faithful to turn their eyes to God, and not to the powers of the world.

sens: Man of the tribe of Judah during the time of the Divided Monarchy
H5834.detail: Ezra is a man of the tribe of Judah mentioned only once in the Bible, at the time when the kingdom of Israel was divided into two rival kingdoms. He is the father of four sons: Jether, Mered, Epher, and Jalon (1 Chronicles 4:17). The name literally means "help" or "aid" in Hebrew.
H5834.origine: The name Ezra comes from the Hebrew עֶזְרָה (ezrah), formed from the root עזר which means "to help" or "to aid." This root evokes the idea of a person who brings help or support. The suffix -ah characterizes Hebrew names. This name was quite common in Hebrew tradition.
H5834.emploi: Ezra appears only once in the Scriptures, in 1 Chronicles 4:17, in a genealogy of the tribe of Judah. He is presented there as the father of four sons. This brief mention is part of the genealogical lists that trace the history of Israelite families during the time of the Divided Monarchy (approximately between the 10th and 6th centuries BC). His role in the Bible is purely genealogical: he is cited only to situate his descendants in the history of God's people.

sens: open space surrounding a religious building, especially the temple
ledge or cornice bordering a structure, such as the altar
H5835.detail:
1. The courtyard primarily refers to the open space surrounding the temple or its buildings, that is, the court or esplanade where the faithful gather and where sacrifices take place. Solomon had a large one built with doors whose leaves were covered in bronze (2 Chronicles 4:9); it was there that he prayed kneeling before all Israel (2 Chronicles 6:13), which shows how central this place was in worship.
2. The word also refers to a ledge, a border, or a protruding frame that runs around an altar or a structure. In Ezekiel's vision, the altar of the future temple had a frame measuring a cubit in width at several levels (Ezekiel 43:17); it was on these ledges that the blood of the sacrifice was placed to purify the altar (Ezekiel 43:20 and 45:19).
H5835.origine: The Hebrew word azarah comes from a root meaning "to surround" or "to enclose." It designates what encloses, confines, or borders an area. The same family of words can denote the idea of an enclosure, of limits that define a sacred space or separate it from the rest.
H5835.emploi: The word appears six times in the Hebrew Bible, always in relation to places or elements of worship. Two uses concern the courts of Solomon's temple (2 Chronicles 4:9 and 6:13), where the courtyard is a structured space, with doors and platforms, intended for public rites and prayer. The other four uses are found in the book of Ezekiel (chapters 43 and 45), which describes the vision of the restored temple altar: there, azarah designates the ledges or cords that bound the structure of the altar at different heights, where sacrificial blood was applied. Its meaning thus varies slightly according to the context: public space in the architecture of the temple, or architectural detail of a ritual object.
H5835.portee: The courtyard reminds the believer that worship does not unfold in secret, but before God and often before the community. It is a place of transparency, where the people see their leaders pray (like Solomon), where sacrifices are offered before witnesses. This visibility invites the Christian to sincere worship, without hidden calculations.

sens: Officer of King David's court
Son of Chelub
Steward of the king's agricultural workers
H5836.detail: Ezri is a man who lived during the time of the divided monarchy in Israel. He is the son of Chelub and appears in the list of David's officers as the overseer of the royal agricultural workers. His role was to supervise the laborers and slaves who tended the king's fields and lands (1 Chronicles 27:26). He held a position of authority in the palace administration, responsible for the agricultural production that fed the king and his court.
H5836.origine: The name Ezri means "Help of God" or "God is my help": it is composed of two Hebrew elements, "ez" (help, aid) and "ri" (variation of "Yah," the divine name). It is a theophoric name, very common in Israel, expressing trust in divine help. Ezri's family, whose father Chelub is also mentioned in Scripture, is part of the Davidic royal administration.
H5836.emploi: Ezri is mentioned only once in the entire Bible, in 1 Chronicles 27:26. He appears in an administrative list enumerating the heads of the various departments of King David's court. His specific title was to command the men who worked in the royal fields (plowmen, farmers, and possibly slaves). This unique mention shows the importance of the administrative structures of the Davidic kingdom and how the king organized the agricultural production of the land. Although little known, Ezri represents the thousands of officers and officials who ensured the daily functioning of King David's kingdom.

sens: Leader of a house of the half-tribe of Manasseh, established beyond the Jordan
H5837G.detail: 1. Azriel is a man who led an important family of the half-tribe of Manasseh, which settled east of the Jordan. During the time of the divided monarchy, he is mentioned among the most prominent and valiant leaders of his tribe, alongside his colleagues Ephraim, Jishai, and Eliel.
H5837G.origine: The name Azriel literally means "My help is God" in Hebrew. It comes from two Hebrew roots: "ezer" (help, assistance) and "el" (God). It is a theophoric name, common in Israel, expressing the trust of the bearer in divine assistance.
H5837G.emploi: Azriel appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 5:24, in a genealogical list of the leaders of Manasseh's houses. The context is that of the genealogical records of the tribes of Israel, documenting families and their leaders at a time prior to the Babylonian exile. This unique mention indicates his local importance but offers no narrative of his actions or personal life.

sens: Tribal leader during the reign of King David
Father of Jerimoth
H5837H.detail:
1. Azriel is an officer during the reign of King David, responsible for the tribe of Naphtali during the royal census. He appears in the list of leaders that David established to administer each tribe of Israel (1 Chronicles 27:19).
2. He is the father of Jerimoth, who himself becomes chief of the tribe of Naphtali during this same period of David's reign.
H5837H.origine: The name Azriel means "My help is God" or "God is my help." It is composed of "azr" (help, assistance) and "El" (God). This name expresses trust in divine assistance, a common conviction among Hebrew names of that time.
H5837H.emploi: Azriel is mentioned only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 27:19, where he is listed among the officials appointed by King David to manage the affairs of the tribes of Israel. The text designates him as the father of Jerimoth, chief of the tribe of Naphtali at the time of the royal census.

sens: Father of Serajah, officer of King Josiah of Judah
Name meaning 'my help is God'
H5837I.detail: Azriel is a character from the Old Testament mentioned only once in the Bible. He is known as the father of Serajah, an officer of King Josiah who was ordered to capture the prophet Jeremiah and his secretary Baruch (Jeremiah 36:26). His Hebrew name means "my help is God," composed of "az" (strength, help) and "el" (God), expressing a trust in divine assistance. Although the source definition mentions three Azriels in the history of Israel, only the father of Serajah actually appears in the transmitted biblical text.
H5837I.origine: The name Azriel literally means "my help is God." It is composed of the root "azar" (to help, to assist) and the word "El" (God), a common structure in Hebrew proper names to express the relationship of the bearer with God. It is a theophoric name, meaning it incorporates the divine name, which was a common practice among Israelites to honor God and place their lives under His protection.
H5837I.emploi: Azriel appears only once in the Bible, in Jeremiah 36:26. He is mentioned as the father of Serajah, an officer whom King Josiah ordered to arrest the prophet Jeremiah and his secretary Baruch after the prophet's message offended the king. This unique passage situates Azriel in the context of Jeremiah's difficult ministry, at a time when Judean authorities opposed the word of God. His name suggests that he lived in the confidence that God was his help, even while serving a king who rejected the prophetic word.
H5837I.portee: This name reminds us that even the simple servants of earthly kings bore names declaring their faith in God. Azriel, despite his position in the royal court, displayed through his name a dependence on God as his source of help. His appearance in the account of Jeremiah's persecution shows how believers in the Old Testament lived out their faith amid political and religious tensions.

sens: Priest, son of Ahimelech and grandson of the high priest Zadok, during the time of King Solomon
H5838G.detail: 1. Azariah is a man from the tribe of Levi who lived during the time of the united monarchy. He is the son of the priest Ahimelech and the grandson of the high priest Zadok. He appears in the genealogies of the priests serving under King Solomon (1 Kings 4:2), where he is mentioned as part of the important leaders of the royal court. His lineage illustrates the priestly authority that extended to the highest offices of the kingdom.
H5838G.origine: The name Azariah comes from Hebrew and means "God has helped" or "the Lord has helped," formed from the word meaning "to help" or "to assist" and the divine name. This name expresses trust in divine assistance and was borne by several important figures in the history of Israel, including a king of Judah and Daniel's renowned friend Abednego. The name reflects the piety and dependence on God that characterized respectable figures in the Old Testament.
H5838G.emploi: Azariah is a name borne by several characters in the Old Testament. The Azariah mentioned in 1 Kings 4:2 is specifically a priest during Solomon's time, son of Ahimelech. The genealogies in 1 Chronicles 6:9 confirm his place in the succession of high priests, between his father Ahimelech and his son Johanan. This Azariah represents an unbroken line of faithful priests who served God through the generations and exerted significant spiritual influence over the kingdom of Israel.
H5838G.portee: This Azariah illustrates the importance of the priestly role in the governance and spiritual life of Israel. His inscription in the genealogies shows how God maintains a succession of faithful servants through generations, ensuring the continuity of worship and mediation between God and His people. For the Christian reader, this reminds us that God uses ordinary men, from priestly families, to accomplish His work, and that commitment to God's service is passed down from generation to generation.

sens: Son of Nathan, officer of King Solomon
Man whose name means 'the Lord has helped'
H5838H.detail:
1. Azaria is a man who lived during the time of the united monarchy in Israel. He was the son of Nathan and held an important position at the court of King Solomon: he was chief of the stewards (1 Kings 4:5), meaning he oversaw the governors and the administration of the provinces of the kingdom.
2. His Hebrew name means "the Lord has helped" or "the Lord has assisted." It expresses the trust that his parents placed in God's divine protection, like many Hebrew names in the Old Testament.
H5838H.origine: The name Azaria comes from Hebrew and is composed of two elements: "azar" (to help, to assist) and "Yah" (abbreviated form of the divine name, the Lord). It is a theophoric name, meaning it contains the name of God, which was common in Israelite families to confess their dependence on the Lord. The same name has been borne by several other important figures in the history of Israel, including a king of Judah and a friend of Daniel.
H5838H.emploi: Azaria appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Kings 4:5. He is presented as the son of Nathan and brother of Zabud. Both served at Solomon's court: Azaria was chief of the stewards responsible for the provincial administration of the kingdom, while Zabud was a state minister and favorite of the king. This mention shows the importance of Nathan's family in Solomon's administration.
H5838H.portee: This brief mention reminds us that faithful service to authorities was an honorable vocation in Israel. Azaria, whose name confessed God's protection, held an important administrative responsibility for the good of the kingdom. This invites us to see all management and administrative work, when done with integrity, as a means of serving the order that God establishes.

sens: Man of the tribe of Judah during the time of the divided monarchy
H5838I.detail: 1. Azaria is a man of the tribe of Judah mentioned only once in the Bible, at the time when the kingdoms of Israel and Judah existed separately. He is identified as the son of Ethan (1 Chronicles 2:8).
H5838I.origine: The name Azaria means "The Lord has helped" or "Jehovah has helped" in Hebrew. It comes from two roots: "azar" (to help, to assist) and "Yah" (the abbreviated divine name). This name expresses the trust that his parents placed in divine help. The same name was borne by several other important figures in biblical history, including a king of Judah and Daniel's friend known as Abednego.
H5838I.emploi: Azaria appears only once in Scripture, in 1 Chronicles 2:8, in a genealogy of the tribe of Judah. He is listed among the sons of Ethan, a descendant of Judah. This brief mention in a genealogical list shows that the author of Chronicles wanted to preserve the record of the families of Judah, even for individuals about whom few other details are provided.

sens: man of the tribe of Judah living during the time of the divided monarchy
H5838J.detail: 1. Azaria is a man of Judah mentioned in the genealogy of the book of Chronicles. He is the son of Jehu and the father of Halets, listed among the descendants of Judah to show the continuity of the family line (1 Chronicles 2:38-39).
H5838J.origine: The name Azaria means "Jehovah has helped" or "Jehovah has assisted." It comes from two Hebrew words: "Azar" (to help, to assist) and "Yah" (abbreviation of the divine name Jehovah). It is a name of trust that expresses the certainty that God helps His people. The same name has been borne by several important figures in the history of Israel.
H5838J.emploi: This Azaria is mentioned only in the genealogy of 1 Chronicles 2, where he is included in the lineage of the tribe of Judah. He is not a major figure, but simply a link in the genealogical chain passed down to establish the origins of the families of Judah. His role is to perpetuate his family's lineage.

sens: Man of the tribe of Levi mentioned in the priestly genealogies
Son of Johanan and father of Amaria
Ancestor of the priest Ezra
H5838K.detail:
1. Azaria is a Levite who appears in the genealogical list of the priests of Israel during the time of the divided monarchy. His name means "The Lord has helped" and evokes trust in divine assistance.
2. He is the son of Johanan and the father of Amaria, placing him in the direct succession of the priesthood (1 Chronicles 6:10-11). He served as a priest in the Temple that Solomon built in Jerusalem.
3. He is an ancestor of the scribe and priest Ezra, who brought the exiles back from Babylon and restored the observance of the Law. His spiritual lineage extends to the days of the restoration of God's people (Ezra 7:3).
H5838K.origine: The name Azaria (עֲזַרְיָה) comes from the Hebrew root עזר (azar), which means "to help" or "to assist." The full name thus means "Yahweh has helped" or "The Lord is my help." It is a common theophoric name in the priestly families of Israel, expressing the belief that God assists His people and servants.
H5838K.emploi: Azaria appears three times in the Segond, always in the genealogies of the Levitical priests. The three occurrences (1 Chronicles 6:10-11 and Ezra 7:3) place him in the continuous chain of the priesthood from the time of Solomon to the return from exile. He is presented as an essential link in this succession: he receives the priesthood from his father Johanan, exercises it in the Temple of Jerusalem, and passes it on to his son Amaria. This genealogical continuity underscores the permanence of the priestly function through the ages.
H5838K.portee: The name Azaria and its presence in the genealogy of Ezra remind the reader that God maintains His help and covenant with His people, even through generations and trials. This Levite illustrates how faithfulness in the service of the sanctuary is passed down from father to son, creating an unbroken chain of devotion to God that extends from Solomon's Temple to the post-exilic restoration.

sens: A priest of the tribe of Levi living during the time of the divided monarchy
Son of Hilkiah, brother of Gemariah, father of Seriah
H5838L.detail: Azaria is a priest of the Levitical lineage who lived during the period of the divided monarchy in Israel. He descends from the priestly line through his father Hilkiah and gives birth to Seriah, who himself fathered Jehozadak. He is a character in the genealogical tree of the priests: Chronicles mentions him as "Azaria, son of Hilkiah, son of Meshullam," who even becomes a prince of the house of God (1 Chronicles 9:11). Many generations later, long after the Babylonian exile, Ezra descends from him through this direct line: Ezra is the son of Seriah, who is the son of Azaria (Ezra 7:1).
H5838L.origine: The name Azaria means "Jehovah has helped" or "God helps." It is composed of the divine name and a root that evokes assistance. This name expresses the trust that the Jewish people placed in God's help for their lives and their descendants. Several characters bear this name throughout the centuries of the ancient Near East.
H5838L.emploi: This Azaria in particular is an ancestor of the high priests of Israel. He appears four times in the Bible: first in 1 Chronicles 6:13-14, where he is placed in the genealogy of the priests between Hilkiah and Seriah. He reappears in 1 Chronicles 9:11 as a prince of the house of God, which shows his high status among the Levites. Finally, in Ezra 7:1, he is mentioned as an ancestor of Ezra the scribe, who will live many centuries later. He is an essential link in the Jewish priestly continuity.

sens: Prophet who spoke to King Asa of Judah
Son of the prophet Obed
H5838M.detail:
1. Azaria is a prophet of Judah who lived during the time of the divided monarchy. The Spirit of God came upon him to bring a message to King Asa (2 Chronicles 15:1). This is the moment when Azaria delivers the divine word to the king to encourage him to turn to God and remove the idols from the land.

2. Azaria is the son of the prophet Obed. His father, also a prophet, marked the prophetic ministry in Judah during the reign of King Asa. Azaria continues the prophetic work of his family by serving God and guiding the king toward righteousness.
H5838M.origine: The name "Azaria" means "the Lord has helped." It comes from the Hebrew root that associates divine help and assistance. It is a name borne by many characters in the history of Israel, including Daniel's companion known as Abednego. The name expresses the belief that God intervenes to support and assist His people.
H5838M.emploi: Azaria appears twice in the Bible, both times in 2 Chronicles 15, during the ministry of King Asa. He is a prophet of Judah who serves during the time of the divided monarchy. He is presented as a bearer of the Spirit of God, capable of delivering the divine word to the king to call him to repentance and religious reform. The Bible provides few details about his life but emphasizes his crucial role with King Asa in bringing him back to God and encouraging religious reforms in Judah.
H5838M.portee: The testimony of Azaria reminds the reader that God speaks through His prophets to guide kings and nations toward justice and faithfulness. It is an example of how God raises up servants to call His people to repentance. His message to King Asa shows that religious reform begins when leaders listen to the voice of God and act courageously to remove idolatry.

sens: High priest of the kingdom of Judah under King Uzziah
Brave man who opposed the king when he attempted to burn incense in the temple
H5838N.detail:
1. Azaria is a high priest of Judah who lived during the time of King Uzziah (also called Ozias). His name means "The Lord has helped." In 2 Chronicles 26:17, he enters the temple with eighty other priests to confront the king.
2. Azaria shows courage by opposing King Uzziah, who wanted to burn incense himself in the temple — a function reserved for the priests according to God's law. After this confrontation, the king is struck with leprosy by the Lord, and Azaria along with the other priests drives him out of the temple (2 Chronicles 26:20). This act demonstrates that Azaria faithfully defends the rights of the priesthood against a king who transgresses divine law.
H5838N.origine: The name Azaria comes from Hebrew and means "The Lord has helped" or "The Lord has aided" (from "Lord" and the verb "to help"). It is a name borne by several characters in the Old Testament, notably by Daniel's companion whom the Babylonians called Abednego. Each Azaria has a different role in the history of Israel.
H5838N.emploi: The name Azaria in these two verses from 2 Chronicles 26 refers to the high priest (chief priest) who served under King Uzziah in Judah. The two biblical occurrences show Azaria at a crucial moment: first, he enters the temple with eighty priests to prevent the king from committing sacrilege (26:17); then, he observes the leprosy that strikes the king as divine punishment and confirms his exclusion from the temple (26:20). This character illustrates the role of the high priest as guardian of the holiness of worship and obedience to the Law.
H5838N.portee: This account reminds us that no one, not even a king, can transgress God's commandments regarding worship without consequence. Azaria and the priests who accompany him show the courage to defend divine truth even in the face of royal power. It is an example of faithfulness to God's principles rather than to the will of men.

sens: Leader of Ephraim who opposed the massacre of Judah's captives
H5838O.detail: 1. Azaria is a military leader of the kingdom of Israel (Northern kingdom) during the time of King Ahaz. Son of Jochanan, he intervenes when the army of Israel returns victorious from battle against Judah, bringing back prisoners. Along with his fellow leaders of Ephraim, Azaria courageously opposes those who want to massacre these captives, instead advocating for their release (2 Chronicles 28:12).
H5838O.origine: The name Azaria means "The Lord has helped" in Hebrew. It is a theophoric name, meaning it contains the divine name (Yah). This name was borne by many figures in the Old Testament, including King Uzziah and Daniel's friend known as Abednego. The same root expresses the help and aid that God provides to His people.
H5838O.emploi: This Azaria is mentioned only once in the Bible, in 2 Chronicles 28:12. He appears in a context of moral and political crisis: after a defeat of Judah against Israel, the Northern leaders consider enslaving the Judean prisoners. Azaria and his companions then intervene to halt this cruelty, reminding that God watches over all Israelites. It is a remarkable example of moral conscience in wartime.
H5838O.portee: This episode shows that at the heart of the division of the kingdom and fratricidal war, there remained good men in Northern Israel, capable of listening to God's voice and defending justice, even against their own comrades in arms. For the reader, Azaria embodies the possibility of repentance and mercy in the face of vengeance, and reminds us that God cares for the protection of prisoners and the defeated.

sens: High priest serving under King Hezekiah of Judah
H5838P.detail: 1. Azaria is a historical figure of the kingdom of Judah who held the position of high priest, that is, the head of worship at the temple. He lived during the time of King Hezekiah and played an important role in the religious administration of the kingdom. In 2 Chronicles 31:10, he is presented as the chief priest, the one who spoke on behalf of the priests and Levites to report on the material blessings received.
H5838P.origine: The name Azaria means "The Lord has helped" in Hebrew: it comes from two elements, one evoking help or aid, the other the divine name (Yah for Jehovah). It is a theophoric name, very common in Israel, which expresses trust in God's help. Several figures bore this name at different times in the history of Israel.
H5838P.emploi: Azaria appears twice in the account of 2 Chronicles regarding the reforms of King Hezekiah. He is first mentioned as the high priest who testifies to God's generosity toward the people through the abundance of offerings brought to the temple. He is then cited as the head of the house of God, overseeing the religious organization alongside Conania and Shimei. His role of great responsibility suggests that he was a respected and trusted figure in the religious governance of the time.

sens: Son of King Jehoshaphat of Judah
Brother of King Joram
H5838Q.detail:
1. Azaria is a prince of the kingdom of Judah, one of the sons of King Jehoshaphat. He lived during the time of the divided monarchy, when the kingdoms of Israel and Judah existed side by side. In 2 Chronicles 21:2, he is named among the brothers of Joram, the eldest son who will become king after Jehoshaphat.
2. Azaria is the brother of King Joram: both are sons of Jehoshaphat. His name appears in the list of royal siblings, alongside Jehiel, Zechariah, Michael, and Shephatiah. These princes of Judah formed the royal family of the southern kingdom.
H5838Q.origine: The name Azaria means "The Lord has helped" or "The Lord has rescued." It comes from the Hebrew root "azar" (to help, to rescue) and the divine name "Yah." This name expresses the Jewish people's trust in God's help, a conviction that the Lord intervenes to rescue His people. Several biblical characters bear this name, expressing this same faith in divine protection.
H5838Q.emploi: Azaria is a prince of Judah, son of King Jehoshaphat who reigned in the 9th century BC. He is mentioned only once in the Bible, in 2 Chronicles 21:2, where he is listed among the sons of Jehoshaphat. After the death of Jehoshaphat, his eldest son Joram became king and reigned over Judah. The Scripture briefly mentions this royal sibling to show the lineage of Jehoshaphat, one of the pious kings of Judah.

sens: Son of King Jehoshaphat of Judah, mentioned in royal genealogies
Name meaning 'The Lord has helped'
H5838R.detail:
1. Azaria is a son of King Jehoshaphat of Judah, living during the time of the divided monarchy. He is cited in 2 Chronicles 21:2 among the brothers of Joram, king of Judah, alongside several other royal children: Jehiel, Zechariah, Michael, and Shephatiah. This name appears in genealogical lists documenting the lineage of the kings of Judah.
2. The name Azaria carries the meaning "The Lord has helped" (from the Hebrew "azar": to help, to rescue, and the divine name "Yah"). This etymology reflects the common practice in Israel of incorporating affirmations of trust in divine help into proper names, revealing how royal families expressed their dependence on God through the very choice of names.
H5838R.origine: The name Azaria comes from the Hebrew root "azar" (עזר) which means "to help" or "to rescue," combined with "yah" (יה), a shortened form of the divine name "Yahweh" or "the Lord." This structure of the theophoric name (containing the name of God) was very common in the royal family of Judah. Several other biblical characters bear the same name, which testifies to its popularity particularly among the priestly and royal elites of Israel.
H5838R.emploi: This Azaria is known only by his mention in 2 Chronicles 21:2, where he appears among the sons of King Jehoshaphat. The genealogical text simply situates him in the sibling group of Joram, his brother who will become king. Unlike other characters named Azaria in the Bible (such as King Uzziah or Daniel's friend Abednego), this one has no other narrative or specific action reported in the Scriptures.

sens: Military leader of Judah during the time of Queen Athaliah
H5838S.detail: Azaria is a name borne by several important men in the history of Israel and Judah. One of the most well-known is the captain mentioned in 2 Chronicles 23:1, who allied with the priest Jehoiada to overthrow Queen Athaliah and restore the young king Joash to the throne. The name means "The Lord has helped" and reflects faith in divine assistance.
H5838S.origine: The name Azaria comes from the Hebrew root meaning "to help" or "to assist," with the divine name Yah (the Lord). It is a theophoric name, meaning it confesses that God helps His people. Several men in biblical history bear this name, including the king of Judah also called Uzziah, and Daniel's friend famously renamed Abednego.
H5838S.emploi: Azaria appears only once in the Segond translation in 2 Chronicles 23:1, where he is cited as one of the military leaders who conspired with the priest Jehoiada. This event marks a decisive turning point: after six years of tyrannical rule by Queen Athaliah, Azaria and his companions rose up to protect the child-king Joash and restore the legitimate worship of the God of Israel. His action illustrates political courage in the service of justice and faithfulness to God.
H5838S.portee: The account of Azaria and his companions reminds us that God raises up men of courage to defend His people and His worship, even in the darkest hours. This alliance between military leaders and the priest shows how faith and civil action can come together to restore divine order and justice.

sens: military leader of Judah during the time of Queen Athaliah
one of Daniel's friends famously renamed Abednego
son of King Amaziah and king of Judah himself
priest and officer in the royal administration
H5838T.detail: Azaria is a name borne by several important figures in the history of Israel. The most well-known is undoubtedly Azaria, friend of the prophet Daniel, whom Nebuchadnezzar renamed Abednego: he refused with his companions to defile themselves by eating the royal food contrary to the purity laws given by God, and he was one of the three young men thrown into the fiery furnace for refusing to bow down before the king's statue, before being saved by an angel. Another Azaria was the son of King Amaziah and reigned over Judah for fifty-two years, also known as Uzziah. Other Azarias held priestly or military positions: thus the one mentioned in 2 Chronicles 23:1 was a captain during the time of Queen Athaliah, among the officers who allied with the priest Jehoiada to restore King Joash. Several priests bore this name, some of whom were high priests.
H5838T.origine: The name Azaria means "The Lord has helped" or "The Lord rescues." It comes from the Hebrew root that expresses divine help and assistance. It is a theophoric name, meaning it is composed with the name of God, very common in the Old Testament to express trust in divine assistance.
H5838T.emploi: Azaria is a very common name in the Old Testament, borne by at least twenty-five different people from the time of the united monarchy to the return from exile. The source mentions Azaria son of Jerocham, a military officer during the time of Queen Athaliah (2 Chronicles 23:1), who was part of the military leaders who allied with the priest Jehoiada to overthrow Athaliah and restore the young king Joash. Several other Azarias were high priests or Levites, showing that this name was particularly borne by priestly families and government figures.
H5838T.portee: The name Azaria reminds the reader that God's help was central to the consciousness of the people of Judah. Through this name borne by military leaders, priests, and Daniel's companion, the Bible illustrates how God rescued His people through trustworthy men, particularly in critical moments: the restoration of worship under Joash, the faithfulness in Babylonian exile with the refusal to defile themselves. It is an invitation to recognize that divine help is manifested through faithful witnesses.

sens: Levite of the Kohathite tribe during the reign of King Hezekiah of Judah
Man whose name means "Jehovah has helped"
H5838U.detail:
1. Azaria is a Levite, meaning a member of the tribe of Levi charged with temple service. He appears in 2 Chronicles 29:12 at the time when King Hezekiah is reorganizing the temple worship after a period of neglect: Azaria, son of Jehallelel, rises with other Levites to carry out this important religious reform.

2. His name means "Jehovah has helped" or "God has assisted," which expresses the conviction that Adonai has granted him help. This name reflects the Israelites' trust in divine support, a trust that Azaria himself practiced by serving in the temple.
H5838U.origine: The name Azaria comes from Hebrew and is composed of two elements: "Azar" (to help, to assist) and "Yah" (Jehovah, the divine name). It is a statement of faith: "Jehovah helps." Several men bear this name in the Old Testament, particularly Levites and temple servants, indicating that this name was valued among those dedicated to the service of God.
H5838U.emploi: Azaria is a Levite mentioned only once in 2 Chronicles 29:12. He is among the Kohathite Levites who rose to assist King Hezekiah in the restoration of the temple and the religious reform. This event takes place around 715 BC, after the temple worship had been neglected during the previous reign. Azaria represents those faithful temple servants who responded to the king's call to renew the worship of God according to the Law.

sens: Levite of the family of the Kohathites, son of Jehallelel, living during the reign of King Hezekiah of Judah
H5838V.detail: Azaria is a Levite mentioned in the Chronicles during the religious reforms of King Hezekiah. He belongs to the family of the Kohathites, one of the three major families of Levites responsible for temple service. He is the son of Jehallelel and is among the Levites who rise to participate in the purification and restoration of the temple during the reign of Hezekiah (2 Chronicles 29:12). His appearance in this passage shows his role in one of the great movements of religious reform in Judah, when the king undertook to cleanse the temple after a period of neglect.
H5838V.origine: The name Azaria means "the Lord has helped" or "the Lord has assisted," composed of two Hebrew elements: "Lord" and "helped." It is a common name in the Old Testament, borne by several important figures, including King Uzziah of Judah (also called Uzziah) and Daniel's friend famously renamed Abed-Nego. The name expresses the trust that the people of God placed in divine help.
H5838V.emploi: Azaria appears only once in the Segond translation, in 2 Chronicles 29:12, where he is named among the Levites who rose to respond to King Hezekiah's call to consecrate the temple. He represents a generation of faithful Levites who participated in this great religious reform. His belonging to the family of the Kohathites connected him to the priestly service of the temple and the care of its sacred objects.

sens: Inhabitant of Jerusalem during the post-exilic reconstruction
Son of Maaseiah, a worker who participated in the restoration of the wall of Jerusalem
H5838W.detail:
1. Azaria is a man's name that appears in the account of the reconstruction of the wall of Jerusalem after the return from exile in Babylon, during the time of Nehemiah. He is a descendant of those who survived the captivity and participates in the restoration of their holy city.
2. The text of Nehemiah 3:23-24 presents him as a construction worker, son of Maaseiah and grandson of Hananiah. He works to repair a section of the wall near his own house, and then his house itself serves as a landmark to delineate the portion that is repaired after him by Binnui son of Henadad. His work extends to the corner and the angle of the wall.
H5838W.origine: The name Azaria means "the Lord has helped" in Hebrew, composed of "azar" (to help) and the reference to God (Yah). It is a common theophoric name in Israel, carrying the assurance that God helps the bearer. Several important figures in the history of Israel have borne this name, including King Uzziah (also called Azariah) and Daniel's friend named Abednego during the captivity.
H5838W.emploi: Azaria appears twice in the Bible in Nehemiah 3:23-24, in the context of the reconstruction project of the wall of Jerusalem led by Nehemiah after the return from exile. These two verses mention him in a list of builders, showing that the wall project was a collective effort where each family contributed to restoring its section. His name and that of his house serve as topographical landmarks to describe the progress of the work around the wall.
H5838W.portee: The mention of Azaria in this reconstruction account illustrates how God restores His people after the judgment of exile: each person, even the simple men of whom we know nothing else, participates in rebuilding what was destroyed. His work to rebuild the walls of Jerusalem symbolizes the renewal of the faith community and the faithfulness of the people to reinvest in their communal life and in the service of God.

sens: One of the leaders who returned from exile in Babylon with Zerubbabel
Priest and scribe who sealed the people's covenant with Nehemiah
One of the leaders who participated in the dedication of the wall of Jerusalem
H5838X.detail:
1. Azaria is one of the principal leaders who accompanied Zerubbabel during the return from exile in Babylon around 537 B.C. (Nehemiah 7:7). His name appears at the head of a list of leaders, indicating his importance in the restoration of the people of Israel.

2. He is also a priest and a scribe who was among those who solemnly sealed the renewed covenant with Nehemiah, the people's commitment to observe the Law of God after the return from exile (Nehemiah 10:2).

3. Finally, he participated in the festive ceremony of the dedication of the wall of Jerusalem, a major reconstruction led by Nehemiah (Nehemiah 12:33). These three mentions present him as a respected figure among the leaders of the return.
H5838X.origine: The name means "God has helped" or "Jehovah has rescued" in Hebrew. It is a theophoric name, meaning it contains the divine name. Several important figures in the history of Israel have borne this name, including King Uzziah (also called Oziah) and especially Abednego, the godly friend of Daniel who refused to defile himself by eating at the king's table.
H5838X.emploi: Azaria is mentioned three times in the book of Nehemiah, during the period of the return from exile and the restoration of Jerusalem in the 5th century B.C. These three occurrences always show him alongside the most prominent leaders and priests. He first appears among the twelve leaders who accompanied Zerubbabel (Nehemiah 7:7), then among those who engaged the renewed people in the covenant with God (Nehemiah 10:2), and finally among the chief musicians or priests who participated in the dedication of the wall (Nehemiah 12:33). His repeated appearance suggests that he was a stable and trustworthy figure during this crucial period of national and spiritual reconstruction.
H5838X.portee: Azaria embodies the faithfulness of the Israelite leaders upon returning from exile: it is through men like him that God restored His people and brought them back to obedience. His commitment to the renewal of the covenant shows that the reconstruction of Jerusalem was not merely a political or architectural matter, but primarily a return to God. For the Christian, he reminds us that all true spiritual restoration requires leaders who place God's covenant at the heart of their actions.

sens: Levite who explained the Law to the people upon their return from exile
H5838Y.detail: Azaria is a Levite mentioned only once in the Bible, during the return of the Jews from exile in Babylon. He appears in Nehemiah 8:7 among the group of Levites tasked with explaining the Law of Moses to the assembled people. His role was that of a teacher and religious instructor, helping the Israelites to understand and rediscover the Word of God after decades of distance from Jerusalem.
H5838Y.origine: The name Azaria means "Jehovah has helped" in Hebrew. It bears witness to divine support: "Azar" (to help) + "Yah" (God). It is a name borne by several figures in the Old Testament, including King Uzziah of Judah and Daniel's companion named Abednego, who all recalled the protective help of the Lord.
H5838Y.emploi: Azaria appears only once in Nehemiah 8:7. He is named among a specific group of Levites – Joshua, Bani, Sherebiah, Jamin, and others – who were given the responsibility of teaching. This event takes place during the public reading of the Law by Ezra, a crucial moment of spiritual restoration after the exile. His presence in this list indicates that he was a reliable man recognized for his ability to convey the Word of God, but the Bible gives us no further details about his life.
H5838Y.portee: Azaria embodies the humble yet essential role of the Levites as teachers of the Law. His example reminds us of the importance of passing on the knowledge of God to future generations and how God uses faithful servants, even those little known, to rebuild the spiritual life of His people. It is a lesson on discreet service in the ministry of the Word.

sens: young Jew from a noble family exiled to Babylon under Nebuchadnezzar
faithful friend of the prophet Daniel
the one who refused to defile himself by eating the king's food against the Law
the one who was thrown into the fiery furnace for not worshiping the idol and was miraculously saved
H5838Z.detail: Azaria is a young man from the tribe of Judah, from a royal family, deported to Babylon after the conquest of the kingdom by Nebuchadnezzar in 606 B.C. (Daniel 1:6). The Babylonian king renames him Abed-Nego, giving him a pagan name, as he does for his three companions Daniel, Hananiah, and Mishael. Azaria is best known for refusing, along with his three friends, to defile himself by eating at the king's table, as this food violated the dietary laws given by God to the Jews (Daniel 1:8 and following). This is an act of faithfulness to the God of Israel in a context of forced assimilation. Later, Azaria and his two companions are thrown into a fiery furnace because they refuse to bow down before the golden statue erected by the king; they miraculously emerge unharmed, saved by an angel of the Lord, which deeply impresses the king and leads him to praise the God of the Jews (Daniel 3).
H5838Z.origine: The name Azaria means "Jehovah has helped" or "The Eternal helps": it combines the divine name Yahweh with a verb meaning to help. It is a typical theophoric name in the Hebrew Old Testament, expressing trust in divine assistance. This name carried within it a profession of faith: even in exile, far from the Temple and the land, the young man recognizes that only the true God can save him. Several other characters in the Old Testament bore this name, including a king of Judah also called Uzziah.
H5838Z.emploi: Azaria appears four times in the Bible, all in the book of Daniel in chapter 1 (verses 6, 7, 11, and 19). He is presented as one of the four young men selected at the court of Nebuchadnezzar for their intelligence and distinction; the four friends are the pivot of the narrative of faithfulness in exile. Although the texts of chapters 2 and 3 of the book of Daniel recount his exploits (notably the refusal of idolatry and the miraculous deliverance from the furnace), in these passages Azaria is called by his Babylonian name, Abed-Nego. His story illustrates how a young believer can remain faithful to God even when forced into assimilation and subjected to the political and religious pressure of a foreign power.
H5838Z.portee: The story of Azaria and his three companions teaches the believer that faithfulness to God has a price, but also that God never abandons those who serve Him with courage. It shows that true power is not that of human empires, but that of the living God, who saves His servants in the most critical moments. For the Christian faced with cultural or social pressures that push him to deny his faith, Azaria offers a model of perseverance and trust: he did not yield to the lies of the world, even at the risk of death.

sens: Levite, son of Elkanah, living during the time of the divided monarchy in Israel
H5838w.detail: Azaria is a man from the tribe of Levi mentioned in the genealogy of the descendants of Korah. He appears in the genealogical list of 1 Chronicles 6:36 as the son of Elkanah and the father of Ahitub, ancestors of the priestly lineage. This name designates a member of the class of Levites, responsible for worship and service in the temple in Jerusalem. Although few details are given about his personal life, his place in this genealogy shows his importance in the transmission of the religious function from one generation to the next during the period of the divided monarchy, when the kingdoms of Israel and Judah existed separately.
H5838w.origine: The name Azaria means "God has helped" or "Jehovah has helped" in Hebrew. It is formed from two elements: "azar" (to help, to assist) and "Yah" (abbreviation of the divine name Jehovah). It is a common theophoric name in Israel, expressing trust in divine assistance. Several biblical characters bear this name, reflecting its popularity among the chosen people.
H5838w.emploi: This Azaria is a Levite from the tribe of Korah, mentioned only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 6:36. He is part of the genealogy of the Levites descended from Korah, an important family in temple service. His specific role in worship is not detailed, but his position in this genealogical line indicates that he likely participated in the liturgical service of the temple during the divided monarchy. The genealogical context shows that the Levites maintained records of their descendants to preserve the order of worship and the purity of the priestly line.
H5838w.portee: This character reminds us that the Church of the Old Testament relied on a faithful transmission from generation to generation, with men whose very names proclaimed God's faithfulness ("God has helped"). These seemingly dry genealogies show us that each had a place in God's plan and that the worship of the Lord rested on the commitment of multitudes of men, many of whom remain unknown to us.

sens: King of Judah, son of Amaziah, who reigned fifty-two years
One of Daniel's three friends, renamed Abednego by Nebuchadnezzar
Several other important characters in the history of Israel: priest, prophet, royal officer, chief Levite
H5838x.detail:
1. Azaria is first the name of the king of Judah established by the people after the death of his father Amaziah, when he was only sixteen years old (2 Kings 14:21). He reigned for a long time — during the thirty-ninth year of his reign, Menahem became king of Israel (2 Kings 15:17). He is also called Uzziah in the New Testament (Matthew 1:8-9), which refers to the same person.
2. Azaria is also the name of the young man from Judah whom the king of Babylon captured and renamed Abednego. Along with Daniel, Hananiah, and Mishael (also renamed), he refused to eat food sacrificed to Babylonian idols and was thrown into the fiery furnace with his companions, from which God miraculously saved them.
3. The Bible also mentions other Azarias: priests of the temple, royal officers during the reign of Solomon, a prophet during the days of King Asa, Levites who assisted Ezra and Nehemiah, and other leaders and servants of God at various times in Israel's history.
H5838x.origine: The name Azaria means "Yahweh has helped" or "God has helped." It comes from two parts: "azar," which means "to help" or "to assist," and "Yah," which is the name of God. It was a common name among the Hebrews, borne by many important figures in the temple and government. Several people in the Old Testament bear this name, reflecting the trust that families placed in divine assistance.
H5838x.emploi: Azaria in the Bible primarily refers to a king of Judah from the 8th century B.C. The six main references in the books of Kings show that this king reigned for a long time and that his reign served as a chronological reference point for dating the kings of Israel — for example, it is said, "the thirty-eighth year of Azaria" (2 Kings 15:8) or "the thirty-ninth year of Azaria" (2 Kings 15:17). Azaria is also one of Daniel's three friends in exile in Babylon, a faithful young man who refused to compromise with the king's religion and was divinely saved. Finally, the name Azaria continually reappears to designate various personalities in the Israelite clergy and government: priests, prophets, Levites, and royal officers. It was an honorable title, borne by men of trust of God and kings.
H5838x.portee: For the reader, King Azaria illustrates the longevity and stability of reign when one remains in the fear of God. But it is Azaria, Daniel's friend, who speaks the loudest: his courage in refusing religious compromise and his miraculous deliverance from the fire show that faithfulness to God matters more than the threats of earthly power. His example, along with that of Daniel, inspires the Christian to remain steadfast in his faith, even in exile or in the face of hostility.

sens: Son of Hoshaiah, a Judean officer during the time of Jeremiah
Arrogant leader who opposes the prophet Jeremiah
H5838y.detail:
1. Azaria is a historical figure from the kingdom of Judah, son of Hoshaiah. He appears only once in the Bible, in Jeremiah 43:2, where he is presented as a powerful man at the end of the Kingdom of Judah's era.
2. Azaria is one of those proud men who, along with Johanan son of Kareah and others, refuse to listen to the word of the Lord delivered by Jeremiah. They accuse the prophet of lying and contradict his divine message (Jeremiah 43:2). His attitude represents the human refusal to submit to God, even when He speaks through His prophets.
H5838y.origine: The name Azaria means "the Lord has helped" in Hebrew. It comes from the combination of two elements: "azar" (to help, to assist) and "Yah" (abbreviation of the divine name). It is a common theophoric name in Israel, borne by many important biblical figures — kings, priests, prophets, and officers. The same individual is also called Jaazaniah, a nickname or another form of the same name, attested in 2 Kings 25:23.
H5838y.emploi: Azaria appears only once in the text of the Bible in the modern French translation: in Jeremiah 43:2. He is a Judean officer from the 6th century B.C., at the time when the survivors of the fall of Jerusalem hesitate about their future. After the death of the governor Gedaliah, Azaria and his companions refuse to believe that God is calling them to remain in the Promised Land. They accuse Jeremiah of being a liar and prepare to flee to Egypt, thus disobeying the prophetic word. The context shows a man of rank, influential among the survivors, but rebellious to the will of God.
H5838y.portee: The character of Azaria illustrates the danger of pride and the refusal to believe the word of God, even when it comes through a recognized prophet. His opposition to Jeremiah shows how the human heart can harden and reject the salvation offered by God, preferring a human plan (fleeing to Egypt) over the divine plan. It serves as a warning for every believer about the importance of humility and obedience to God.

sens: king of Judah during the divided monarchy
H5838z.detail: Azaria was a king of Judah, son of King Joram and Queen Athaliah. He reigned during the period when the kingdom was divided between Judah in the south and Israel in the north. He is known by several names: Azaria, Ahaziah, and also Uzziah. The only usage retained in the Segond refers to him as "Azaria, son of Joram, king of Judah," who went down to Jezreel to see Joram, king of Israel, who was ill (2 Chronicles 22:6).
H5838z.origine: The name Azaria means in Hebrew "Jehovah has helped" (from "azar" which means "to help"). It is a theophoric name, meaning it invokes the name of God to express trust in His help. It was a common name among the Hebrews for kings and priests.
H5838z.emploi: Azaria appears only once in the Segond translation in 2 Chronicles 22:6, where he is referred to as king of Judah and son of King Joram. The Bible speaks of this character under other names as well: Ahaziah (the most common name) and Uzziah. These different names refer to the same man, the young king of Judah who visited his uncle Joram, king of Israel, in Jezreel.

sens: Young Jew from the tribe of Judah deported to Babylon during the exile
Companion and friend of Daniel during captivity
The one whom Nebuchadnezzar renamed Abednego
H5839.detail:
1. Azaria is a young Jewish man of noble lineage, deported to Babylon during the Babylonian exile. His name means "Jehovah has helped," expressing his people's hope in divine protection even far from Jerusalem. He appears in Daniel 2:17 as one of Daniel's three faithful companions.
2. Along with Daniel, Hananiah, and Mishael, Azaria refused to defile himself by eating the royal food, in accordance with the dietary laws given by God to the Jews. This faithfulness to God's law, even in exile and under foreign domination, characterizes Azaria's heart.
3. King Nebuchadnezzar imposed the name Abednego on him, thus attempting to erase his Jewish identity and his relationship with God. But this name change did not alter his heart: he refused to bow down before the golden statue and was thrown into the fiery furnace, from which he was miraculously saved by the angel of the Lord.
H5839.origine: The name Azaria comes from Hebrew and literally means "Jah has helped" or "Jehovah has helped," composed of the divine name and the verb "to help." It is a typically Jewish theophoric name, expressing trust in divine assistance. Nebuchadnezzar replaced this name with Abednego (in Aramaic Abed-Nego), meaning "servant of Nebo" (the Babylonian god), an act of political and spiritual domination.
H5839.emploi: Azaria is mentioned only once by his Hebrew/Jewish name in the Bible, in Daniel 2:17, where he is presented as one of Daniel's three companions. The biblical narrative knows him mainly by the Aramaic name Abednego, used from Daniel 2:49 and throughout chapters 2 and 3, notably during the dramatic episode of the fiery furnace (Daniel 3). The use of the double name highlights the conflict between Jewish spiritual identity (Azaria) and the assimilation imposed by Babylonian power (Abednego). Azaria represents one who, despite exile and the pressure of a pagan context, maintains his faithfulness to God and His law.
