H5839.portee: The story of Azaria challenges Christians on faithfulness to God in a foreign land and under pressure. Like this young exile, believers may find themselves in contexts that tempt them to renounce their convictions: Azaria shows that remaining faithful to God's principles, even when socially or politically costly, leads to divine protection and glory. His miraculous rescue from the furnace speaks of God's power to preserve those who fear Him and trust Him, beyond any human threat.

sens: Son of Neariah, descendant of Zerubbabel in the royal lineage of Judah
H5840G.detail: Azrikam is a man from the people of Judah living during the time of the Divided Monarchy. He appears in the genealogy of 1 Chronicles 3:23 as the son of Neariah and brother of Elioenai and Hezekiah. His name means "help against the enemy" in Hebrew. He is part of the lineage of Zerubbabel, who was the leader of the return from exile and represented the continuation of the royal dynasty of Judah after the destruction of the Temple.
H5840G.origine: The name Azrikam comes from Hebrew and literally means "help against the enemy" (composed of a word meaning "help" and a word meaning "enemy"). This type of compound name was common in Israel and expressed trust in divine protection.
H5840G.emploi: Azrikam appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 3:23, where he is mentioned in the genealogy of the descendants of David after the return from exile. He is presented as one of the three sons of Neariah, alongside Elioenai and Hezekiah. This genealogical mention shows the importance of maintaining family lineage records in Judah after the exile, even for the distant descendants of the royal house.

sens: son of Azel, from the tribe of Benjamin, living during the time of the divided monarchy
H5840H.detail: Azrikam is a proper name designating a man from the tribe of Benjamin mentioned in the royal genealogies. He is presented as one of the six sons of Azel, himself a descendant of Saul. His name appears in two parallel passages in Chronicles that list the descendants of Saul and the genealogy of Benjamin.
H5840H.origine: The name Azrikam means "help against the enemy" or "help in the face of the adversary," formed from the Hebrew "azr" (help) and "qam" (to rise, to stand against). It is a Hebrew theophoric name that expresses trust in God as protector and helper.
H5840H.emploi: Azrikam appears twice in the biblical text, in 1 Chronicles 8:38 and 9:44, in parallel genealogical passages that list the descendants of Saul. These passages are part of the genealogical records of the people of Israel after the return from exile, intended to establish the lines of descent and the dynastic legitimacy of the tribe of Benjamin and the royal house of Judah.

sens: Levite from the time of the Exile and return, ancestor of Schemaeja
H5840I.detail: 1. Azrikam is a Levite mentioned in the lists of priests and temple servants who returned from Babylonian captivity. He is the ancestor of Schemaeja and belongs to the family of the sons of Merari, one of the three major Levitical families (1 Chronicles 9:14; Nehemiah 11:15).
H5840I.origine: The name Azrikam means "help against the enemy" or "mighty aid." It is composed of two Hebrew elements: help or aid, and the notion of strength or protection. This name reflects trust in divine assistance, typical of Levitical names from the time of the return from exile.
H5840I.emploi: Azrikam appears in two parallel or close passages in the Book of Chronicles and Nehemiah, both listing the Levites who returned after the Babylonian captivity. Each time, he is presented as the father of Schemaeja and the son of Hashabia, a descendant of Merari. These mentions reflect the genealogical importance of Levitical families for the reorganization of worship at the temple after the Exile.

sens: Figure from the Divided Kingdom, chief of the royal house of King Ahaz of Judah
H5840J.detail: Azrikam was the governor of the palace of King Ahaz of Judah. He was killed during an invasion by Ephraim, struck down by the warrior Zicri (2 Chronicles 28:7). His name literally means "help against the enemy," but the irony of the text suggests that despite his prestigious title as chief of the royal house, he was unable to defend himself against the northern enemies.
H5840J.origine: The Hebrew name עַזְרִיקָם is composed of two elements: עָזַר (azer, "to help, support") and קָם (qam, "to rise, stand"). It evokes the image of help that stands up to fight. It was a name borne by several important figures in the genealogy of Judah and in royal administration.
H5840J.emploi: Azrikam appears only once in the Bible, in 2 Chronicles 28:7, where he is presented as "chief of the royal house" (sar habbayit, governor of the palace) during the reign of Ahaz. He is mentioned among the victims of the battle fought between Judah and Northern Israel, alongside the son of King Maaséja and the prince Elkana. This dramatic context places Azrikam among the prominent figures of his time, even though his name does not appear elsewhere.

sens: Inhabitant of the city of Gaza
Belonging to Gaza or its inhabitants
H5841.detail:
1. A Gazite is an inhabitant of the city of Gaza, one of the five major cities of the Philistines on the coast of Canaan. In Joshua 13:3, Gaza is mentioned as one of the Philistine strongholds that the Israelites must conquer; in Judges 16:2, the people of Gaza seek to capture Samson by lying in wait at the city gate.

2. The adjective refers to anything concerning Gaza or its inhabitants: the prince of the Gazites, the ambushes of the Gazites, their way of life and warfare.
H5841.origine: The word comes from the name of the city of Gaza (עַזָּה, azzah), whose original probable meaning is "the strong" or "the fortified" — Gaza was indeed an important fortified city of the Philistines. The suffix אִי (i) adds the idea of belonging to a place, similar to "Egyptian" coming from Egypt. Gaza already appears in ancient Egyptian texts as a major strategic point.
H5841.emploi: This term appears only twice in the Bible (Joshua 13:3 and Judges 16:2), designating the inhabitants or authorities of Gaza. In Joshua 13:3, it is in the political and military context: Gaza is one of the five Philistine principalities that God promises to Israel, but which it has not conquered. In Judges 16:2, the Gazites embody the threat: they attempt to capture Samson at night at the gate of their city. In both passages, the Gazites represent the Canaanite and Philistine enemies resisting Israel.
H5841.portee: Understanding this term helps to see that Gaza is not a biblical abstraction, but a concrete Philistine city with its inhabitants, leaders, and army. It reminds us that God's promises to Israel concerned the possession of real territories, occupied by real peoples, and that biblical history is rooted in the geography and politics of the ancient Levant.

sens: Pointed iron tool, hardened with diamond, for engraving on stone or metal
Cut reed or other instrument for writing in ink on a scroll of papyrus or parchment
Figuratively: the ability to write, the art of writing
What engraves or marks deeply, like sin engraved in the heart
H5842.detail:
1. The iron burin with a diamond tip is the tool of the engraver: it must be struck hard to carve lasting lines in stone or metal. Job wishes that his words be thus engraved "in the rock" (Job 19:24), as an indestructible testimony.
2. The pen is the cut reed that the scribe dips in ink to trace characters on the unrolled papyrus or parchment. It is the instrument of the copyist and secretary, much lighter and quicker than the burin.
3. By extension, the word designates the writer's talent itself: "my tongue be like the pen of a skilled writer" (Psalms 45:2) means that the speaker will speak with the elegance and precision of a literate person.
4. The image of the burin that engraves deeply in stone serves to describe how sin is inscribed in the human heart, impossible to erase (Jeremiah 17:1) — it is a mark as lasting as the engraving on the altar.
H5842.origine: The Hebrew word עֵט comes from a root that evokes the action of pointing, pricking. It is an ancient term for any pointed instrument used to mark or write. In the daily life of the ancient Near East, it was a crucial tool: the burin for monuments and engraved contracts, the pen for administration and records. Both meanings coexist in the same word because they share the idea of leaving a trace.
H5842.emploi: The word appears four times in the Hebrew Bible, always with solemnity. In Job 19:24, it refers to the burin that would engrave Job's words for eternity — an image of the desire for immortality. Psalms 45:2 uses "pen" to describe royal eloquence. Jeremiah 8:8 denounces "the lying pen of the scribes" who falsify the Law — here, it is the tool of political deceit. Jeremiah 17:1 returns to the burin, but in a figurative sense: the sin of Judah is engraved in the heart like an indestructible inscription. The biblical usage often contrasts the authentic (the eternal engraving, the pen of the skilled writer) with the deceitful (the pen of false scribes).
H5842.portee: This word reminds us that words — whether written or spoken — leave lasting marks. They engrave something in us and around us. The Bible uses it to show the importance of truth (the Word of God, Job's innocence) in the face of the lies of corrupt scribes. It also emphasizes that sin is inscribed deeply in the heart like an engraving — but this invites reflection on what we allow to be engraved in us and what we communicate to others through our words.

sens: Practical wisdom, the ability to judge well and act with discernment
Thoughtful advice, counsel given with common sense
Discretion and restraint in speech and action
H5843.detail:
1. Prudence is that practical wisdom which allows one to judge a situation well and make the right decision. In Daniel 2:14, Daniel addresses Arioch "in a prudent manner": he does not react in panic to the threat of death, but with calm and common sense, which enables him to negotiate and save his life.
2. This word also refers to wise counsel, advice given with reflection and judgment. Prudence is the quality of one who weighs their words and actions before acting.
3. It also evokes discretion and restraint: prudence leads one to weigh their words, not to speak lightly, and to measure the impact of what is said.
H5843.origine: The Hebrew word עֵטָא (éta) expresses the idea of practical wisdom and good decision-making. It is rare in the Hebrew Bible. It belongs to the semantic field of terms denoting wisdom and good judgment, such as חָכְמָה (hokhma, "wisdom"). Its usage reflects the importance, in biblical thought and particularly in the book of Daniel, of the ability to discern truth from falsehood and to act intelligently in the face of challenges.
H5843.emploi: This word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Daniel 2:14. Daniel perfectly illustrates it by adopting a prudent and thoughtful attitude towards Arioch, who came to execute him. Instead of succumbing to panic, Daniel speaks "in a prudent and sensible manner," which allows him to request a delay from the king and thus resolve the problem. This usage shows that prudence is not a weakness, but a strength: it allows one to avoid the worst and find a solution.
H5843.portee: For the Christian reader, Daniel's prudence is a model. It shows how to face crises, injustices, or unreasonable orders without panicking, but by keeping one's composure and discernment. It is an invitation to cultivate practical wisdom in trials, confident that God helps those who think before acting.

sens: To wrap one's body in a garment or fabric
To drape oneself in something
To clothe someone or something with an outer layer
To be figuratively enveloped (shame, disgrace, dignity)
H5844A.detail:
1. To wrap one's body in a garment or fabric: the word describes the action of draping oneself in clothing, wrapping up for protection or coverage. In Leviticus 13:45, the leper must "cover his beard," meaning to veil or wrap it as a sign of mourning and ritual impurity.
2. To drape oneself in something: this refers to enveloping oneself as one wraps in a coat. In Jeremiah 43:12, the prophet mentions Nebuchadnezzar who "wraps himself in the land of Egypt like a shepherd wraps himself in his garment": the image is of someone draping themselves, adorning themselves with something like a robe.
3. To clothe someone or something with an outer layer: the word can also mean to dress, to cover with a veil or protection. In Isaiah 59:17, the text states that God "clothes Himself with righteousness as with a breastplate."
4. To be enveloped in a figurative sense: the word is used to mean being covered by a spiritual or moral reality, particularly shame. In Psalms 71:13, it is wished that those who threaten the righteous be "covered with shame and disgrace," as if shame were a garment with which they would be draped.
H5844A.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that evokes the idea of folding, wrapping, enveloping. It describes a movement of covering: one takes something (a strip of fabric, a garment) and drapes oneself or drapes another. The image is concrete: that of someone who wraps themselves or is wrapped. It extends metaphorically to express being covered by an invisible reality (shame, glory, peace).
H5844A.emploi: This verb appears about 14 times in the Hebrew Bible, primarily in the Psalms and the prophetic books. Its concrete usage predominates: covering the beard as a sign of mourning (Leviticus 13:45), wrapping oneself in a garment (Jeremiah 43:12). But the Bible mostly uses it in a figurative sense: being covered with shame (Psalms 71:13, 89:46), being clothed with a quality or divine power (Isaiah 59:17, where God is clothed with righteousness and salvation). The context defines the meaning: it can refer to protection, adornment, or a mark of humiliation or mourning.
H5844A.portee: This word reminds us that the Bible expresses spiritual realities through physical images: one is "covered" with shame or glory just as one is with a garment. This shows that our moral and spiritual states are visible, concrete, and envelop us entirely. Meditating on this vocabulary helps us understand that faith is not invisible: it is clothed in fruits, it is shown in actions, and it can completely drape us.

sens: To seize and wrap something around oneself or someone else
To envelop, to carry away in a swirling motion (notably a thrown projectile)
H5844B.detail:
1. The verb primarily means to seize something to wrap it around oneself: it is the action of draping, enveloping oneself in a garment or fabric. The image is one of taking and wrapping.
2. In Isaiah 22:17, the prophet uses this word to describe how the Lord will throw someone "like a ball" — that is, by enveloping or wrapping them in the motion of the throw, as one rolls and throws a ball. The word thus also evokes the action of swirling and being carried away by a force.
H5844B.origine: The Hebrew root עָטָה (ʿatah) expresses the idea of taking and turning around, rolling into a ball. It describes the concrete gesture of seizing something to envelop or roll it. It is a verb that paints an action of the body: to take, to wrap, and by extension, to be seized and carried away.
H5844B.emploi: The verb appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Isaiah 22:17. There it describes how the Lord will throw a man like a ball — that is, by enveloping or seizing him in the motion of projection. This context of divine judgment gives the word a connotation of power and irresistible seizing. The translation "ball" captures the meaning well: it is a sphere that one rolls and throws.
H5844B.portee: This word reminds us of God's power in the face of our resistances. Enveloped, seized, carried away "like a ball" — this is the biblical image of one who cannot escape divine will. For the believer, it speaks both of the fear of God and the certainty that nothing can thwart His plan.

sens: The lateral part of the body, between the rib and the hip
The fleshy part of the belly or torso
A part of the body mass, particularly as a measure of strength or well-being
H5845.detail:
1. The flank refers to the lateral area of the human body, located between the ribs and the hip. In Job 21:24, the expression "the flanks loaded with fat" paints the image of a rich and well-fed man, whose body manifests opulence and material prosperity.

2. More broadly, the word can evoke the belly or torso as a whole, the fleshy part of the body that accumulates reserves and life. It is a concrete way of speaking about bodily substance.

3. By extension, the flanks represent the vital force or the state of health of the body: "the flanks loaded with fat" and "the marrow of the bones filled with sap" go hand in hand to depict a man in the fullness of his physical vigor.
H5845.origine: The Hebrew word עֲטִין (atin) comes from a root expressing the idea of what is dense, filled, or robust. It belongs to the family of terms designating the fleshy and substantial parts of the body. The original image is that of the visible and tangible body mass, the side of the body where energy and physical strength accumulate.
H5845.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible, in Job 21:24. It is found in a passage where Job describes the wicked man who prospers despite his impiety: his flanks are "loaded with fat," a symbol of wealth and material well-being. The context does not serve to express a spiritual notion, but rather to paint the image of carnal abundance and overflowing physical health.
H5845.portee: This word reminds us that the Bible views the body realistically: it sees in it the visible sign of life and material ease. However, the context of Job invites caution: the physical prosperity of the wicked is not true wealth. It urges us to distinguish between the satisfaction of bodily needs and the satisfaction of the soul.

sens: sudden expulsion of air through the nose and mouth
involuntary physiological phenomenon
sign of life or living presence
H5846.detail: 1. Sneezing is the sudden and noisy expulsion of air through the nose and mouth — an involuntary physical reaction of the body, often caused by irritation of the respiratory tract. In Job 41:9, this word describes the sneezes of Leviathan, a fabulous and fearsome creature: "His sneezes make light shine." 2. Figuratively, sneezing becomes a manifestation of the raw power and intense life of an extraordinary creature. The sneezes of Leviathan are so violent and bright that they emit light, symbolizing the superhuman strength and chaotic energy of this monstrous beast. 3. More broadly, the word evokes any phenomenon that proves a creature lives and acts — a tangible sign of presence and vitality, even when describing a mythological or unreal beast.
H5846.origine: The Hebrew word עֲטִישָׁה comes from a root expressing the idea of a sudden and involuntary expulsion. The term is formed to specifically designate this physiological phenomenon characteristic of living beings. It is a rare word in biblical Hebrew, attested only once, which underscores its concrete and observational nature: it is used only to describe a real physical act.
H5846.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Job 41:9. It is in the discourse where God describes Leviathan, a terrifying and almost mythological creature presented as one of the wonders of divine creation. By using this ordinary and physiological term ("sneezes") to describe a fabulous beast, the Bible blends the image of the monstrous with that of the living: Leviathan is not a fantasy, but a real creature, even if superhumanly powerful. The effect is both ironic and impressive — the ordinary sneeze becomes grandiose.
H5846.portee: This passage reminds us that God knows and masters creatures that we find terrifying or incomprehensible. The use of such an ordinary and living detail as sneezing to describe Leviathan helps us imagine its tangible reality and incomparable strength. It invites the reader to recognize the immensity and wisdom of the Creator who has formed even the most fearsome creatures.

sens: Nocturnal flying animal with skin wings
Impure creature according to the law of Moses
Image of refuge in darkness and rejection
H5847.detail:
1. The bat is a flying mammal that moves in the night. In Israel, this animal was well known and its comings and goings were observable. Leviticus 11:19 and Deuteronomy 14:18 classify it among the impure animals that are forbidden to eat.
2. In the two identical legal passages of Leviticus and Deuteronomy, the bat appears alongside the heron and the hoopoe in the list of creatures that the Israelites must not consume. It embodies a category of beings that the law judges ritually impure, probably due to its nocturnal nature or hidden habits.
3. In Isaiah 2:20, men throw their gold and silver idols "to the rats and the bats": the image evokes rejection in darkness and abandonment, as if the abandoned idols return to the creatures of the night. It is a figure of degradation and contempt.
H5847.origine: The Hebrew word עֲטַלֵּף (ataleph) specifically designates the bat. Its etymology is uncertain, but the word is ancient and consistently attested in biblical Hebrew. The name likely evokes a compound describing the animal by its distinctive traits, particularly its nocturnal activity or unique flying ability.
H5847.emploi: The word appears only three times in the Bible, always in defined contexts. Two occurrences are found in the law of the pure and the impure (Leviticus 11 and Deuteronomy 14, parallel and close texts) where it is classified among the animals that should not be eaten. A third occurrence, in Isaiah 2:20, uses it symbolically to express the rejection and ruin of idols. These three uses show that the bat, known as an animal unsuitable for consumption, is also charged with a metaphorical value of degradation and darkness.
H5847.portee: For the reader, the mention of the bat reminds us that divine law distinguished the pure from the impure and that this distinction affected the daily life of the people. In Isaiah, the image of the idol thrown to the bats suggests that false gods, abandoned and despised, return to nothingness and darkness. It is a motif of consolation: the powers that one fears are nothing before the living God.

sens: To turn aside, to turn away to escape notice
To escape sight, to remain invisible
H5848A.detail:
1. To hide means to turn aside, to turn away in order to escape the gaze of another person. The image is that of someone who turns away, who evades: one thinks of someone hiding behind something or turning away so as not to be seen. In Job 23:9, Job speaks of God who "hides" in the north or the south, meaning that God escapes his perception, his anxious gaze, despite all his efforts to seek Him.
2. More broadly, to hide means to remain invisible or out of reach. It is to be present but imperceptible, absent from the sight or knowledge of the one who seeks. In the text of Job, this expresses the anguish of the righteous who cannot find God, who is as if veiled, hidden from his eyes.
H5848A.origine: The Hebrew verb עָטַף (ataph) comes from a root that evokes the idea of turning, turning away, veiling, or wrapping. The basic image is that of rotation, of diversion: one turns to avoid being seen. This verb belongs to a family of words related to the notion of covering and concealment, such as to envelop or to cover.
H5848A.emploi: This verb appears only once in the Bible, in Job 23:9. Job, in his distress, seeks God but finds Him nowhere: "Is He occupied in the north, I cannot see Him; Is He hiding in the south, I cannot discover Him." The context is that of a desperate quest for the divine presence. Job uses this verb to express that God seems to evade him, turning away from him, becoming invisible and inaccessible. It is a cry of suffering in the face of God's apparent silence.
H5848A.portee: This word speaks to us of the painful experience of God's silence. When we pray and God seems distant or hidden, Job tells us that we are not alone in this trial. However, the verb also reminds us that God is never truly absent: He may seem hidden, but His presence remains real, even when our faith is tested and our eyes do not see Him.

sens: To wrap oneself in something, to cover completely
To wear or display a quality, a feeling as one wears a garment
H5848B.detail:
1. The word primarily denotes the action of wrapping oneself, covering oneself completely with a material or garment. It is a very concrete image: just as one puts on a garment that covers the body, one "clothes" oneself with something that surrounds you. In Psalms 65:14, the valleys "are clothed with wheat" meaning they are covered, filled with golden harvests that completely adorn them.
2. By extension, this verb applies to wearing or displaying a quality, a feeling, an attitude as if it were a garment. It is no longer physical covering, but the act of presenting oneself clothed in a certain nature. In Psalms 73:6, pride and violence are what the wicked "clothe themselves with" — they visibly wear them, like an ornament.
H5848B.origine: The Hebrew verb עָטַף comes from a root that expresses the idea of wrapping, covering, or overlaying. The basic image is that of draping, veiling, that which surrounds and conceals. The same family includes nouns related to clothing and that which covers. This verb is used to speak of what physically envelops a body or, figuratively, an abstract reality.
H5848B.emploi: This verb appears twice in the Old Testament, both in Psalms. In Psalms 65:14, it depicts the valleys covered with an abundance of harvest: they "are clothed" with wheat, as if the harvest were a garment adorning them. In Psalms 73:6, it describes the adornment of the wicked — the pride and violence they "clothe themselves with" — showing how they publicly display these evil traits. In both cases, the word emphasizes the idea of total and visible covering: what envelops is apparent, ostensible.
H5848B.portee: This verb reminds us that our qualities and attitudes are visible, that we "clothe" ourselves as in a garment. For the believer, this invites reflection on what he chooses to wear: does he wrap himself in justice, peace, virtue, or does he allow himself to be clothed by pride and evil? The image of clothing also emphasizes that God sees what covers us, what we display.

sens: To be physically weak or exhausted
To lose strength, to wither
To be morally discouraged, to have a heavy spirit
To be on the verge of fainting or passing out
H5848C.detail:
1. To be physically weak or exhausted: the word primarily denotes a bodily weakness, a lack of vigor. The "sickly" sheep of Genesis 30:42 are thin and without strength, unable to thrive, unlike the strong sheep.
2. To lose strength, to wither: this is the gradual weakening of the body or soul. In Lamentations 2:11, the children in "fainting" in the streets are exhausted and dying of hunger.
3. To be morally discouraged, to have a heavy spirit: the word applies to the inner state. The psalmist says in Psalms 77:4: "My spirit is downcast," expressing a state of melancholy or desolation in the face of suffering.
4. To be on the verge of fainting or passing out: this is extreme weakness where one loses consciousness. In Psalms 107:5, the "fainting" souls from hunger and thirst are at the end of their strength.
H5848C.origine: The Hebrew root עטף (ataf) expresses the idea of covering or wrapping, from which the image of weakening derives: the vital energy "covers" or fades away. The word belongs to the family of verbs that describe the loss or obscuring of strength. This root produces only a limited number of derivatives in biblical Hebrew.
H5848C.emploi: The verb appears twelve times in the Old Testament, mainly in the Psalms (Psalms 61, 77, 102, 107, 142, 143) and in Lamentations (2:11, 2:12, 2:19). It describes both physical exhaustion — the sickly sheep (Genesis 30:42) or the children dying of hunger (Lamentations 2:19) — and the emotional distress of the psalmist in the face of trials. Isaiah 57:16 uses it to express the feeling of weakness of the human spirit. It is a word of lamentation and distress.
H5848C.portee: This word helps the reader name the feeling of being drained, crushed by circumstances — physically, emotionally, or spiritually. It legitimizes the laments of those who suffer and does not hide their fragility. For the Christian, it reminds us that weakness is a biblical reality that God knows and hears, inviting us to acknowledge our need for His strength.

sens: To close around something or someone by forming a barrier or enclosure
To invest someone, to surround them to prevent escape
To cover, protect by encompassing like a benevolent armor
H5849A.detail:
1. The literal meaning is to form a circle around a person or thing to close or encircle it: it is the action of arranging in a circle to control or capture. In 1 Samuel 23:26, Saul and his men "surrounded" David and his companions to stop and seize them — this is a hostile and strategic encirclement.
2. From there, the verb means to invest or surround someone to control or block them. The image is that of a vise: one gradually closes the grip around the prey.
3. In a benevolent and metaphorical context, to surround means to cover, protect, or fill by completely encompassing. In Psalms 5:13, the Lord "surrounds" the righteous with His grace like a shield — not to capture him, but to keep and defend him from all sides.
H5849A.origine: The verb comes from a simple Hebrew root that paints the image of a circular movement of closure. The word family groups the idea of closure, enclosure, and protection. The basic meaning is physical and spatial: to form a circle around something.
H5849A.emploi: The verb appears only twice in the Hebrew Bible. It first expresses military and hostile action: in 1 Samuel 23:26, Saul deploys his men in a circle around David to capture him — it is a verb of threat and trap. In Psalms 5:13, the same verb changes color: it speaks of God's blessing that "surrounds" the righteous with His grace like a protective armor. The context determines whether the surrounding is hostile or benevolent.
H5849A.portee: This word helps to understand two realities of the life of faith: first, that God may allow His children to be "surrounded" by threats and enemies (like David encircled by Saul), without being abandoned. Secondly, that true protection comes from God who "surrounds" the righteous with His grace — an invisible and perfect barrier. It is an invitation to move from the fear of being encircled by evil to the trust of being kept by the love of God.

sens: To place a crown on someone's head
To honor, magnify someone
To complete, finish an action with magnificence
H5849B.detail:
1. To place a crown on someone's head: it is the material and visible act of putting a royal crown. In Song of Solomon 3:11, the mother of King Solomon crowns him on the day of his betrothal, a solemn gesture that acknowledges his dignity and authority.
2. To honor, magnify someone: to crown also means to bestow honor and glory. In Psalm 8:6, God has crowned man with glory and majesty, which means He has granted him a place of honor in creation, little lower than God Himself.
3. To complete, finish an action with magnificence: to crown can also mean to accomplish or perfect. In Psalm 65:12, God crowns the year with His goodness, meaning He completes the year by filling it with abundance and blessings.
H5849B.origine: The Hebrew verb עָטַר comes from a root that evokes the idea of placing something on top, of overcoming. The crown is what overcomes the head and distinguishes the one who wears it. The word belongs to the family of Hebrew terms related to honor, dignity, and exaltation. It is an action verb: to crown is to perform a significant act that changes the status of the one who receives it.
H5849B.emploi: The verb to crown appears 5 times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in the Psalms and the Song of Solomon. Three usages are in the Psalm (8:6, 65:12, 103:4), where God crowns humanity or the faithful with glory, goodness, and mercy — all signs of divine love and generosity. One usage in the Song of Solomon (3:11) describes the concrete crowning of King Solomon by his mother. A final usage in Isaiah 23:8 speaks of Tyre as the "dispenser of crowns," meaning a center of power and honor in ancient trade. The word thus expresses both a real gesture (putting on a crown) and a divine action (honoring, exalting, filling).
H5849B.portee: For the biblical reader, to crown reminds us that honor and glory come from God. Whether crowned with glory, goodness, or mercy, the faithful discover that God elevates, magnifies, and enriches them. It is an invitation to recognize the dignity that God gives to those who believe in Him, and to live this reality in trust and gratitude.

sens: Head ornament worn by kings and great figures, made of precious metal and adorned with stones
Mark of dignity, honor, or power
Reward, victory, or distinction obtained
Beauty, brilliance, or glory of a person or thing
Honor or pride that crowns a life
H5850.detail:
1. The crown is primarily a concrete object: a circle of precious metal, often gold, worn by kings on their heads (2 Samuel 12:30 reports that the crown of the Ammonite king "weighed a talent of gold and was adorned with precious stones"). It symbolizes royal power and the supreme dignity of a nation.

2. Beyond the physical object, the crown represents the honor, glory, and authority of the one who wears it. When Job laments, "He has taken the crown from my head" (Job 19:9), he is not speaking of an accessory, but of his lost honor and ruined status.

3. The crown also becomes the symbol of the reward and victory achieved. "She will place on your head a crown of grace" (Proverbs 4:9): this is the fruit of wisdom and virtue, the mark that God grants to the one who faithfully follows Him.

4. Natural beauty and brilliance can also be referred to as a "crown": "Gray hair is a crown of honor" (Proverbs 16:31). Here, the dignity that radiates from age and experience is compared to a crown.

5. Finally, the crown can signify the glorious culmination of a life: for the saved people, God will make a "glorious crown" (Isaiah 62:3), a manifestation of His glory and love that everyone will see shining.
H5850.origine: The Hebrew word עֲטָרָה (atarah) comes from a root that means "to encircle" or "to surround." The original image is that of an object that goes around the head to crown it. In Hebrew, the verb from the same family was already used to speak of encircling or crowning. This root expresses the idea of a circle of honor that encircles and distinguishes the one who wears it.
H5850.emploi: The word appears 23 times in the Old Testament, especially in the poetic books (Proverbs, Psalms, Job) and prophetic books (Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, Zechariah). It first denotes the concrete royal crown: that of the king of Ammon (2 Samuel 12:30), the crowns mentioned in the context of royal festivities (Esther 8:15, Zechariah 6:11). Then, especially in Proverbs, the term is used figuratively to express the honor that a quality or a virtuous life confers: the virtuous woman is "the crown of her husband" (Proverbs 12:4), experience and wisdom form a "crown" (Proverbs 17:6). Among the prophets, the crown becomes the image of divine glory and the honor that God bestows upon His people (Isaiah 62:3). The meaning thus varies from the concrete object to the symbol of dignity, reward, or even the glorious intention of God towards His people.
H5850.portee: For the Christian reader, the crown reminds us that true honor comes from God and is earned through faithfulness, not through human wealth or power. Proverbs shows that wisdom and virtue "crown" a life far more than royal gold. This image invites us to seek the eternal reward that God prepares for those who obey Him, not the fragile honors of the world. Meditating on the crown encourages the believer to value a life of righteousness rather than fleeting glory.

sens: Woman from the tribe of Judah during the time of the united monarchy
H5851.detail: Athara is a woman from the time when Israel was united under a king. She was the wife of Jerachmeel, an important member of the tribe of Judah, and the mother of their son Onam. She is mentioned only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 2:26, in the context of a genealogy that lists the descendants of Judah.
H5851.origine: The name Athara means "crown" in Hebrew, an image of dignity and beauty. This name was borne by this high-ranking woman from the tribe of Judah.
H5851.emploi: Athara appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 2:26. She is mentioned solely to identify her lineage: she is the mother of Onam, son of Jerachmeel. She is included in the official genealogy of the descendants of Judah, indicating the importance of her family position, even though the Bible reports nothing else about her.

sens: City in Transjordan, in Gilead, east of the Jordan
H5852G.detail: Atharoth is a city located east of the Jordan, in the region of Gilead. Its name means "crowns" in Hebrew, possibly evoking heights or fortifications. This city was taken and rebuilt by the tribe of Gad during the conquest of Canaan (Numbers 32:34), after Moses had given his approval for Gad to settle in Transjordan rather than enter the Promised Land with the other tribes.
H5852G.origine: The Hebrew name עֲטָרוֹת (Ataroth) derives from the root עטר (atar), which means "to crown" or "to place a crown." This image of a crown may suggest ridges or crown-like fortifications, characteristic of this mountainous region of Gilead.
H5852G.emploi: Atharoth appears twice in the Bible, both times in chapter 32 of the book of Numbers. In Numbers 32:3, it is listed among the cities that the tribe of Gad desired to take in Transjordan. In Numbers 32:34, we learn that the sons of Gad actually rebuilt and fortified it, making it one of the fortified cities of their territory.

sens: Locality located on the border between Ephraim and Benjamin
Place in the mountainous region of Ephraim
H5852H.detail: Atharoth is a small locality marking the border between the territories of Ephraim and Benjamin, in the central region of Canaan. Its name means "crowns" in Hebrew, probably because the terrain was mountainous or featured notable heights. It is mentioned twice in the description of the borders of the territory of Ephraim (Joshua 16:2 and 16:7), which shows its importance as a geographical landmark for delineating the lands promised to this tribe.
H5852H.origine: The name Atharoth comes from the Hebrew root "atar" (עטר), which means "to crown" or "to encircle." The word is related to "atara" (crown, diadem). The plural or form of the name thus evokes "crowns," perhaps suggesting peaks or heights that dominate the surrounding landscape.
H5852H.emploi: Atharoth appears only twice in the Bible, both in the book of Joshua in chapter 16, which lists the borders of the territory allocated to the tribe of Ephraim. Joshua 16:2 mentions it as the starting point on the border, while Joshua 16:7 places it again in the delineation of territorial limits. These two references show that Atharoth was a well-known and identifiable locality, serving as a reliable landmark for generations who needed to understand and maintain the boundaries of their tribal heritage.

sens: Fortified city located on the western border of the territory of Benjamin
H5853.detail: 1. Atharoth-Addar is a city of ancient Israel, mentioned as a landmark in the descriptions of boundary lines. Its name means "crowns of glory" in Hebrew, possibly evoking an elevated or fortified site. It appears twice in the book of Joshua to mark the borders: it is cited as the eastern boundary of the inheritance of Ephraim (Joshua 16:5) and also as a point of passage in the description of the borders of Benjamin (Joshua 18:13). This dual mention shows that it was a strategic point at the junction between these two territories, near Beth-Horon.
H5853.origine: The name "Atharoth-Addar" combines two Hebrew terms: "Atharoth" (crowns, plural) and "Addar" (glory or majesty). This type of double geographical name suggests either an important locality or a distinction from another Atharoth. The presence of the word "crowns" evokes heights or fortifications, which corresponds to its mountainous location according to biblical texts.
H5853.emploi: Atharoth-Addar is mentioned only in the book of Joshua, in chapters 16 and 18, in the context of the division of the promised lands among the twelve tribes. These two passages describe the territorial boundaries of Ephraim and Benjamin after the conquest of Canaan. It served as a geographical landmark to delineate tribal inheritances, located near Beth-Horon in the mountains. Its double mention indicates that it was a well-known and easily identifiable place for the contemporaries of Joshua.

sens: Region or locality of Judah associated with the house of Joab
H5854.detail: Athroth-Beth-Joab is a place located in Judah, mentioned in the genealogy of the descendants of Salma. The name literally means "the crowns of the house of Joab" — a geographical and genealogical description that links this territory to the family of Joab, one of the major military leaders of Israel. In 1 Chronicles 2:54, it appears in a list of Judean localities, alongside Bethlehem and the Nethophathites, indicating that it was a region or administrative subdivision of the tribe of Judah.
H5854.origine: The compound name combines two elements: "ataroth" (עַטְרוֹת), which means "crowns" or "diadems," and "beth-Joab" (בֵּית יוֹאָב), which means "house of Joab." This onomastic structure — uniting a descriptive word with a patronymic — was common in biblical Hebrew to designate territories controlled or inhabited by an important family. Joab was the nephew of King David and the commander-in-chief of his armies.
H5854.emploi: Athroth-Beth-Joab appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 2:54, within the genealogy of the descendants of Salma. It is listed among the cities or regions of Judah, suggesting that it was a possession or habitation area of the lineage of Joab. The genealogical context indicates that this place was recognized as an important territorial or administrative center, associated with one of the great military families of the kingdom.

sens: City in the region of Gad, east of the Jordan
H5855.detail: Atroth-Shophan is a city located in the territory allocated to the tribe of Gad, east of the Jordan. Its name literally means "crowns of plunder" or "crowns of their robbery," a common poetic formulation in biblical place names. The city is mentioned only once in the Bible, in Numbers 32:35, at the time when Moses lists the cities that the tribe of Gad has rebuilt or fortified after conquering the region.
H5855.origine: The name consists of two Hebrew elements: "'atroth" (עַטְרוֹת) meaning "crowns" or "crowned ramparts," and "shophan" (שׁוֹפָן) evoking plunder or robbery. This type of compound name reflects the ancient practice of giving cities names evocative of their defensive function or history. The suffix "-an" or "-on" is common in toponyms of the Levant.
H5855.emploi: Atroth-Shophan appears only once in the preserved biblical texts: in Numbers 32:35. It is cited in the context of the land distribution after the conquest of Canaan. The tribes of Reuben and Gad, along with the half-tribe of Manasseh, receive the lands east of the Jordan that the Israelites conquered from the kingdoms of Sihon and Og. Atroth-Shophan is among the cities that Gad built or restored in this region.
H5855.portee: This geographical location recalls the fulfillment of God's promise: each tribe receives its inheritance. Although little known, Atroth-Shophan bears witness to the historical reality of the Israelite conquests and the organization of the territory of God's people.

sens: Pile or accumulation of stones and debris
City or sanctuary completely destroyed and ravaged
State of total destruction and abandonment
Moral or spiritual ruin
H5856.detail:
1. The word primarily designates a heap, a confused mass of stones and collapsed debris. This is the most concrete image: when a structure collapses, only an amorphous pile remains. Jeremiah speaks of Jerusalem which "will become a heap of stones" (Jeremiah 26:18), an accumulation of rubble where nothing can be recognized anymore.
2. By extension, the word refers to a city or sanctuary completely destroyed, reduced to a state of abandoned ruins. Micah prophesies that Samaria will be reduced to a heap of stones, a field of desolation where one can "plant a vineyard" (Micah 1:6) — the image is that of a city razed to the ground, left to abandonment.
3. The word also evokes the state of a plundered and desecrated city: Jerusalem and its holy temple become a heap after the foreign invasion (Psalms 79:1), marking the total rupture with what was sacred and holy.
4. Figuratively, the word can apply to the perdition of a person, to their moral collapse. In Job 30:24, the one who "is about to perish" — whose existence is collapsing — is compared to one who stretches out their hands in distress.
H5856.origine: The Hebrew root עִי evokes collapse, complete ruin. It is related to the idea of things that have collapsed and been destroyed. The word belongs to the family of terms that describe violent and irreversible destruction, the final state of a city or a people reduced to nothing. It is a word rich in biblical imagery of divine judgment.
H5856.emploi: The word appears five times in the Old Testament, mainly in the prophetic books (Jeremiah, Micah) and the Psalms. It primarily designates the ruins of Jerusalem and the temple, or those of cities like Samaria, prophesied by Micah. The prophets use it to express God's judgment on the sin and unfaithfulness of His people: a prosperous city becomes a heap of stones, a visible symbol of the rupture with God. In Job 30:24, the word takes on a more personal and moral nuance: the one who "is about to perish" is one whose existence is collapsing. The context is always that of destruction, of irreversible collapse.
H5856.portee: This word reminds the believer of the reality of divine judgment on sin and pride. The ruins of once powerful and holy cities become a visible sign of what it means to distance oneself from God. It is also an invitation to vigilance: what may seem unshakeable — a temple, a nation — can be reduced to nothing. For the believer, the word invites them to build their life not on sand, but on the solid foundation of the word of God.

sens: City of Canaan located east of Bethel
Second city conquered by Israel during the invasion of Canaan
Strategic location near Jericho
H5857G.detail:
1. Ai is a city of ancient Canaan, positioned east of Bethel and near Jericho (Genesis 12:8). It is a fortified city with its gates and inhabitants capable of fighting (Joshua 7:5, 8:1).
2. Ai is famous in Israel's history as it was the second city that the Israelites conquered after Jericho during their invasion of Canaan under Joshua. The first attempt to take the city failed, but Joshua employed a trap strategy that led to the complete destruction of the city and its inhabitants (Joshua 8:10-25).
3. The name literally means "heap of ruins" or "debris," which likely reflects the state of the city after its destruction during the conquest (Joshua 8:28-29).
H5857G.origine: The Hebrew name עַי (ay) literally means "heap of ruins" or "pile of debris." This descriptive name evokes a city whose ruins are visible, perhaps an ancient site that was destroyed. The name also has variants Ajja and Ajjath in some biblical passages.
H5857G.emploi: Ai appears about 33 times in the Bible, primarily in the book of Joshua, which details the conquest and destruction of this city (Joshua 7-8). It is also found in passages where Abraham and Jacob stopped (Genesis 12:8, 13:3). The city is mentioned in lists of conquered cities (Joshua 12:9) and in records of inhabitants returning from exile (Ezra 2:28, Nehemiah 7:32, 11:31). The prophet Isaiah also mentions it in a prophecy (Isaiah 10:28). Ai thus remains a key site in the history of the conquest of Canaan and an important geographical landmark in biblical geography.
H5857G.portee: The account of the conquest of Ai teaches believers the importance of obedience to God and divine judgment against sin: the first defeat occurs due to the hidden sin of Achan in the camp of Israel (Joshua 7), while the final victory comes from obedience and trust in divine strategy. This story also shows that God guides His people with wisdom and power, and that He fulfills His promises for those who obey Him.

sens: City of the Ammonites east of the Jordan
H5857H.detail: Ai is a city belonging to the Ammonite people, located east of the Jordan, probably associated with Heshbon. Its name literally means "heap of ruins," which evokes the fate of many cities in the ancient Near East, often destroyed and rebuilt. In the only passage where it appears in the Bible (Jeremiah 49:3), the prophet Jeremiah announces its destruction during divine judgment against the Ammonites: the inhabitants are called to lament and to put on sackcloth, signs of mourning, for the city will be ravaged during captivity.
H5857H.origine: The Hebrew name עַי (Ai) literally means "heap of ruins" or "pile." This name likely reflects the troubled history of the city, which has experienced successive destructions. Although this word appears only once as a proper name in the provided biblical text, it is associated with other Ammonite cities and the region of Heshbon, an important center of Ammonite territory in biblical times.
H5857H.emploi: Ai appears only once in the canonical Bible, in Jeremiah 49:3, in a prophetic oracle against the Ammonites. The prophet lists the cities that will be struck during divine judgment, and Ai is among them. This passage is part of a series of oracles against the enemy nations of Israel. The context shows that the city is significant enough to be named alongside Heshbon and other Ammonite centers during announcements of destruction. This unique mention suggests that Ai was a known but secondary locality compared to Heshbon, the Ammonite capital.
H5857H.portee: This passage reminds us that God's judgment extends over all nations, including those that have oppressed the people of Israel. The mention of Ai invites the reader to meditate on the vanity of earthly powers and the certainty of divine judgment. It is also an invitation to recognize that no human refuge can shield us from God's justice, and that only repentance can preserve us from it.

sens: Son of Joktan and grandson of Shem
H5858A.detail: 1. Ebal is an ancestor of the Arab peoples, son of Joktan (who himself was a son of Eber) and brother to a dozen other sons including Sheba and Ophir. He is mentioned in the genealogy of the descendants of Noah in 1 Chronicles 1:22, where he appears alongside his brothers.
H5858A.origine: The name "Ebal" means "stone" or "bald mountain" in Hebrew, evoking a landscape of rocky or barren heights. This name designates a figure from the patriarchal era, an ancestor of a tribe or people from Arabia.
H5858A.emploi: Ebal appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 1:22, in the genealogical list of the sons of Joktan. This passage recaps the genealogy from Genesis 10:28 to summarize the ancestors of the peoples of the Middle East. Ebal represents a branch of the Semitic descent that populated the Arabian Peninsula.

sens: Son of Schobal, man of the time of the Patriarchs
H5858B.detail: Ebal is a man mentioned in the ancient genealogies of Esau. He is the son of Schobal and the brother of Alvan, Manahath, Shepho, and Onam. Nothing is known about him except that he belongs to the lineage of Esau, the ancestor of the Edomites, and that he appears in the enumerations of descendants given in Genesis 36 and repeated in 1 Chronicles 1.
H5858B.origine: The name means "stone" or "bare mountain" in Hebrew, an evocative image of solidity and nakedness. It is a name from the family of Esau, the ancestor of the Edomites, a people established in the south of the Promised Land.
H5858B.emploi: Ebal appears twice in the Bible, always in genealogies: in Genesis 36:23 among the sons of Schobal, and in 1 Chronicles 1:40 in a parallel enumeration. These lists aim to preserve the memory of the neighboring peoples of Israel and their origins. Ebal plays no active role in the biblical narrative; he is simply a link in a genealogical chain.

sens: mountain in the West Bank, located north of Shechem
place designated for the pronouncement of the curses of the covenant
site of the first altar built by Israel in the Promised Land
H5858C.detail:
1. Ebal is a mountain in the land of Canaan, positioned north of the city of Shechem, facing its neighbor, Mount Gerizim (Deuteronomy 11:29). The name literally means "stone" or "bare mountain," which well describes its rocky and arid appearance.

2. God commanded Israel to pronounce the curses of the covenant on Mount Ebal, while the blessings would be declared from Mount Gerizim (Deuteronomy 27:13). Six tribes stood on Ebal to pronounce the curses against all who would violate God's commandments.

3. It is on Mount Ebal that Joshua erected the first altar in the Promised Land, after crossing the Jordan (Joshua 8:30). There, all Israel gathered — elders, officers, judges, priests, and Levites — to renew the covenant with the Lord, half of the people on each side of the mountain (Joshua 8:33).
H5858C.origine: The Hebrew name עֵיבָל (Ebal) means "stone" or "bare mountain." It refers to the rocky and infertile nature of this mountain in Samaria. This designation evokes the bare and austere aspect of the place, which corresponds well to its symbolic role: it is where the curses are proclaimed, while Gerizim, the "mountain of grace," stands opposite.
H5858C.emploi: Ebal appears 5 times in the Bible, all in the context of the renewal of the covenant at Sinai. Moses commands Israel to pronounce the blessings on Gerizim and the curses on Ebal upon entering Canaan (Deuteronomy 11:29; 27:4, 13). After crossing the Jordan, Joshua carries out this order: he builds an altar on Ebal and gathers all the people on each side of the two mountains to renew their commitment to the Lord (Joshua 8:30, 33). These passages show that Ebal is never just a geographical site, but a symbol of divine judgment against sin.
H5858C.portee: Mount Ebal reminds the people of God that the covenant is not without consequences: alongside the blessings promised to the obedient rise the curses against disobedience. It is a call to moral and spiritual responsibility. For the believer, this means that following God requires a conscious choice: one cannot be indifferent to divine commandments without suffering the consequences.

sens: fortified city in northern Israel
territory of the tribe of Naphtali
city conquered and destroyed
H5859.detail: 1. Ijjon is a fortified city located in northern Palestine, within the territory of the tribe of Naphtali. It was one of the important cities in this northern region. 2. It was part of the northern centers of Israel and served to control this border region. 3. Ijjon met the tragic fate of several cities in the north: it was taken and its inhabitants deported, first by Ben-Hadad (1 Kings 15:20), then by the Assyrian king Tiglath-Pileser (2 Kings 15:29), who carried its inhabitants into captivity.
H5859.origine: The name Ijjon literally means "a ruin" in Hebrew, evoking the final state of this city after the destructions it suffered. This name reminds us that human fortifications, no matter how significant, can fall before the power of surrounding empires. The Hebrew used here conveys a concrete reality: what was built can be reduced to rubble.
H5859.emploi: Ijjon appears three times in the Old Testament, always in the context of war and conquest. In the first mention (1 Kings 15:20), it is taken by the army of Ben-Hadad, king of Aram, during a conflict between the kingdoms of Israel and Judah. The second occurrence (2 Kings 15:29) reports its capture by Assyria under Tiglath-Pileser, who deports its population. The third mention (2 Chronicles 16:4) recalls the same event as the first, showing the military and strategic importance of this northern stronghold. These three references testify to the vulnerability of Israelite cities before regional powers.
H5859.portee: Ijjon illustrates how kingdoms and cities, no matter how well fortified, remain under the sovereign control of God. Its very name — "a ruin" — anticipates its fate. For the Christian reader, this city serves as a reminder that true security does not lie in walls and armies, but in faithfulness to God.

sens: to shout at someone with violence and contempt
to treat someone with brusqueness and harshness of speech
H5860A.detail:
1. The verb evokes the action of shouting at someone, not just a simple call, but a harsh, contemptuous cry intended to rebuke or intimidate. It is the tone of a person who raises their voice to humiliate or reject the one they are addressing. In 1 Samuel 25:14, Nabal "rudoys" the messengers of David by shouting at them with disdain.
2. More broadly, it means to treat someone with brusqueness and harshness, to reject them verbally. The word captures verbal aggression: not a simple polite refusal, but an insult delivered in an aggressive tone, often accompanied by harsh words or a gesture of rejection.
H5860A.origine: The Hebrew verb עִיט (it) comes from a root expressing a sharp cry or a howl. The word evokes a voice that rises, expressing hostility or contempt. It is a cry of rejection, close to the idea of "driving" someone away by voice. The biblical context associates it with attitudes of denial and pride: the one who rudoys someone refuses to acknowledge them and humiliates them with their cries.
H5860A.emploi: This verb appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in 1 Samuel 25:14. It describes Nabal's behavior towards David's messengers: while David, before becoming king, was a powerful military leader, Nabal "rudoys" him by refusing to help with harsh and humiliating words. This act of insolence and verbal contempt is presented as highly offensive and provokes a reaction of anger from David. The word emphasizes the brutal and contemptuous nature of the insult rather than its simple expression.
H5860A.portee: This word shows us the devastating power of harsh and contemptuous speech. Nabal, by his "rudoying," insults not only the messengers but also David himself, by refusing a basic courtesy. It is a reminder that treating someone with contempt, especially without justified reason, constitutes a serious offense. For the Christian reader, this illustrates the importance of mastering one's tongue and not humiliating others, as taught in the Epistle of James.

sens: to pounce on something eagerly and quickly
to seize or take possession of a spoil
to act without restraint or respect for established order
H5860B.detail:
1. The verb paints the image of an animal or person rushing upon prey or goods with sudden and impatient voracity: it is to pounce on, to charge at. In 1 Samuel 14:32, the hungry soldiers "rushed upon the spoil," meaning they pounced on the captured sheep, oxen, and calves to devour them immediately.
2. The word also designates the act of seizing or taking possession of something by the force of desire or greed, without waiting for an order or authorization. It is to violate the established order or law out of impatience or covetousness.
3. In a figurative or moral sense, "to rush upon" the spoil means to commit an act of disobedience or contrary to divine will. In 1 Samuel 15:19, Saul "committed what is evil in the eyes of the Lord" precisely by rushing upon the spoil against the received order.
H5860B.origine: The Hebrew verb עִיט comes from a root that expresses the idea of sudden movement, haste, and covetousness. The image is that of a rapid and insatiable rush. The word belongs to the family of verbs denoting abrupt and impatient action, and its root evokes the swiftness of the gesture and the intensity of desire.
H5860B.emploi: The verb appears twice in the first book of Samuel, in the story of Saul. In both cases, it describes the same fault: the soldiers (or Saul himself) rushing upon the war spoil with greed, in violation of divine order. These two uses illustrate how greed and impatience constitute disobedience to God. The context is always one of a blamed action: the hungry army, then the rebellious king, acting without restraint.
H5860B.portee: This word shows how greed and impatience lead us to disobey God, even when the received order seems difficult. It reminds us that yielding to immediate desire, without waiting for divine order or respecting His will, is to commit evil. For the believer, it is a call to master one's covetousness and to obey, rather than to rush upon what attracts our gaze.

sens: Carnivorous bird that captures and devours other animals
Predator that swoops down on its prey quickly
Figuratively: a being or people that preys on others
Figuratively: instrument of divine punishment
H5861.detail:
1. The word literally designates a carnivorous bird — hawk, eagle, vulture — that hunts other animals for food. In Genesis 15:11, the "birds of prey" immediately swoop down on the carcasses offered in sacrifice, showing their natural propensity to devour the remains. Job 28:7 emphasizes that even the bird of prey, with its keen eyes, has no access to hidden wisdom — a trait that makes the word effective in evoking the visual acuity and swiftness of this animal.
2. The image of the "swooper" captures the characteristic movement: the bird soars high and then suddenly dives on its prey. This predatory and violent movement is very present in biblical imagery.
3. Figuratively, the word applies to a people or nation that devours others through conquest and oppression. In Jeremiah 12:9, the people of Israel become "a bird of prey, a hyena," meaning they have become like the predators that threaten them — they devour as they are devoured.
4. In Isaiah 46:11, the "bird of prey" that God calls from the east symbolizes a conqueror (probably the Persian Cyrus) that God uses to accomplish His plans of judgment and deliverance. The word then evokes a divine instrument, as effective and inevitable as a predator on the hunt.
H5861.origine: The Hebrew word עַיִט (ayit) is related to roots meaning "to fly quickly" or "to swoop down." The basic image is that of rapid and violent aerial movement. The word fits within the lexical field of predators and danger in the Hebrew Bible. It is a common term for all birds of prey (eagles, hawks, vultures) without precise species distinction.
H5861.emploi: The word appears six times in the Old Testament, primarily in the prophetic books (Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel) and wisdom literature (Job). In concrete contexts, it simply designates the bird of prey that devours carcasses (Genesis 15:11; Isaiah 18:6; Ezekiel 39:4) or hunts ruthlessly (Job 28:7). In figurative and prophetic contexts, the word becomes a metaphor for destructive power: a people or nation that ravages others (Jeremiah 12:9), or an instrument of divine vengeance (Isaiah 46:11). The usage varies little: the word always retains its connotation of violent and rapid predation, whether referring to a real animal or a human power.
H5861.portee: This word reminds us that the Bible does not hide the reality of violence and natural predation — they are part of the created world. At a deeper level, the bird of prey becomes an image of the vanity of human power that seeks to devour others: it is subject to the will of God, who can divert it from its ends or use it for His own purposes. This teaches humility in the face of forces that seem invincible: no earthly power escapes divine control.

sens: Cave or rocky refuge in Judah
Fortified place of retreat
H5862G.detail:
1. Etam is a cave or shelter carved into the rock, located in Judean territory. Samson takes refuge there after defeating the Philistines: he "withdrew to the cave of the rock of Etam" (Judges 15:8), probably to escape retaliation.
2. This place becomes a well-known refuge, significant enough for three thousand men of Judah to come down and seek it out (Judges 15:11). It is a naturally fortified place, difficult to access, offering protection to those who hide there.
H5862G.origine: The name literally means "den of wild beasts" — the image is that of a rocky cave where fearful creatures hide. Etam designates a natural cavity in the rock, a primitive place of refuge. The word reflects the rugged and rocky landscape of Judah, with its many caves and cliffs.
H5862G.emploi: Etam appears only twice in the Bible, both passages in chapter 15 of Judges. It is the setting for the conflict between Samson and the Philistines: Samson hides there after his vengeance (Judges 15:8), and it is there that the men of Judah come to find him (Judges 15:11). The context shows that it is a natural refuge, accessible but difficult, known to the local inhabitants.

sens: Village of the tribe of Simeon
H5862H.detail: Etham is a village located in the territory of the tribe of Simeon, in the southern part of the Promised Land. The name evokes the idea of a den or refuge — literally "lair of wild beasts" — reflecting the character of this region, perhaps rocky or wooded. It appears in the genealogy of the descendants of Simeon as one of the localities that this tribe possessed and inhabited.
H5862H.origine: The Hebrew word עֵיטָם (étam) literally means "lair," a refuge or hiding place — the image of a den where wild animals retreat. This place name likely reflects the rugged or covered terrain that characterized this region of Simeon in ancient times.
H5862H.emploi: Etham is mentioned twice in the genealogical and territorial lists of Simeon in 1 Chronicles 4. The first mention (1 Chronicles 4:3) identifies it as the name of an ancestor or patriarch of Simeon. The second (1 Chronicles 4:32) lists it among the five main cities that the tribe of Simeon possessed: Etam, Ain, Rimmon, Tokein, and Ashan. These two mentions show that Etam was an important geographical and genealogical landmark for the tribe of Simeon.

sens: fortified city of the kingdom of Judah
H5862I.detail: Etham is a city that King Rehoboam of Judah fortified and garrisoned with troops. It was located between Bethlehem and Tekoa, two other cities in southern Judah. The text of 2 Chronicles 11:6 mentions it among the strongholds that Rehoboam built to defend his kingdom after the schism of Israel.
H5862I.origine: The name literally means "den of wild beasts," suggesting that the place may have originally been a deserted or sparsely populated area before becoming a fortress. The Hebrew name עֵיטָם reflects this image of refuge or fortified shelter.
H5862I.emploi: Etham appears only once in the Bible, in 2 Chronicles 11:6, in the list of cities that King Rehoboam fortified after the kingdom of Israel separated from Judah (around 930 B.C.). Rehoboam consolidated his borders by establishing several strongholds, including Etham, to protect his kingdom from external incursions. Its position between Bethlehem and Tekoa made it a strategic point in southern Judah.

sens: Israel's station in the desert, on the southeast border of Moab
H5863.detail: Ijjé-Abarim is a stop on the journey of the Israelites in the desert after their exodus from Egypt. The name literally means "ruins of Abarim": this place was located near the region of Abarim, a mountain range east of the Jordan. The Israelites camped there after leaving Oboth, heading toward the territory of Moab (Numbers 21:11). It was a strategic waypoint in their progression toward the Promised Land.
H5863.origine: The compound name combines the Hebrew word "ijjim" (ruins) and "Abarim" (mountainous region of Transjordan). Abarim means "passages" or "crossings," evoking a place of crossing. This geographical name refers to a well-known landmark for the peoples of the ancient Levant.
H5863.emploi: Ijjé-Abarim appears twice in the Bible, both in the book of Numbers, in the account of the desert stages. In Numbers 21:11, the Israelites camp there after Oboth, in the desert facing Moab, toward the east. In Numbers 33:44, the same route is precisely listed: they depart from Oboth and camp at Ijjé-Abarim, on the border of Moab. These two passages trace the same path, confirming that this place was an important stop during the forty years of wandering in the desert.

sens: Camping station of Israel in the desert
Location east of Moab during the Exodus
H5864G.detail: Ijjé-Abarim was a site where the people of Israel established their camp during their forty years of crossing the desert after leaving Egypt. The name literally means "ruins of the passages" or "ruins of the crossings," evoking remnants of fortifications or inhabited areas that the Israelites found there. It is one of the many stops that Moses enumerates in Numbers 33, the detailed record of Israel's journey to the Promised Land.
H5864G.origine: The Hebrew name עִיִּים (iyim) means "ruins" or "desolations." It is composed of the word עִי (i) which denotes a ruin, and may refer to remnants of construction. The term "Abarim" comes from the root עבר (avar), meaning "to pass" or "to cross," suggesting crossings through a mountainous region. Ijjé-Abarim thus combined the idea of ancient ruins in a difficult passage area.
H5864G.emploi: Ijjé-Abarim appears only once in the Bible, in Numbers 33:45. This verse mentions it as one of the desert stops where Israel camped after leaving Nebo and before arriving at Dibon-Gad. This site corresponds to the final phases of the forty-year journey, placing Israel at the moment when it was finally approaching the Promised Land, in the region east of the Jordan and Moab.

sens: city of Judah mentioned as a locality in the territory assigned to the descendants of Judah
H5864H.detail: Ijjim is a small city in the southern territory of Judah, listed among the cities of the tribe in the land distribution after the conquest (Joshua 15:29).
H5864H.origine: The name Ijjim means "ruins" in Hebrew, possibly evoking a site marked by ancient remnants or simply a settlement of little importance.
H5864H.emploi: Ijjim appears only once in the Bible, in Joshua 15:29, in the list of cities in the Negev (southern Judah) that Moses and Joshua assigned to the tribe of Judah after the conquest of the land.

sens: for an unlimited time, without end
at all times, permanently
in a constant and enduring manner
H5865.detail:
1. The word expresses the idea of unlimited duration, that which lasts forever and never stops. In 2 Chronicles 33:7, God says He wants to place His name "forever" in the temple of Jerusalem: this affirms an eternal presence, an intention that will never end.
2. It also denotes a moral permanence or constancy: God's commitment to His people, His faithfulness that persists without interruption.
3. The word can also qualify that which dates back very far in the past, that which is from the beginning (the "ancient," the "eternal"), for that which lasts forever extends both into the past and into the future.
H5865.origine: This Hebrew word comes from a root that expresses the idea of secrecy or hiddenness — that which is concealed, hidden, or distant. From this arose the meaning of "remoteness in time": that which is far back (antiquity) and that which extends beyond (eternity). The same family produces other Hebrew words meaning "century," "age," "world." In the Greek Bible of the Old Testament, this word is often rendered by "aïôn" (αἰών), which has the same range of meanings: duration and eternity.
H5865.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible as an adverb indicating infinite duration: in 2 Chronicles 33:7. It is a word from God addressed to David and Solomon regarding the temple of Jerusalem. The usage is solemn, liturgical: it emphasizes the permanence of the divine covenant with the house of David and the centrality of the sanctuary in God's plan for Israel. Although rare in this exact form, the idea it carries — that of divine eternity and unending faithfulness — is fundamental in biblical theology.
H5865.portee: This word invites the believer to grasp the stability and eternity of God's plan. When God says He will place His name "forever" in the temple, it is a promise of lasting presence, even beyond human failures and historical destructions. For the Christian, this speaks of God's constancy: His word endures forever, His salvation is permanent, and His faithfulness has no beginning or end.

sens: elite warrior in the service of King David
H5866.detail: Ilaï is one of the thirty mighty warriors of David, also known as his "valiant men." He belongs to the clan of the Ahohites, a family of renowned warriors. The text of 1 Chronicles 11:29 mentions him in the official list of the king's elite fighters.
H5866.origine: The name Ilaï means "exalted" or "elevated" in Hebrew. In 2 Samuel 23:28, he appears in another form, showing that ancient scribes sometimes recorded the same name in slightly different ways. The Ahohites formed a group of warrior clans recognizable at that time in the united kingdom.
H5866.emploi: Ilaï is mentioned only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 11:29, where the list of David's thirty warriors appears. This list showcases the king's personal army, his most loyal and competent men in battle. The absence of detailed accounts of his exploits contrasts with the prestige associated with these titles — being counted among David's mighty men was a considerable honor.

sens: Ancient region located east of Babylon
Military and political power rivaling Israel and Babylon
People whom the Lord announces judgment upon through the prophets
H5867A.detail:
1. Elam is a historical region in the Middle East, located east of Babylon and northeast of the lower Tigris River. It is an ancient territory with its own kings and a formidable army. Genesis 14:1 mentions it as early as the time of Abraham, when Kedorlaomer, king of Elam, participates in a coalition of kings against the cities of Sodom and Gomorrah.
2. Elam is a notable military power, equipped with chariots and armed horsemen. Isaiah 22:6 describes its warriors carrying the quiver and its battle chariots, demonstrating its capacity for war. It is among the nations that God enumerates in His prophetic warnings.
3. Several prophets announce that the Lord will judge Elam. Jeremiah 49:34-38 reports the word of the Lord against Elam: God will bring four winds to scatter its inhabitants and will establish His throne to destroy the king and the leaders. This judgment shows that even distant powers are under the authority of the Lord.
H5867A.origine: The name "Elam" literally means "eternity" or "that which is high," which could evoke the antiquity and greatness of this civilization. Elam is one of the oldest regions in the world, inhabited and powerful long before the rise of Babylon. Its history dates back to the very origins of Mesopotamian civilization, which explains the weight of the name in biblical texts.
H5867A.emploi: Elam appears about fifteen times in the Bible, mainly in the prophetic books (Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, Daniel) and once at the beginning of Genesis. It first appears as a political and military power alongside other kings (Genesis 14:1, 14:9). Over the centuries, as Babylon grows in power, Elam becomes a subject of prophecies of divine judgment. The prophets Isaiah and Jeremiah announce that the Lord will scatter His people and break their government, illustrating divine sovereignty over all nations, great or small. In Ezekiel and Daniel, it is mentioned among the peoples judged or in connection with visions of eschatological judgment.

sens: Several individuals who bore this name during the time of exile and the return of the Jews to Jerusalem
H5867B.detail: The name Elam actually refers to several different individuals living at the time of the Babylonian exile and the return to Jerusalem under Zerubbabel and Nehemiah. The Bible calls them this because they are ancestors of families or leaders of groups: some are mentioned as heads of families of exiles who returned (Ezra 2:7; Ezra 2:31), others as men who participated in the return or the renewal of the covenant (Ezra 8:7; Ezra 10:2), and still others as leaders who signed the commitment with Nehemiah (Nehemiah 7:12). The context shows that these distinct Elams are recognizable by their genealogies or their role in the events of that time.
H5867B.origine: The name Elam means "eternity" or "age" in Hebrew. Its etymology suggests a notion of duration or permanence. This name, borne by several ancestors of families, was quite common in Israel after the exile.
H5867B.emploi: The name Elam appears seven times in the Hebrew Bible, exclusively in the books of Ezra and Nehemiah, which recount the return of the exiles from Babylon (around 538 BC). Each mention refers to a different Elam: some are heads of families whose descendants are listed during the count of returns (Ezra 2:7; Ezra 2:31; Nehemiah 7:12), others are individuals active in the spiritual renewal of the people, such as Shecaniah son of Jehiel, himself a son of an Elam, who calls for repentance and separation from mixed marriages (Ezra 10:2). These passages show that several lineages bore this name and played a role in the reconstruction of the Jewish community after the exile.

sens: Son of Shem, ancestor of the peoples of antiquity
H5867C.detail: Elam is one of the five sons of Shem listed in the genealogy of the peoples after the Flood (Genesis 10:22). He also appears in the parallel list of 1 Chronicles 1:17. These biblical genealogies establish the lineages of the nations that dispersed after Babel, and Elam represents the supposed ancestor of the people of the same name, significant in the ancient history of the Near East.
H5867C.origine: The name Elam literally means "eternity" in Hebrew. The historical people of Elam, established in the region of Khuzestan (western Iran today), were well known to Mesopotamian civilizations. The biblical name refers to this founding ancestor, anchoring the history of the people in the universal genealogy descending from Noah through Shem.
H5867C.emploi: Elam appears only twice in the Bible, both in genealogical lists of the sons of Shem: in Genesis 10:22 and 1 Chronicles 1:17. These two passages essentially provide the same information, listing his brothers Asshur, Arphaxad, Lud, and Aram, confirming that Elam held an important place among the ancestors of the eastern peoples recognized in biblical tradition. No specific account is provided about his personal life.
H5867C.portee: This name reminds us that the Bible considers the peoples of antiquity as stemming from one human family, descended from Noah. It emphasizes the unity of humanity and God's plan that embraces all peoples in the history of salvation.

sens: Son of Shashak, of the tribe of Benjamin
H5867G.detail: He is a Benjaminite mentioned only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 8:24, among the descendants of Shashak. He had several brothers, including Ishpan, Eber, and Eliel. This character lived during the time of the divided monarchy, but nothing else is known about him except his name and his place in the genealogy of Benjamin.
H5867G.origine: The name means "eternity" in Hebrew. It is a theophoric name that expresses the idea of an endless duration, a quality attributed only to God.
