H5867G.emploi: Elam is a proper name that appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 8:24. It designates a man of the tribe of Benjamin, son of Shashak, of whom nothing else is known except his genealogical listing. No act or particular event is attached to him.

sens: Son of Meshelemiah, temple porter during the divided monarchy
H5867H.detail: Elam is a Levite, son of Meshelemiah, who served as a porter (gatekeeper) of the temple in Jerusalem during the divided monarchy of Israel. He appears in the genealogy of the temple porters established during the time of King David, and was one of the brothers in a large family (Zechariah, Jediael, Zebadiah, Jathniel, Jehohanan, and Elihoenai) all engaged in the service of the temple (1 Chronicles 26:3).
H5867H.origine: The name Elam literally means "eternity" in Hebrew. It is a theophoric name that reflects faith in the permanence and stability of God. This same name was borne by other biblical figures, including an ancestor of the peoples mentioned in patriarchal times (Genesis 10:22).
H5867H.emploi: Elam son of Meshelemiah appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 26:3, where he is named as the fifth son of Meshelemiah among the temple porters. This mention fits within the context of the organization of the temple servants established by David, revealing the administrative and religious structure of Israelite worship. His brief but precise appearance in this genealogical record shows the importance of Levitical service and the transmission of sacred responsibilities within temple families.

sens: Leader of the people during the restoration after the Babylonian exile
H5867I.detail: Elam is a character mentioned only once in the entire Bible, in Nehemiah 10:14, among the leaders of the people who seal the covenant with God at the time of their return from exile. He is listed among the notable figures who solemnly commit to observing the Law of the Lord.
H5867I.origine: The name Elam means "eternity" in Hebrew. It is a proper name that also appears in the Old Testament to designate an ancient territory and people (see Genesis 10:22), but this character in Nehemiah is distinct from those earlier usages.
H5867I.emploi: This character Elam appears only once in the Scriptures: in Nehemiah 10:14, during the return from exile. He is counted among the leaders who acknowledge God's authority and commit to respecting His Law. Nothing else is known about him other than this official role at this pivotal time in Israel's history.

sens: A man from the time of the Exile and the Return
Temple singer during Nehemiah's time
H5867J.detail:
1. Elam is a man mentioned only once in the Bible, during the return from exile to Jerusalem. He is part of a list of musicians and temple singers (Nehemiah 12:42). His name appears among those involved in the celebrations of the restoration of the walls of Jerusalem, alongside other names that sound like Levites or worship singers.
2. The name Elam means "eternity" in Hebrew. It is a theophoric name (bearing a divine reality) that evokes stability and permanence, qualities deemed precious at a time when Israel was rediscovering its roots after exile.
H5867J.origine: Elam is cited only once in the Bible, in Nehemiah 12:42, among the musicians who participated in the celebration of the restoration of the walls of Jerusalem after the return from the Babylonian exile. The context indicates that he was one of the temple singers, a member of the Levitical community responsible for liturgical service. His singular appearance in this account reflects the reorganization of Israelite worship at the time of reconstruction.
H5867J.emploi: Elam is mentioned only once in the Bible, in Nehemiah 12:42, among the musicians who participated in the celebration of the restoration of the walls of Jerusalem after the return from the Babylonian exile. The context indicates that he was one of the temple singers, a member of the Levitical community responsible for liturgical service. His singular appearance in this account reflects the reorganization of Israelite worship at the time of reconstruction.

sens: Hot and violent breath
Fervor of the wind
Desiccating force
H5868B.detail:
1. The word refers to the hot and powerful breath that escapes as a force. In Isaiah 11:15, the Lord raises His hand "blowing violently" upon the river of Egypt: it is a fierce, hot, and drying breath that divides the waters like a burning desert wind.
2. This burning breath also evokes the action of intense heat that dries and exhausts. It is the image of a powerful natural force, one that renders the land arid and strips it of its moisture.
3. By extension, the word can express any fervor or desiccating force — a breath of death or judgment, which consumes and destroys.
H5868B.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root evoking heat and breath. It is related to the idea of burning respiration, of ardent breath. Hebrew uses this word to depict intense natural forces: the desert wind, the heat of the sun, anything that emanates from a burning and desiccating energy.
H5868B.emploi: This word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Isaiah 11:15. It is found in a vision of future judgment and restoration: the Lord, in His omnipotence, dries up the river of Egypt by a sovereign gesture, as He breathes violence and authority. It is a poetic and rare word, used to express the superhuman energy of divine judgment.
H5868B.portee: This passage reminds the reader that God has control over all the forces of nature: a simple breath of His will transforms the course of waters. It is an image of His absolute sovereignty over the created world and the judgment that is to come. For the Christian, this verse invites recognition that no earthly power can resist the word of God.

sens: The physical organ of vision, located in the face
The act of seeing, looking, observing something
The ability to perceive, understand, discern
Interest, attention, consideration given to someone or something
Presence, being under someone's gaze
Expression, the brightness of the face that reveals feelings or inner nature
H5869A.detail:
1. The eye is primarily the physical organ of vision. In Genesis 3:5, the serpent promises that Adam and Eve's eyes "will be opened" — meaning they will see with clarity. The Bible also speaks of the aging of this organ: in Genesis 48:10, Isaac's eyes "had grown dim."

2. To look means to fix one's attention on something. When it says "with your own eyes you will look" (Psalms 91:8), it means one will contemplate an event. It is the action of looking, the movement of attention.

3. The eye symbolizes the ability to understand and judge. In Deuteronomy 16:19, it warns against accepting bribes, as this "blinds the eyes" — meaning one loses discernment, the ability to judge rightly.

4. The eyes express interest or favor towards someone. "Finding grace in someone's eyes" (Genesis 6:8, Genesis 39:4) means being looked upon with favor, being appreciated.

5. The "presence" is often rendered by "eyes": "under your eyes" or "before your eyes" means "in your presence." For example, in Deuteronomy 11:12, the land is "under the eyes of the Lord."

6. The expression of the face reflects the soul. In Song of Solomon 4:9, the "gaze" (the expressive eyes) of the beloved captivates the heart of the lover. It is the beauty and brightness of the eyes that speaks.
H5869A.origine: The Hebrew word עַיִן comes from an ancient root meaning "to see" or "to look." Ancient Semitic peoples associated the eye with the act of seeing, but also with consciousness and discernment. In Hebrew, several expressions use "eyes" to speak of understanding: "the eyes of your heart" (expression in Ephesians 1:18, translated from Greek) follows this logic. The Hebrew word will be translated into Greek in the New Testament as ὀφθαλμός (ophthalmos), from which our French term "ophtalmologie" derives.
H5869A.emploi: The word "eye" appears 443 times in the Hebrew Bible, making it an extremely common word. It primarily denotes the physical organ (Genesis 3:5, 3:7; Leviticus 24:20: "eye for eye"). But very quickly, the eye becomes a metaphor: to see means to know, understand, judge. "Finding grace in the eyes" (Genesis 6:8, Genesis 39:4) expresses favor and esteem. In the Psalms and poetry, the eye embodies vigilance and moral discernment — God's gaze watches over all (Deuteronomy 11:12). The closed or dimmed eye symbolizes the inability to perceive truth or justice. The context shows that the Bible uses this word to speak of physical vision, certainly, but also of intelligence, will, and spiritual consciousness.
H5869A.portee: Understanding the biblical symbolism of the eye helps us discern how the Bible speaks of spiritual perception. When Jesus says, "Blessed are the eyes that see what you see" (Matthew 13:16), He speaks of faith — the ability to recognize God's presence. Meditating on the eye in Scripture reminds us that our inner life — what we think, what we value — is reflected in our eyes and in our gaze upon the world. It is a call to purify our vision, to see as God sees.

sens: Natural water point from which water springs
Access to a water reserve, well or fountain
Gate of a city providing access to a water source
H5869B.detail:
1. A spring is a place where water naturally flows from the ground — it is the origin of the living water that supplies the area. It is a precious resource in an arid country like Judea.
2. The word also refers to a water reserve or an artificially constructed well: a water point built to accumulate or draw water, like the king's pool mentioned in Nehemiah 2:14.
3. In Jerusalem, the "gate of the spring" (Nehemiah 3:15) is one of the main gates of the wall: it gets its name from the fact that it provides access to a vital water source for the city. It is through this gate that one would go down to the spring of Siloam.
H5869B.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root meaning "to see" or "to look" — the basic image may evoke a place that is watched or observed, or simply a visible location where water appears. The same Hebrew root can also mean "eye" in other contexts, maintaining the idea of "that which appears" or "that which is seen to emerge."
H5869B.emploi: The word appears in the Bible only three times, all in Nehemiah 2-3 and 12, during the reconstruction of the wall of Jerusalem after the exile. It systematically refers to the "gate of the spring" — one of the gates of the city. Nehemiah 3:15 specifies that it is the gate leading to the spring of Siloam, the main water reserve of Jerusalem. The three occurrences show that this gate was an important landmark in the city's topography. The context is always practical and urban: fortifications, gates, city paths.
H5869B.portee: This gate of the spring reminds readers that water is a vital issue in the life of Jerusalem. It is also a symbol: in the Bible, living water often represents life, blessing, the Spirit of God. This gate, a passage to the water source, invites one to seek in God the true source of life.

sens: Water point where groundwater naturally springs
Place where water flows permanently and regularly
That which feeds, that which provides a continuous supply
H5869G.detail:
1. A spring is a place where water naturally emerges from the ground, fed by underground reserves. It is living water that springs forth, unlike a cistern that simply collects rainwater. In Jerusalem, the dragon's spring (Nehemiah 2:13) was a strategic water point that Nehemiah inspects while surveying the ruined walls.
2. By extension, a spring refers to any water supply that flows continuously and regularly. These water points were vital in dry lands: they allowed a city to survive during a siege, hence their military and political importance. This is why Nehemiah carefully examines them during his reconnaissance of Jerusalem.
3. Figuratively, a spring represents the origin from which something comes — that which sustains, that which gives life. In the Bible, God is presented as the source of life, forgiveness, and wisdom.
H5869G.origine: The Hebrew word עַיִן ('ayîn) literally means "eye," probably explaining its application to the spring: a point through which water "looks" at the world, or from which visible water emerges from the underground world. This image of water springing from the earth, emerging like a gaze, explains why the same word designates both the organ of vision and the spring. In Hebrew thought, freely flowing water is always a sign of life and blessing, which is why the springs of cities are so precious.
H5869G.emploi: The word appears here to describe an identifiable water point in Jerusalem. Nehemiah, the governor sent to restore the city, first inspects its fortifications by passing through the dragon's spring — a known geographical landmark, probably one of the springs that Jerusalem used for its supply. The context shows that springs were of primary importance for the defensive integrity of a city, as they provided essential fresh water and their control was crucial.
H5869G.portee: For the Christian reader, this detail reminds us that God cares for the physical needs of His people. The springing water that God provides becomes a symbol of His generosity and the life He gives. It is an invitation to recognize how God provides for essential resources, both materially and spiritually.

sens: Organ of vision of the human body
One who looks, one who sees
Expression of the face that reveals inner feelings
Gaze, attention, consideration of someone
That which pleases or displeases, value judgment
Presence, sight (being in someone's presence)
H5869H.detail:
1. The eye is the physical organ that allows one to see: it is the opening through which one looks at the world. Thus, a man may have a blemish on his eye, a visible infirmity (Leviticus 21:20).
2. The eye represents the person who sees, the one who observes and judges. When it is said that something is done "in the eyes" of someone, it is that person who sees and evaluates the action (1 Kings 21:20).
3. The eye expresses the feelings of the one who looks: a gaze can show pride, disdain, or tenderness. For example, when Hagar becomes pregnant and looks at her mistress with disdain, it is the inner feeling that is reflected in her gaze (Genesis 16:4).
4. The eye designates the gaze and attention that someone gives to a person: "to find favor in the eyes of" means to be looked upon with favor, to have the esteem of the one who looks (Genesis 39:4).
5. That which pleases or displeases is what finds favor or contempt in the eyes of God or men. Doing what is wrong "in the eyes of the Lord" means acting contrary to what God considers good (Deuteronomy 12:25).
6. The eye can signify concrete presence: "in the presence of" (literally "under the eye of") expresses being before someone, visible to their eyes (Genesis 23:11).
H5869H.origine: The Hebrew word עַיִן comes from a very ancient root that expresses the idea of seeing and looking. It is one of the simplest and most universal words in Semitic languages. The basic image is that of the physical organ of vision, but the word quickly extended to denote anything related to sight: attention, judgment, presence. It is a very vivid word in Hebrew texts, omnipresent in the stories of Genesis and in the Law.
H5869H.emploi: The word "eye" appears about 196 times in the Old Testament, making it one of the most frequent terms in the Hebrew Bible. Its uses are distributed across all narrative and legislative books: Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, Deuteronomy, Judges, Samuel, Kings. Its physical use is direct (a blemish on the eye, having a good or bad eye). But the meaning unfolds especially in frequent expressions: "to find grace in the eyes of," "to be beautiful in the eyes of," "to displease in the eyes of." The eye metaphorically becomes the seat of judgment, esteem, and moral value. In God, the "eyes" represent His ability to see what is hidden, to know and judge justly.
H5869H.portee: For the believer, understanding that our actions are done "in the eyes of the Lord" is crucial: it reminds us that God sees everything, even what is hidden from men, and that He judges with justice. The word "eye" also invites us to examine what "finds grace" in His sight, that is, how to live in a way that is pleasing to the Lord. This notion transforms the Christian's conscience by reminding them of God's vigilant and benevolent presence in their life.

sens: Organ of vision of the body
What appears, what seems good or bad to someone
The judgment, the appreciation of a person
Favor, approval
H5869I.detail: 1. The physical organ that allows one to see: "we were in their sight like grasshoppers" (Numbers 13:33) evokes real sight, but also how one sees oneself and how others see us. 2. What pleases or displeases someone's view, their opinion on what is good or acceptable: "this displeased him" (1 Samuel 18:8) or "this would be pleasing in your sight" (2 Samuel 19:6) show that one judges something based on the feeling it provokes. 3. The moral or personal judgment of a person: "He did what was right in the sight of the Lord" (2 Kings 22:2) means he acted according to what God judges as good and just. 4. Kindness and approval towards someone: "The young woman pleased him" (Esther 2:9) means she found favor, that she was looked upon with kindness.
H5869I.origine: The Hebrew word עַיִן (ayin) is very ancient and comes from a root meaning the organ of sight. But from biblical times, this word extends from the concrete meaning (the physical eye) to the abstract meaning: the eye becomes the seat of judgment, taste, and favor. That is why "in his eyes" means "in his judgment" and "to find favor in his eyes" means "to be approved." This extension makes the word a bridge between physical sensation and thought.
H5869I.emploi: The word eye appears 142 times in the biblical Hebrew text, primarily in the literal sense (to see, to look). But very often it takes on a figurative meaning: to judge something as good or bad, pleasing or displeasing. One says "this pleases his eyes" or "this does not please his eyes"; one does "what is good in his eyes" or "what is right in the eyes of God." This metaphorical use is particularly frequent in historical narratives (1 and 2 Samuel, 2 Kings). The legal context also shows the eye as the seat of judgment in decisions (Deuteronomy 24:1: the husband who finds "a cause for divorce" in his eyes).
H5869I.portee: For the Christian, this word invites reflection on judgment: what our physical eyes see profoundly influences us, but the essential is what our heart and the eye of God think. The expression "in his eyes" reminds us that every action can please or displease God, whose gaze sees beyond appearances. It is an invitation to seek what is right "in the eyes of the Lord," and not just in our own eyes.

sens: The organ of the body that allows one to see
What is presented to view, what is perceived directly
The presence or gaze of a person (being before their eyes)
The intention, judgment, favor, or suspicion of a person
Mental and spiritual faculties (discernment, attention, conscience)
H5869J.detail:
1. The eye is the physical organ of vision. It is the simplest and most direct sense of the word in Hebrew, describing the instrument by which we see the world.

2. What is before the eyes is what is visible, what appears on the surface. In Exodus 10:5, the locusts will cover the "surface" of the land — literally, what shows to the eyes.

3. Being in someone's eyes means being in their presence, under their direct gaze. When Moses says to Israel "according to all that He has done for you in your sight in Egypt" (Deuteronomy 1:30), he speaks of the visible and attested wonders before them.

4. The eye represents a person's judgment and appreciation: what is "good in their eyes" pleases, what is "bad in their eyes" displeases. It is the intention recognized in the other: in 1 Samuel 21:13, David appears mad "in their eyes," he shows madness through his actions.

5. The eye symbolizes the faculties of the heart, soul, and spirit — conscience, discernment, spiritual attention. God "sets everything before your eyes" (Psalms 50:21) means He makes you see the truth and makes you aware of your actions.
H5869J.origine: The Hebrew word עַיִן (a.yin) is ancient and universal in Semitic languages. It designates the physical organ, but quickly acquired figurative meanings: the eye as the seat of judgment, intention, desire, and conscience. This extension of meaning comes from observation: the one who looks at you judges and evaluates you; the one who sees something approves or rejects it.
H5869J.emploi: The word appears 28 times in the provided passages, mainly in the Pentateuch (Genesis, Exodus, Deuteronomy) and the books of the Old Covenant. In Genesis 23:18, "in the eyes of" means "in the presence of and with the approval of" (the Hittites). In Deuteronomy 1:30, "in your sight" means "you who have seen." In 1 Samuel 21:13, "in their eyes" describes how others perceive him. The expression "good/bad in the eyes of" is very common to indicate whether something pleases or displeases God or a person. The word thus transitions from the concrete (the organ, the surface) to the abstract (the presence, judgment, conscience).
H5869J.portee: Understanding the biblical use of "the eye" enriches our spiritual reading. When the Bible speaks of seeing in the eyes of God, it means that God sees and judges — we are responsible before His gaze. The eye also symbolizes our spiritual discernment: do we have our eyes open to perceive the reality of God and His will? It is an invitation to honesty, transparency, and a living awareness of the divine presence.

sens: Evil, sin, injustice
The weight of sin seen as a burden or affliction
What offends God and troubles the conscience
H5869K.detail:
1. The word designates moral evil, sin, injustice towards God or one's neighbor. It is the opposite of justice and righteousness. In 2 Samuel 16:12, David speaks of his affliction and asks God to compensate for it, which shows that iniquity weighs on the one who suffers it or commits it, like a burden to bear.
2. Iniquity is seen as something palpable, objective, that exists in the land or in the hearts of people. In Zechariah 5:6, the prophet sees a measure (the ephah) containing the iniquity of an entire people, as if sin were a substance that can be contained, weighed, and from which one must rid oneself.
3. It is also the state of guilt and separation from God that sin produces: iniquity afflicts the one who bears it and demands restitution or forgiveness.
H5869K.origine: The Hebrew word עַיִן (ayîn) comes from a root meaning "to turn aside," "to deviate." Iniquity is therefore what deviates from the right path, what turns away from justice. This same word appears in the psalms and the prophets to describe guilt and moral evil, often in parallel with other terms for sin (like חטא, sin proper). The image is one of deviation, of perversion.
H5869K.emploi: This word appears 2 times in the provided passages. In 2 Samuel 16:12, it describes the affliction that David endures as a consequence of iniquity (the curses of others), and he hopes that God will see it and compensate him. In Zechariah 5:6, it refers to the collective iniquity of the people, symbolically contained in a measure and destined to be removed from the land. These two uses show that iniquity is not abstract: it has concrete consequences (affliction, trouble) and concerns the heart of God.
H5869K.portee: Understanding this word invites the reader to see that sin is not a mere moral failing, but a reality that afflicts, weighs, and from which only God can deliver us. It is a call to recognize the weight of evil within us and around us, and to seek justice and forgiveness from God. The symbol of iniquity being contained and removed (Zechariah 5) speaks of hope: God acts to remove evil from the world.

sens: A water source that springs from the ground
A place where water is drawn
An image of fertility and abundance
The one who is the origin of something
H5869M.detail:
1. A source is a point of water that naturally springs from the ground, where water emerges from the heart of the earth. This is a phenomenon that every traveler in Israel knows well: when crossing arid regions, one seeks these life-saving sources. In Genesis 16:7, the angel finds Hagar "near a spring of water in the desert." 

2. It is also the concrete place where people come to draw water daily. Rebekah, in Genesis 24:16, goes down to the source with her pitcher to fill it — this is an ordinary act in ancient life, but it is there that she meets Abraham's servant. 

3. A source represents life, nourishment, and prosperity. When it is said in Genesis 49:22 that Joseph is "the branch of a fruitful tree near a source," he is imagined surrounded by fruits and abundance, blessed and fruitful like this place of water that makes plants grow. 

4. Figuratively, a source denotes the origin or cause of something — the one upon whom everything depends, like a source from which waters spring.
H5869M.origine: The Hebrew word "ayin" comes from the root "ayin" (עַיִן) which evokes the idea of that which emerges, that which comes out. A source is literally what "comes out" or "springs" from the earth. It is a simple and universal word: every ancient civilization in a land of springs and streams knows this vital phenomenon.
H5869M.emploi: This word appears mainly in the narratives of the patriarchs and in the descriptions of the landscapes of Israel. It occurs 16 times in the Segond translations, concentrated in the early books. It always designates a natural, concrete water source — never figurative in Hebrew. It appears especially where water is scarce: in the desert (Genesis 16:7), or as a treasure of a region (Numbers 33:9: "at Elim, twelve springs of water and seventy palm trees"). It is also the setting for encounters: Elisha goes there (2 Chronicles 32:3), one comes to fetch water. Genesis 49:22 uses it as an image of blessing.
H5869M.portee: The source reminds us that life comes from God alone, just as water springs from the earth. In a desert land, a source is a daily miracle and a gift without which one would not survive. It speaks to us of dependence and grace: we do not create water; it is given to us. Meditating on the source invites us to see in the small goods of each day a generous hand that nourishes us.

sens: The organ of the body that allows seeing
That which sees, observes, vision
The appearance, the aspect of something
The gaze, attention, surveillance
H5870.detail:
1. The eye is the physical organ of vision. When Nebuchadnezzar "lifted his eyes to heaven" (Daniel 4:34), he turned his gaze in a direction to see. The eye can also refer to the eyes as features of the face: the little horn had "eyes like the eyes of a man" (Daniel 7:8), which gave it a human and terrifying appearance. 

2. The eye represents the ability to observe, to see what is happening. When it is said that "the eye of God was watching over the elders of the Jews" (Ezra 5:5), it means that God saw everything, that He watched over and protected His people — the eye of God is His vigilant attention. 

3. The eye can also evoke the general appearance of a creature. The horn had "a greater appearance than the others" (Daniel 7:20): literally, it "had eyes" and a more imposing presence. The eyes contribute to the aspect that is judged when seen.
H5870.origine: The Aramaic word עַיִן (ayin) is the Aramaic form of the Hebrew word עַיִן (ayin). Both come from an ancient root meaning the eye, the organ of vision. It is a very ancient word, shared by Semitic languages. The Aramaic word appears in the Aramaic sections of Daniel and Ezra.
H5870.emploi: The word appears four times in the Aramaic texts of the Bible: twice in Daniel and twice in Ezra. It is used in the literal sense (the eyes of Nebuchadnezzar, the eyes of the horn) and also in the figurative sense, particularly to describe the eye of God that watches and protects. In the visions of Daniel, the eye or eyes characterize supernatural creatures, giving these creatures a strange and unsettling appearance. The word is rare in Biblical Aramaic, as these books contain few passages in Aramaic.
H5870.portee: The expression "the eye of God watches" reminds believers that God sees everything, that nothing can be hidden from Him, and that He protects His people even in the midst of captivity. It is a comfort for those who suffer: they are not forgotten. The eyes of the strange creatures in the visions highlight their strange nature and chaotic power, in contrast to the watching eye of the eternal God.

sens: a water source in the region of Canaan
a landmark on the eastern border of the Promised Land
H5871G.detail: 1. Aïn is a source, that is, a place where water springs from the ground, a precious resource in arid land. In Numbers 34:11, it appears in the description of the borders of the Promised Land: "it shall descend from Shepham to Riblah, on the east of Aïn" — this water point precisely marks where the eastern boundary of Canaan lies. 2. For the people of Israel receiving their inheritance, this source serves as a geographical landmark, like a visible and permanent signal that cannot be ignored. It is also called Rimmon, which may indicate that it was located near a place of that name.
H5871G.origine: The Hebrew word עַיִן (ayin) literally means "source" or "fountain" — the place where water springs from the earth. It is also the word that designates the "eye," as both are openings through which flows that which gives life (water for the earth, vision for man). In Canaan, where water is scarce, a source bears a proper name and becomes a landmark known to all.
H5871G.emploi: Aïn appears only once in the Bible, in Numbers 34:11, where God enumerates the precise borders of the Promised Land to the Israelites. It is mentioned as an eastern boundary point, between Riblah and the Sea of Kinnereth (the Sea of Galilee). It is a real, geographically identifiable place that helps readers visualize the contours of the promised territory.

sens: City in the south of Judah, in the Negev
City allotted to the tribe of Simeon
City given to the Levitical priests
H5871H.detail:
1. Aïn is a city located in the southern region of the territory of Judah, in an area called the Negev (the dry region of the south). It appears in the lists of holy cities as an identified and named locality, often mentioned alongside Rimmon (Joshua 15:32; Joshua 19:7). 
2. During the division of the land among the twelve tribes of Israel after the conquest, Aïn was allotted to the tribe of Simeon as part of its territorial inheritance (Joshua 19:7; 1 Chronicles 4:32). 
3. Although initially given to Simeon, Aïn was later ceded to the Levitical priests for them to dwell in and serve, according to Moses' instructions: it thus figures among the cities of refuge and the cities of priests (Joshua 21:16).
H5871H.origine: The Hebrew word עַיִן ('ayin) literally means "source" or "fountain" — a point of water springing from the earth. It is a descriptive name: Aïn was likely an oasis or a water-providing place, a precious and rare resource in the desert of the Negev. This geographical name reflects a vital reality of the landscape.
H5871H.emploi: Aïn appears four times in the Hebrew Bible, exclusively in texts related to the division of territory among the tribes after the conquest (Joshua 15 and 19, and 1 Chronicles 4). It is systematically cited with Rimmon, with the two names sometimes merged into "En-Rimmon" (fountain of the pomegranate). Its status evolves in the narrative: first a city of Simeon, it becomes a Levitical city. These administrative mentions show its administrative importance in the territorial organization of the kingdom of Judah.

sens: City of Israel located in the Judean desert, on the western shore of the Dead Sea
H5872.detail: 1. En-Gedi is a city in the Judean desert, situated on the western shore of the Dead Sea. Its name means "spring of the kid" in Hebrew, evoking the freshwater springs that burst forth in this arid place. It appears in the list of cities of the tribe of Judah (Joshua 15:62).
H5872.origine: The Hebrew name עֵין גֶּדִי (En-Gedi) is composed of two elements: עֵין (en, "spring" or "fountain") and גֶּדִי (gedi, "kid"). This name reflects the geography of the place, rich in water springs in the midst of the desert, a vital resource that allowed an oasis to develop. The city was also known as Hazazon-Tamar, "cut palm" (2 Chronicles 20:2), two names designating the same site.
H5872.emploi: En-Gedi is mentioned six times in the Bible. It is first cited as one of the fortified cities of Judah (Joshua 15:62). It becomes famous in the story of David, who finds refuge in the caves and "strongholds" during his flight from Saul (1 Samuel 24:1-2). The Song of Songs praises the beauty of its vineyards (Song of Songs 1:14), suggesting the remarkable fertility of this oasis in the desert. In Ezekiel's prophetic vision, En-Gedi marks the starting point of abundant fishing along the transformed waters (Ezekiel 47:10), an image of restoration and blessing.
H5872.portee: In the Bible, En-Gedi symbolizes both a refuge in times of trial and an oasis of grace in a dry land. The story of David seeking asylum there illustrates how God provides for our needs in the very heart of spiritual desert. The prosperity of its vineyards and the abundance of fish prophesied remind us that God's blessing transforms barren lands into sources of life.

sens: City in the plain of Judah
H5873G.detail: En-Gannim is a small city in the low region of Judah, mentioned in the list of cities allocated to the tribe of Judah during the division of the territory after the conquest of Canaan (Joshua 15:34). It was located in the coastal plain, between Zanoach and Tappuah.
H5873G.origine: The Hebrew name literally means "spring of the garden" or "fountain of the garden": "en" means "spring" or "fountain" in Hebrew, and "gannim" means "gardens." This name likely evokes the presence of a spring and irrigated crops in this locality.
H5873G.emploi: En-Gannim appears only once in the Bible, in the enumeration of the cities of the tribe of Judah (Joshua 15:34). It is listed among the towns in the region of the Shephelah, the low plain of Judah, between cities like Zanoach and Tappuah. This administrative context suggests that it was a locality of modest importance, well identified geographically by the biblical authors.

sens: City in the territory of Issachar allocated to the Gershonite Levites
H5873H.detail: 1. En-Gannim (whose name means "Fountain of the Garden") was a city located on the border of the territory of Issachar. It is mentioned during the division of the promised land among the tribes of Israel (Joshua 19:21), where it is listed among the cities allocated to Issachar. This city was later designated as one of the Levitical cities given to the Gershonites, Levites responsible for the service of the Tabernacle (Joshua 21:29), which shows its religious importance in the life of Israel.
H5873H.origine: The Hebrew name עֵין גַּנִּים (en gan.nim) is composed of two words: עֵין (en, "fountain" or "spring") and גַּנִּים (gan.nim, "gardens"). This name evokes a water source in a planted or cultivated area, a common image in Palestine where water was precious. The city bore this descriptive name due to its geographical location, likely near an abundant spring allowing for the cultivation of gardens.
H5873H.emploi: En-Gannim appears only twice in the Bible, both in the book of Joshua at the time of the land division. First, it is listed among the cities of the territory of Issachar (Joshua 19:21), during the systematic description of the borders and cities of each tribe. Secondly, it is mentioned as one of the Levitical cities given to the sons of Gershon (Gershonites) with its suburbs (Joshua 21:29). These two appearances show that En-Gannim was a secondary locality, recognized for its status as a Levitical city rather than for major events.
H5873H.portee: This city reminds us that God had planned places of rest and properties for the Levites who served the people in worship and teaching. The fact that a city without its own territory (the Levites did not receive land inheritance as a tribe) still received cities and pastures shows divine providence towards those who dedicated themselves to His service.

sens: City of Canaan in the territory of Issachar
Place where a woman who conjured the dead resided
Site of a battle where Israel's enemies were defeated
H5874.detail:
1. En-Dor is a city located in Canaan, in the territory of the tribe of Issachar, but it was conquered and possessed by the tribe of Manasseh (Joshua 17:11). It was one of several fortified cities with their surrounding villages that Manasseh occupied.

2. En-Dor is best known as the place where a woman capable of conjuring the dead lived, a necromancer whom King Saul secretly consulted to know his future (1 Samuel 28:7). It is here that Saul asked this woman to summon the deceased prophet Samuel.

3. En-Dor is also the site of a victory for Israel against its enemies: the psalmist recalls that the adversaries of God's people were destroyed there and became "dung for the earth" (Psalms 83:11), an image of total defeat and humiliation.
H5874.origine: The name En-Dor literally means "fountain of Dor" or "spring of Dor" ("en" meaning "fountain" and "Dor" likely designating a place or region). It is a Hebrew geographical name that precisely designates this locality in Upper Galilee, near Mount Tabor.
H5874.emploi: En-Dor appears three times in the Bible. In Joshua 17:11, it is listed among the cities in the territory of Issachar that Manasseh possessed with their surrounding villages. The most famous usage is in 1 Samuel 28:7, where Saul seeks to consult a woman who "conjures the dead" at En-Dor to know his fate before battle. This is a dramatic moment where the king of Israel, desperate and rejected by God, transgresses his own law by resorting to necromancy. Finally, in Psalms 83:11, the psalmist invokes the destruction of God's enemies at En-Dor as an act of divine justice.
H5874.portee: En-Dor reminds us of the limits of human power and the spiritual danger of seeking to circumvent God. The account of Saul at En-Dor shows how despair and a lack of listening to God can lead to resorting to forbidden practices. It is also a symbol of God's victory over the enemies of His people, encouraging the believer to trust in divine justice and protection.

sens: Water source in ancient Israel, near Lehi
H5875.detail: En-Hakkoré is the name of a spring that God caused to gush forth from the rock to quench Samson's thirst after he had killed a thousand enemies with a donkey's jawbone. The account in Judges 15:19 specifies that God "split open the hollow place that is at Lehi, and water came out from it" — a miracle of deliverance and support from the Lord for his weary servant.
H5875.origine: The Hebrew name עֵין הַקּוֹרֵא literally means "the spring of the one who cries" or "the spring of the call." It comes from the word עֵין ("spring") and the verb קרא ("to cry, to call"). This name reminds us that Samson, thirsty and exhausted, cried out to God, and God answered his call by causing this miraculous water to flow from the rock.
H5875.emploi: This spring appears only once in the Bible, in Judges 15:19. It marks a key moment in the story of Samson: after his feat of killing a thousand Philistines, the Israelite hero finds himself exhausted and dying of thirst. God does not abandon him but intervenes directly to refresh him. The text even notes that this spring "exists to this day at Lehi," suggesting that it was a real geographical landmark known to ancient Israelites and the contemporaries of the author of the Book of Judges.
H5875.portee: This spring testifies to God's faithfulness to those He has called to serve Him. By responding to Samson's desperate call, God shows that He does not leave His servants without help, even in their greatest distress. It is a symbol of divine provision and the Lord's support in times of trial.

sens: Border town of the territory of Issachar
H5876.detail: En-Hadda is one of the towns assigned to the tribe of Issachar during the division of the land of Canaan among the twelve tribes of Israel (Joshua 19:21). Its name literally means "swift spring" or "living fountain," suggesting the presence of a clear and abundant water source at this location — a valuable resource in the region of Mount Gilboa.
H5876.origine: The Hebrew name עֵין חַדָּה (En-Hadda) is composed of עֵין ("spring" or "fountain") and חַדָּה, which expresses the idea of liveliness and swiftness. This composition reveals the importance of water for the inhabitants and the topography of the place.
H5876.emploi: En-Hadda appears only once in the Bible, in the passage where Joshua lists the towns of the territory of Issachar. It is mentioned alongside Remeth, En-Gannim, and Beth-Patsets, four towns that mark the boundaries or constitute important points of the territory assigned to this tribe. Its absence from the rest of the Bible suggests that it was a minor locality, though strategically positioned on the border of the tribe.

sens: Fortified city in the territory of Naphtali
H5877.detail: En-Hatsor is a fortified city assigned to the tribe of Naphtali during the division of the Promised Land. Its name means "fountain of Hatsor" or "spring of Hatsor," which likely indicates a connection to another locality called Hatsor. It appears in the list of walled cities intended for the defense of the territory (Joshua 19:37).
H5877.origine: The name En-Hatsor is composed of two Hebrew elements: "en" means "fountain" or "spring" of water, and "Hatsor" is the name of another city. This compound suggests that this locality was known for its water source or that it depended on another city called Hatsor. Localities bearing the name Hatsor existed in northern Israel.
H5877.emploi: En-Hatsor appears only once in the Bible, in Joshua 19:37, as one of the fortified cities assigned to the tribe of Naphtali during the division of the Promised Land. It is mentioned amidst a list of cities intended to serve as defensive strongholds for this northern tribe of Israel.

sens: Water source in Israel, camping site
Strategic place where Gideon gathered his army
H5878.detail: Harod is a spring (well or fountain) located in Israel, probably in the Jezreel Valley. It is the place where Gideon and his army camped before fighting the Midianites (Judges 7:1). The name literally means "spring of Herod" or "spring of trembling." This strategic site, near the hill of Moreh, served as a gathering point for the Israelite troops before their miraculous victory against the Midianite invaders.
H5878.origine: The Hebrew word עֵין (en) means "spring" or "eye" (water gushing forth like an eye from the ground), and חֲרֹד (charod) refers to the idea of trembling or fear. The place bears a name that perhaps evokes the gushing spring or an association with the fear and combat that took place there.
H5878.emploi: Harod appears only once in the Bible, in Judges 7:1, where it is mentioned as the camping site of Gideon and his people before the battle against Midian. It is a precise geographical landmark: the spring is located near the hill of Moreh, in the valley. This site holds historical and strategic importance, as it is where God selected Gideon's warriors for victory over a much larger army.
H5878.portee: This place reminds us that God chooses His moments and places to manifest His power. The camping at Harod marks the starting point of a miraculous deliverance: with only 300 men, Gideon defeated the Midianites through divine strategy. For the believer, Harod symbolizes the place where God shows that victory does not depend on numbers or strength, but on trust in Him.

sens: Town in the lowlands of Judah
H5879G.detail: 1. Énaïm is a small town located in the lowland region (the Shephelah) of the territory of Judah. Its name literally means "double spring" or "two springs," probably because it was situated near two water sources. It is where Tamar sat by the roadside to Timnah (Genesis 38:14).
H5879G.origine: The Hebrew name עֵינָם (Énaïm) comes from עַיִן (aïn), which means "spring" or "eye," in the plural with the possessive suffix forming the dual "two springs." This geographical name simply describes the landscape of the place, characterized by the presence of flowing water.
H5879G.emploi: Énaïm appears only twice in the Bible, both in the account of Genesis 38, the story of Tamar and Judah. The town serves as a geographical landmark: it is mentioned as a reference point on the road leading to Timnah. These two occurrences inform us simply that it was a known place, significant enough to serve as a passageway.

sens: Town in the lowlands of Judah
H5879H.detail: Énam is a small town located in the low hills of the territory of Judah, to the west. It appears in the list of towns that God gave to the tribe of Judah during the conquest of Canaan.
H5879H.origine: The name "Énam" literally means "double spring" or "two springs" in Hebrew, likely evoking a geographical feature of the place: two water sources that sprang forth there. This descriptive name, like many names of ancient towns, reflects a notable characteristic of the landscape.
H5879H.emploi: Énam is mentioned only once in the Bible, in Joshua 15:34, in the enumeration of towns assigned to the tribe of Judah. It is among the localities of the lowlands in southern Judah, a fertile and well-watered region. The biblical list of ancient towns helps historians and archaeologists reconstruct the geography of the territory of Judah after the conquest of Canaan.

sens: Place in Palestine located in the south, also called Kadesh
H5880.detail: En-Mischpath is a Hebrew name that literally means "spring of judgment." It is a location situated in ancient Egypt (Genesis 14:7), identified as the same as Kadesh, an important oasis in the southeast of Palestine, a desert region where Moses and the Israelites often camped.
H5880.origine: The name En-Mischpath combines two Hebrew words: "en," which means "spring" or "fountain," and "mishpat," which means "judgment." This name evokes the idea of a source or a place of justice. It is a double name for the same place: Kadesh (קָדֵשׁ) means "holy" or "sacred."
H5880.emploi: En-Mischpath appears only once in the Bible, in Genesis 14:7. It is mentioned as the place where the allied kings from the North (Amraphel and his companions) defeated the Amalekites during a military expedition in the time of Abraham. It is an ancient geographical landmark, identified as Kadesh, an important archaeological site in the Sinai desert.
H5880.portee: This passage recalls the existence and activity of the peoples of Canaan long before the Exodus from Egypt. The connection between En-Mischpath and Kadesh helps us understand biblical geography and the historical significance of certain places where God guided His people in the desert.

sens: Father of the prince Ahira of the tribe of Naphtali
H5881.detail: 1. Enan is a man from the time of the Exodus and the desert, mentioned for the first time around Sinai. He is the father of Ahira, who is designated as prince (chief) of the tribe of Naphtali during the census of Israel at Mount Sinai (Numbers 1:15). Ahira represents his tribe in all official acts: during the second census (Numbers 2:29), during the presentation of offerings at the sanctuary (Numbers 7:78 and 7:83), and finally at the head of his tribe during the departure from the desert to Canaan (Numbers 10:27). Although Enan himself is never directly cited, his name is preserved in the history of Israel because he fathered the one who led his tribe.
H5881.origine: The name Enan means "having eyes" in Hebrew, formed from the root עַיִן (ayin, the eye). It is a theophoric name that evokes the idea of vision or the ability to see—perhaps an allusion to insight or clairvoyance. Names with similar meanings were common in ancient Israel to evoke desired qualities in a man.
H5881.emploi: Enan appears five times in the book of Numbers, always in the formula "Ahira, son of Enan." These five occurrences correspond to the main moments of the organization of Israel at Sinai and the beginning of the desert journey: the first census (Numbers 1), the order of march of the tribes (Numbers 2), the offerings of the princes during the dedication of the sanctuary (Numbers 7), and finally the departure from Sinai (Numbers 10). Enan is significant only through his relationship to Ahira: he is an ancestor, a genealogical link that establishes the identity and authority of the prince of Naphtali. His name is memorial, a signature of a family that served as tribal chief in Israel.

sens: Place on the shore of the Dead Sea
H5882.detail: En-Eglaim is a location situated on the shores of the Dead Sea, in the Holy Land. The name literally means "spring of the two calves" or "source of the two heifers," suggesting that there was a water source there, possibly with traces of ancient animal worship or simply a notable geographical marker. In Ezekiel 47:10, the prophet mentions it as the eastern boundary of a miraculous fishing area along the Dead Sea: it serves as a reference point to indicate the extent of this future transformation of these barren waters into fish-filled waters.
H5882.origine: The Hebrew name עֵין עֶגְלַיִם (en eglaïm) consists of עֵין ("spring, fountain") and עֶגְלַיִם ("calves, heifers"), in the dual form, meaning "two." It is a place name formed on the image of a water source—well visible in arid land—associated with a local detail (perhaps two young cattle that came to drink there, or an ancient cultic practice). Place names in the Holy Land often bear traces of natural landmarks or human activities that have marked them.
H5882.emploi: En-Eglaim appears only once in the Bible, in Ezekiel 47:10. The prophet describes a vision where the waters of the Dead Sea miraculously transform: they become fish-filled and attractive to fishermen. En-Eglaim is cited as a boundary point, on the side of the land of Israel, to show the extent of this miracle. It is a concrete geographical marker that anchors the vision in the real topography of the Holy Land, making God's promise of restoration all the more tangible for the exiles who listened to the prophet.
H5882.portee: This place, mentioned only once in a vision of transformation, carries a message of hope: even the most barren and hostile regions (the Dead Sea was known to be lifeless) will be renewed by God's action. For the Christian reader, it is a reminder that the restoration promised by God reaches forgotten places and the most desperate situations.

sens: Water source near Jerusalem, at the boundary between Judah and Benjamin
Place serving as a landmark in tribal borders
Location where messengers hid to relay information to King David
H5883.detail:
1. En-Roguel is a permanent water source located near Jerusalem, at the boundary between the territories of Judah and Benjamin. Its name means "spring of the fuller" (the one who prepares fabrics). It was an important water point in this arid region.
2. This spring served as a geographical marker to delineate tribal boundaries. In Joshua 15:7 and 18:16, it is mentioned as one of the landmarks that marked the boundary between the lands of Judah and those of Benjamin, showing its role as a well-known reference point.
3. In the time of King David, En-Roguel became a hiding place for royal messengers. In 2 Samuel 17:17, Jonathan and Ahimaaz, who were bringing news to King David, stood at En-Roguel because they could not enter Jerusalem openly without being spotted.
H5883.origine: The compound name "En-Roguel" literally means "spring (en) of the fuller (roguel)." It likely refers to the current Gihon spring, which is indeed located near Jerusalem and is the permanent source of the Pool of Siloam. It was a vital source in a region where water was precious.
H5883.emploi: This locality is mentioned four times in the Bible, all in the Old Testament. It first appears in the description of tribal boundaries (Joshua 15:7 and 18:16), where it serves as a marker to delineate the lands. It then reappears in two significant historical events: as a refuge for messengers of King David fleeing Absalom's supporters (2 Samuel 17:17), and as the place where Adonijah celebrated a sacrifice before rebelling against Solomon (1 Kings 1:9). These uses show that En-Roguel was a well-known and frequented place, strategically located on the outskirts of Jerusalem.

sens: City of Judah inhabited by exiles returning from Babylon
H5884.detail: En-Rimmon is a locality in Judah mentioned in Nehemiah 11:29 among the cities where Jews resettled after their return from Babylonian captivity. It is another name for Ain (עַיִן), a spring or fountain in the land.
H5884.origine: The Hebrew name עֵין רִמּוֹן means literally "spring of the pomegranate" or "fountain of the pomegranate": עֵין (en) = spring, fountain, and רִמּוֹן (rimmon) = pomegranate. The pomegranate was a precious and symbolic fruit in the Old Testament, associated with the fertility and abundance of the land. The name recalls the richness of the waters and vegetation of the place.
H5884.emploi: En-Rimmon appears only once in the Bible, in Nehemiah 11:29, in the context of the return of the exiles. The list enumerates the cities and villages where Jews returning from Babylon settled to repopulate the land. En-Rimmon is mentioned among these localities in Judah, testifying to the gradual restoration of the people to their territory. It is also another designation for Ain, showing how the same locality could be known by different names.

sens: Source or fountain located at the border between Judah and Benjamin
H5885.detail: En-Shemesh literally means "fountain of the sun." It is a water source that marks the boundary between the territory of Judah in the south and that of Benjamin in the north. It is mentioned in the description of the territorial limits of these two tribes after the conquest of Canaan (Joshua 15:7 and 18:17).
H5885.origine: The name is composed of two Hebrew words: "en" (עֵין) means "fountain" or "source," and "shemesh" (שֶׁמֶשׁ) means "sun." The image evokes a source illuminated by the sun or springing toward the sun. This type of geographical name was common in Canaan, often given to notable water points.
H5885.emploi: En-Shemesh appears twice in the Bible, in the book of Joshua. It is cited as a landmark during the delineation of territorial boundaries: in Joshua 15:7, it marks a point on the southern boundary of Benjamin and northern boundary of Judah, and in Joshua 18:17, it again appears as a major geographical reference for establishing borders. These two passages show that it was a well-known and easily identifiable water point for the ancient Israelites.

sens: Place located at the border between Ephraim and Manasseh
H5887.detail: 1. En-Tappuah is a locality situated at the boundary between the territory of Ephraim and that of Manasseh in the Promised Land. Its Hebrew name literally means "fountain of the city of the apple tree": "En" means "source" or "fountain," and "Tappuah" refers to the city of the apple tree. It is mentioned to precisely mark where the border between the two tribes passes (Joshua 17:7).
H5887.origine: The name is composed of two elements: "En" (עֵין), which means "source" or "fountain" in Hebrew, and "Tappuah" (תַּפּוּחַ), the name of a city whose original meaning refers to the apple tree or the region of apple trees. These geographical names often reflect a physical characteristic of the place: the presence of a water source and apple orchards.
H5887.emploi: En-Tappuah appears only once in the Bible, in Joshua 17:7, where it serves as a landmark for delineating tribal territory. It marks the northwestern boundary of Manasseh, near Shechem. This type of border locality was important for the Israelites during the division of the Promised Land after the conquest.

sens: To lack physical strength, to be exhausted by effort
To be weakened, succumbing under weight or suffering
H5888.detail:
1. To lack physical strength, to be exhausted by effort: this is the fatigue that comes from combat, work, or fasting. David is weary after fighting the Philistines (2 Samuel 21:15). The people of Israel, hungry and exhausted from marching and battle, can no longer continue (1 Samuel 14:31).

2. To be weakened, succumbing under weight or suffering: beyond physical fatigue, the word describes a state of moral or spiritual overwhelm, when one no longer has the strength to resist. Sihon, deeply asleep and overwhelmed with weariness, cannot defend himself (Judges 4:21). The daughter of Zion succumbs under the murderers, crushed by misfortune (Jeremiah 4:31).
H5888.origine: The Hebrew verb עִיף comes from a root that expresses the idea of falling, collapsing under weight. The word describes the state of one who has no more strength, physically or morally. It is a simple verb in the Qal (basic form), without the addition of a suffix: the state is passive, it is endured rather than acted upon.
H5888.emploi: This verb appears five times in the Hebrew Bible, always to describe exhaustion in battle or under suffering. It is used for warriors (David, the people of Israel) fatigued after battle, or for people overwhelmed by circumstances. The context is always concrete: the fatigue is visible, immediate, linked to dramatic events. There is no figurative or spiritual use detached from physical reality.
H5888.portee: This word reminds us that physical and moral fatigue is a reality that God acknowledges. It weakens our defenses and makes us vulnerable. It is a call to rest and seek our strength in God, not in ourselves.

sens: Lacking physical strength, exhausted by effort or deprivation
Thirsty, lacking water or moisture
Weary, discouraged, weakened in one's soul
H5889.detail:
1. The word first describes someone whose body can no longer continue: the legs can no longer support them, strength abandons them. Esau returns "weary" from hunting (Genesis 25:29), Gideon pursues his enemies and his men are "weary" (Judges 8:5). It is the exhaustion that comes from prolonged action, travel, or running.
2. The word can also refer to thirst: a soul "dried up" (Psalms 143:6), the man "thirsty" who asks for a drink (Job 22:7). The image is that of dry land needing water, or of a body that has lost its humors.
3. More broadly, it expresses weakening: not only of the body but also of courage and will. The "weary" man has lost the energy to act or even to hope.
H5889.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that evokes the idea of weakening, losing one's strength or humors. It is found in contexts where the body is drained of its energy — whether by effort, heat, thirst, or simply the passage of time. It is a word that describes the state of one who has nothing left to give.
H5889.emploi: This word appears seventeen times in the Old Testament, mostly to speak of physical fatigue during travels or pursuits (Genesis 25:29-30, Deuteronomy 25:18, Judges 8:4-5, 2 Samuel 16:14). But it also extends to the idea of drying up or exhausting resources: a dry land (Psalms 143:6), a man who is thirsty (Job 22:7, Psalms 63:2). Isaiah uses it negatively: the servant of the Lord will not be "weary" in his mission (Isaiah 5:27, Isaiah 28:12). Thus, it is a word that covers both physical fatigue and that of the soul.
H5889.portee: This word reminds the reader that human energy has limits. It shows the importance of mutual help: giving bread to the hungry, water to the thirsty, rest to the exhausted (2 Samuel 17:29). For the believer, it also emphasizes that God never grows weary and can fill with strength those who trust in Him.

sens: the absence of light, the dark state
the thickness of shadow, that which veils
doubt, confusion of the mind
H5890.detail:
1. The word primarily designates physical darkness, the absence of light — what one sees when it is night or in a closed place. In Job 10:22, it is the darkness of the abode of the dead, that underground land where shadow and confusion reign, where light itself seems black.
2. It is also the thickness of that which veils and envelops. Amos 4:13 speaks of one who "turns the dawn into darkness": the image evokes a sudden change, the withdrawal of morning light, the darkening of the sky.
3. Figuratively, this word can denote trouble, doubt, misunderstanding that darken the mind — everything that leaves us without clarity, without a clear vision of things.
H5890.origine: The Hebrew word belongs to a family of terms expressing darkness and shadow. It evokes the primitive image of that which is dark, veiled, imperceptible to sight. In the Greek Old Testament, this word often translates ideas related to the absence of divine light or the distance from the presence of God.
H5890.emploi: The word appears twice in the provided biblical texts. In Job 10:22, it describes the darkness of the abode of the dead, that place without light where death dwells. In Amos 4:13, it expresses the dramatic change that God brings about, transforming light into darkness — an image of divine judgment that withdraws its blessing. In both cases, darkness is not neutral: it is linked to death, judgment, or the absence of God's face.
H5890.portee: This word invites the reader to meditate on the power of divine light and what it means to live in darkness — whether physically or spiritually, that is, far from the presence and guidance of God. It reminds us that only God gives clarity and direction to life.

sens: son of Midian, ancestor of the Ephahites
man of the tribe of Judah
H5891G.detail:
1. Ephah is one of the five sons of Midian, born to Keturah, Abraham's second wife (Genesis 25:4). He is mentioned in the genealogy of the peoples who populated Arabia and the surrounding regions during the patriarchal times.
2. Another Ephah appears in the genealogy of Judah as the son of Jahdai (implicitly mentioned by tradition). He is a figure from the people of Israel, distinct from the first one.
H5891G.origine: The name Ephah means "dark" or "sad" in Hebrew, possibly evoking a difficult birth or circumstance. The name is borne by several men in biblical genealogies, which was common in antiquity.
H5891G.emploi: Ephah appears twice in the Bible, always in genealogical lists. The first mention (Genesis 25:4) presents him as one of the sons of Midian, brother of Epher, Enoch, Abida, and Eldaa. This genealogy establishes the origins of the Arab and Moabite peoples. The second mention (1 Chronicles 1:33) reproduces the same genealogical list. A third Ephah, son of Jahdai, belongs to the lineage of Judah (mentioned in 1 Chronicles 2:47).

sens: woman of the tribe of Judah
concubine of Caleb
mother of Haran, Motsa, and Gazez
H5891H.detail: Ephah is a woman of the tribe of Judah mentioned only once in the Bible, during the divided monarchy. She was the concubine of Caleb, the powerful and faithful man known for his faith in God. She bore three sons: Haran, Motsa, and Gazez (1 Chronicles 2:46). Her name means "dark" or "morose" in Hebrew.
H5891H.origine: The name Ephah comes from a Hebrew root meaning "darkness" or "sadness." This name appears in the genealogy of Judah, among the women who contributed to the lineage of God's people. The same name also designates a son of Midian and a Judahite son of Jahdai, but it is to Caleb's concubine that the unique biblical usage of the word refers in this sense.
H5891H.emploi: Ephah appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 2:46, in the detailed genealogy of the tribe of Judah. She is presented as a concubine (a woman of lower status than a primary wife) of Caleb, the powerful leader of Judah. This verse lists her three sons and continues by mentioning that one of them, Haran, fathered Gazez. Thus, she figures in the genealogical chain of God's people, testifying that even women of less privileged status played a role in the transmission of the line of Judah.

sens: figure from the Old Testament, son of Jahdai and member of the tribe of Judah
H5891I.detail: Ephah is a man from the tribe of Judah mentioned only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 2:47. He is presented as the son of Jahdai and belongs to the lineage of Caleb. His name appears in a genealogy that also lists his brothers: Regem, Jotham, Geshan, Peleth, and Shaaph. He is a distant ancestor of whom nothing else is known except his place in the genealogical tree of God's people.
H5891I.origine: The name Ephah means "dark" or "gloomy" in Hebrew. It may evoke a dark or somber hue. Several biblical figures bear this name: a son of Midian (son of Abraham by Keturah), and this Judahite son of Jahdai. The name, although rare, reflects the variety of proper names in biblical genealogies.
H5891I.emploi: Ephah appears only once in the entire Bible, in 1 Chronicles 2:47, where he is listed among the descendants of Caleb and son of Jahdai. He is included in a long genealogy tracing the ancestors of Judah during the time of the Divided Monarchy. This unique usage tells us nothing more than his name and his place in the family lineage.

sens: region or people associated with Sheba and Midian
H5891J.detail: 1. Ephah designates a region or people from the ancient Arab world, mentioned alongside Sheba and Midian. It is a place or community involved in luxury trade and the riches of the East. In Isaiah 60:6, Ephah appears among the peoples bringing gold and incense to honor restored Jerusalem.
H5891J.origine: The name Ephah comes from the Hebrew עֵיפָה and literally means "dark" or "obscure." It designates a territory or people from the Arabian desert, probably a tribe or region in the southeast of the Arabian Peninsula. This name appears in biblical lists of distant peoples with whom Israel had trade relations.
H5891J.emploi: Ephah appears only once in the Bible, in Isaiah 60:6. In this prophetic passage, the prophet describes the future glory of Jerusalem by listing the nations that will come to bring her riches. Ephah is mentioned among the desert Arab peoples — Sheba, Midian, and others — known for their trade in gold, spices, and incense. This context shows that Ephah was a prosperous and influential region, participating in the great commercial exchanges of the time.

sens: deep trouble caused by fear or alarm
fierce anger, fit of intense rage
H5892A.detail: 1. Anguish is a feeling of dread and alarm that grips the soul in the face of danger or threat. In Jeremiah 15:8, it is a sudden calamity that befalls the city: God "suddenly brings anguish and terror upon her," an image of overwhelming misfortunes that paralyze with fear. 2. This word also denotes fierce anger, the fit of rage that rises up in someone. In Hosea 11:9, God says: "I will not act according to my fierce anger," where anguish is this burning passion that drives one to destroy — an intense and concentrated fury.
H5892A.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root related to the idea of tightening, pressing, suffocating. It literally describes this physical sensation of oppression that accompanies extreme fear or violent anger. It is the feeling that knots the throat and strangles the heart.
H5892A.emploi: This word appears twice in the Hebrew Bible. In Jeremiah 15:8, it evokes collective anguish in the face of God's judgments — those sudden terrors that fall upon a people. In Hosea 11:9, it describes an inner disposition, the divine anger that God restrains by His holiness: unlike humans who act under the influence of anger, God refuses to let His fury dominate Him.
H5892A.portee: This word reminds us that anguish and anger are real powers that threaten to overwhelm us — but also that God, in His holiness, is master of these passions. For the believer, this is a promise: our God, infinitely powerful, masters His anger out of love.

sens: A populated and fortified place, surrounded by walls, with a center of collective life
A collection of houses and public buildings where populations of varying sizes live
The population that inhabits a city
The center of political and administrative power of a region
The refuge, the place of protection and asylum
H5892B.detail:
1. A city is primarily a constructed and defended place: it is a location where people gather, where walls protect them, and where communal life and governance are organized. Cain built a city and named it after his son (Genesis 4:17); during the conquest of Canaan, Joshua is commanded to take the city of Ai along with its inhabitants and fields (Joshua 8:1).
2. A city gathers an organized human community: it has gates (Genesis 24:11 speaks of the well near the city gates), leaders who govern it (Nehemiah 11:9), and houses where its inhabitants live. It is a structured space, different from a nomadic camp or an isolated village.
3. The word "city" sometimes also refers to its inhabitants themselves: "they struck the whole city with the edge of the sword" (Judges 20:37) means that all those who lived there were killed.
4. A city is often the seat of government and power: it is the residence of the king, the center of decision-making, and also the place where judgments are rendered; this is why Jerusalem, the City of David, is at the heart of the kingdom.
5. A city offers protection and security: the cities of refuge in Numbers 35:2-7 are a perfect example; they are places where a fugitive can find asylum and be protected by the community.
H5892B.origine: The Hebrew word עִיר (ir) comes from a root that evokes the idea of "watching" or "staying awake," which reflects the essence of a city: a inhabited place where life is organized and where one must remain vigilant. This word is very ancient in Hebrew and appears in the earliest narratives of Genesis. It is linked to the idea of a conscious space, guarded and animated by collective life, as opposed to an empty or deserted territory.
H5892B.emploi: The word עִיר (city) is one of the most frequent in the Old Testament, used 928 times, present in almost all books. It refers to the cities of Canaan that the Israelites conquer (Joshua), the cities of refuge for those who have committed homicide (Numbers 35), the cities that kings build and fortify (2 Kings), and also the cities of the enemy that are destroyed or besieged (Jeremiah 32:29 speaks of Jerusalem besieged by the Chaldeans). The word applies to Jerusalem, the holy capital, as well as to foreign cities; it can refer to an important large city or a more modest settlement. Its richness comes from the fact that it names both the physical place, its population, and its role in the social order.
H5892B.portee: Meditating on the "city" in the Bible means understanding how God organizes communal life: He approves of organized collective life (Cain builds a city), He establishes laws to protect the inhabitants (the cities of refuge), and He makes them centers of judgment and government. For the Christian, this sheds light on the importance of the church community as a place of shared life and refuge. Jerusalem, the city of David where the Temple stands, also becomes an image of the Church as a community gathered around God.

sens: A fortified human settlement, a populated center of some importance
A locality with its inhabitants, its collective life
An organized architectural and social ensemble
H5892G.detail:
1. A city is a fortified settlement, a center of habitation more significant than a simple village. It is a place where many people live together, with its ramparts, gates, streets, and institutions. In Isaiah 19:18, the "city of destruction" refers to an Egyptian city that will be transformed and will speak the language of Canaan.

2. The word also evokes the community and social life that unfolds there: not only the buildings and walls, but the inhabitants who live there and form a community tied to this place. This is why the Bible often speaks of a city through its history, its deeds, and its destinies.
H5892G.origine: The Hebrew word עִיר (ir) is the fundamental root for designating a city in biblical Hebrew. It appears hundreds of times in the Old Testament, particularly in conquest narratives and geographical descriptions. Its initial image is that of a fortified city, a stronghold where power, commerce, and social life concentrate. In the provided passages, this word specifically designates a city in Egypt in relation to the sacred city of On (Heliopolis).
H5892G.emploi: The word עִיר (city) is extremely frequent in the Old Testament. It refers to the cities of Canaan that the Israelites conquered, royal cities, cities of refuge, and cities of the known world. In Isaiah 19:18, it is a prophecy concerning a future transformation: an Egyptian city, symbolically called the "city of destruction," will one day speak the language of Canaan and worship the God of Israel. This passage shows that the city is not only a geographical place but also political and religious, the seat of decisions and beliefs.
H5892G.portee: The notion of city in the Bible reminds us that God governs peoples and centers of earthly power. The fact that an Egyptian city is called to speak the language of Canaan and to swear by the God of Israel means that divine authority transcends the boundaries and powers of the world. This promise invites the believer to see beyond political appearances and to recognize that God's plans are fulfilled in the history of nations.

sens: A fortified or inhabited human settlement
An urban center with its inhabitants and institutions
People or community of a city
H5892H.detail:
1. A city is a fortified or densely populated settlement, built as a center of collective life. In 1 Chronicles 4:12, Techinnah is called "father of the city of Nachash," which means he founded or governed this urban community.
2. The word also designates all the institutions and civil life that characterize a city: its administration, commerce, and social life. This is why one can speak of "the city" to evoke not only the walls but everything that makes it a populated center.
3. By extension, "city" can also refer to the inhabitants themselves, the community that lives together: one says "the city has decided" just as one says "the people have voted."
H5892H.origine: The Hebrew word עִיר (ir) comes from a root that evokes the idea of staying, dwelling, or living for a long time. A city is therefore primarily a place where one stays, where one establishes oneself durably. The word is very ancient and very common throughout the Hebrew Bible.
H5892H.emploi: The word appears only once in this text from Chronicles, where it qualifies Techinnah as "father of the city of Nachash." This unusual expression designates either a founder or a governor who has given his name or authority to this locality. In a broader biblical context, a city can be the capital of a region, a commercial center, or a fortified refuge, always presented as the seat of organized communal life.
H5892H.portee: Understanding that Techinnah left a lasting mark by founding or governing a city reminds us that our actions can have generational consequences. A city is a legacy, a bequest that we leave to future generations: it is a call to build solidly, not just for oneself, but for those who will come after us.

sens: Man of the tribe of Benjamin, ancestor of the families of Schuppim and Huppim
H5893G.detail: Ir is a man of the tribe of Benjamin mentioned only once in the Bible, at the time when the text lists the genealogies of the sons of Bela. He is the father of Schuppim and Huppim, two sons whose names appear in the list of Benjaminite descendants (1 Chronicles 7:12). His name means "one who belongs to the city," which evokes a connection to urban life, a notable characteristic for the patriarchal era.
H5893G.origine: The name Ir comes from the Hebrew root meaning city (עִיר). This name suggests an association with urban life, which was uncommon in the patriarchal era when pastoral and nomadic life predominated. This choice of name may reveal the importance of urban life for this Benjaminite family.
H5893G.emploi: Ir appears only once in the Old Testament, in 1 Chronicles 7:12, in the context of the genealogies of the tribe of Benjamin. The text mentions him as the son of Bela and the father of Schuppim and Huppim, to document the genealogical continuity of the descendants of Benjamin. This unique and brief mention fits within the narrative function of Chronicles, which systematically traces the tribal lineages of Israel.

sens: Ancient city of Mesopotamia, mentioned alongside Nineveh and Calah
H5893H.detail: 1. Hir is an ancient city of Mesopotamia (the region of the ancient Near East, between the Tigris and Euphrates rivers, corresponding to present-day Iraq). It is mentioned in the account of the beginnings of human civilization, alongside Nineveh and Calah, all three built or developed by Asshur according to the text of Genesis 10:11. The name "Hir" literally means "the city" or "belonging to a city" in Hebrew — it is a geographical term that designated this important city of the ancient world.
H5893H.origine: The word עִיר (ir) means "city" in Hebrew. The name "Hir" is formed from this word, often combined with other elements to create compound geographical names. In this case, "Rehoboth-Hir" literally means "Rehoboth, the city" — Rehoboth (רְחֹבוֹת) meaning "the places" or "the wide spaces." It is common in Hebrew to add the word "city" to a place name to specify or reinforce its identity.
H5893H.emploi: Hir appears only once in the Bible, in Genesis 10:11, in the context of the Table of Nations that lists the descendants of Noah and the cities they founded. It is among the major urban centers of ancient Mesopotamia, built or developed under the authority of Asshur (the Assyrian god and empire). This passage establishes Hir as one of the three major cities of the ancient world, alongside Nineveh (the Assyrian capital) and Calah. Hir thus represents a center of power and civilization in the antediluvian and postdiluvian world according to biblical chronology.

sens: To be vigilant, attentive, in a state of wakefulness
One who remains awake to watch or guard
Celestial being who observes and executes God's orders
H5894.detail:
1. The word fundamentally designates the state of vigilance and attention: to remain awake, on the lookout. It is the opposite of sleeping or being asleep — someone who watches does not doze off but remains aware and attentive to what is happening around them.
2. By extension, the watcher is a guardian, a sentinel: they are responsible for watching over something or someone. It is one who refuses rest to fulfill a task of vigilance (Daniel 4:17, where the "watchers" are described as executors of the divine sentence).
3. In Nebuchadnezzar's vision, the word designates a celestial creature, a supernatural being in angelic form that descends from heaven to convey divine orders (Daniel 4:13 and 4:23). These "watchers" embody God's perpetual attention and obedience to the human world.
H5894.origine: The word comes from the Hebrew root meaning "to awaken" or "to remain awake." It is formed to describe one who is in a state of wakefulness, one who does not sleep. In Hebrew texts, this term appears mainly in the book of Daniel, where it takes on a mystical dimension by designating celestial beings. The root expresses the idea of active vigilance and maintained awareness.
