H5894.emploi: The word appears only three times, all in the book of Daniel (4:13, 4:17, 4:23), in the context of King Nebuchadnezzar's vision. Daniel reports the royal vision and explains that celestial creatures called "watchers" observe the affairs of men and execute God's decrees. These beings are presented as holy, powerful, and authorized to give orders (to cut down the tree, to bind the king with chains). They act as intermediaries of the divine will to humans, always attentive, never distracted or asleep.
H5894.portee: This word reminds the believer that the universe is not abandoned to itself: celestial creatures watch, observe, and execute God's plans. It is an invitation not to doubt divine sovereignty, even when God's plans seem incomprehensible or painful (as for the humiliated King Nebuchadnezzar). The vigilance of these celestial beings is a sign that God never sleeps and never loses control of earthly kingdoms.

sens: young donkey or foal, particularly the male
adult donkey, male of the species
beast of burden and mount
symbol of humility and poverty
H5895.detail:
1. The word primarily designates the young male donkey, the foal. In Judges 10:4 and 12:14, the sons of Jair and Ibzan "rode on thirty donkeys" and "seventy donkeys": these are young animals, agile and light, suitable for travel or quick movement in the mountains.
2. It can also refer to the adult male donkey, as opposed to the female donkey. In Genesis 32:15, Jacob separates "twenty she-donkeys and ten donkeys": the first animals to breed, the latter to carry or ride.
3. As a useful animal, the donkey is an indispensable beast of burden in the Near East: humble, sturdy, capable of carrying heavy loads on difficult paths. In Isaiah 30:6, travelers "carry their riches on the backs of donkeys." 
4. In the messianic prophecy of Genesis 49:11 and Zechariah 9:9, the donkey takes on unexpected dignity: the Messiah "ties his donkey to the vine" or "rides on a foal, the offspring of a she-donkey." The humble animal becomes the symbol of the peaceful and humble coming of the King of Israel, not as a warrior on horseback, but as a servant mounted on a beast of the poor.
H5895.origine: The Hebrew word עַיִר comes from a root that expresses the idea of youth and vigor. It belongs to the same family as other words designating young animals. In Hebrew, the distinction between the adult donkey (חמור, chamor) and the young donkey (עַיִר, ayir) was clear, although the context sometimes allows for confusion. The Greek translation of the Old Testament uses the word ὄνος (onos, "donkey") for both.
H5895.emploi: This word appears 8 times in the Old Testament, mainly in narrative and poetic passages. In Genesis and Judges, it describes transport animals or mounts for important figures (the sons of the judges). In Job 11:12, the wild donkey becomes an ironic comparison to humiliate the man who claims to be wise. In Isaiah, the animal appears as a pack animal for caravans. It is in Genesis 49:11 and especially Zechariah 9:9 that the donkey acquires symbolic significance: the prophetic text of Zechariah speaks of the Messiah "riding on a foal," which the Gospels apply to Jesus' triumphant entry into Jerusalem. The New Testament (Greek) retains this image.
H5895.portee: For the believer, the image of the donkey in messianic texts reveals the character of Jesus Christ: not a conqueror riding a war horse, but a humble and gentle King, serving before reigning. It reminds us that God honors humility and simplicity, and that true greatness comes through self-denial. The burden-bearing donkey also teaches that everyone, in their humble condition, is useful to God's plan.

sens: David's officer
David's mighty warrior
H5896G.detail: Ira is a proper name that designates several characters from the time of the united kingdom under David, all linked to the royal court. The most well-known is Ira the Jairite, who was a state minister of David (2 Samuel 20:26) — an important position that placed him among the king's great officers. The name means "vigilant of a city," evoking someone who watches over and protects. Two other men named Ira also appear in the list of David's mighty warriors: one is a Tekoite, son of Ikkesh. These three Iras represent different functions in service to the king — administrative for the state minister, and warrior for the other two.
H5896G.origine: The name Ira literally means "vigilant of a city" or "one who watches." It expresses an idea of surveillance, attention, and protection. This type of name was common in Israel to express qualities or social roles. Several characters bear this name in the Old Testament, showing its widespread use during the monarchical period.
H5896G.emploi: Ira appears in the Old Testament as the name of three different characters, all linked to David. The only one explicitly mentioned in the provided verses is Ira the Jairite, designated as a state minister of David in 2 Samuel 20:26. This administrative role places him at the heart of the royal government. The other two Iras are mentioned in the lists of David's mighty warriors, showing that this name was borne by several of the king's loyal followers.

sens: Elite warrior in the service of King David
Military chief responsible for a division of the army
H5896H.detail: Ira is one of the most renowned warriors during the time of King David, during the united monarchy of Israel. He is identified as the son of Ikkesh and from Tekoa, a town in Judah. He ranks among David's great officers and warriors, indicating his military and political importance. In 1 Chronicles 27:9, we learn that he commanded a division of twenty-four thousand men during the sixth month of the year, indicating a high responsibility in the organization of the royal army.
H5896H.origine: The name Ira means "vigilant over the city" (literally "watchful of a city"), evoking the image of an attentive and vigilant person, tasked with watching over and protecting. Although the modern transliteration is "Ira," the Hebrew name עִירָא (ira) carries this connotation of vigilance and guard. It belongs to a time when names had descriptive significance, reflecting the qualities or function of the person.
H5896H.emploi: Ira appears three times in the Old Testament, always in the lists of David's warriors. In 2 Samuel 23:26, he is mentioned among the great officers and warriors of King David. This same passage also appears in 1 Chronicles 11:28, confirming his place in the royal military elite. In 1 Chronicles 27:9, we discover that he had administrative responsibilities: he was the chief of a military division of about twenty-four thousand men during the sixth month of the year, demonstrating his role in the structured organization of King David's standing army. These three mentions converge to present Ira as a major military figure during David's reign.

sens: Officer and warrior of David
Military chief of King David
H5896I.detail: Ira is the name of a man who lived during the time of the united monarchy and served King David. He is mentioned in the lists of David's great officers and mighty warriors (2 Samuel 23:38 and 1 Chronicles 11:40), where he is referred to as "Ira of Jether," which likely indicates his origin or family. The context suggests that he held an important role in the royal army.
H5896I.origine: The name Ira literally means "vigilant of a city" or "one who watches over the city," evoking the image of an attentive, capable, and responsible person. This etymology fits well for a military officer with significant responsibilities to the king.
H5896I.emploi: Ira is mentioned twice in the Bible, both times in lists of David's warriors: first in 2 Samuel 23:38, and a second time in 1 Chronicles 11:40. These two passages essentially provide the same information: Ira, of Jether, was part of the mighty warriors and great officers of King David. He is not the subject of a detailed narrative, but his appearance in these prestigious lists attests to his importance and status with the king.

sens: Descendant of Cain before the Flood
H5897.detail: Irad is a man who lived before the Flood, in the lineage of Cain. He is the son of Enoch (son of Cain) and the father of Mehujael. The Segond names him "Metuschaël" in Genesis 4:18, where the antediluvian genealogy of Cain is given: "Enoch fathered Irad, Irad fathered Mehujael, Mehujael fathered Metuschaël, and Metuschaël fathered Lamech."
H5897.origine: The name Irad literally means "swift" or "one who runs fast," evoking agility or speed. It belongs to the genealogy of Cain, whose descendants are listed in Genesis 4, and is situated in the mythical period before the Flood.
H5897.emploi: Irad appears only once in the Bible, in Genesis 4:18. He is part of the genealogical chain of Cain — Cain, Enoch, Irad, Mehujael, Metuschaël, Lamech — which shows the continuity of the cursed lineage before the judgment of the Flood. This genealogy contrasts with that of Seth (in Genesis 5), which leads to Noah and the ark.

sens: City of Judah, in the desert
Place of salt or salty region of the desert
H5898.detail: Ir-Hammélach literally means "the city of salt." It is a locality in the desert of Judah, listed among the cities of the tribe of Judah. It derives its name from the presence of salt in this arid region, likely related to mineral deposits or saline springs in the Judean desert. The geographical context suggests a small town or settlement in an inhospitable area.
H5898.origine: The Hebrew name is composed of two words: 'ir (עִיר), which means "city" or "town," and melach (מֶלַח), which means "salt." The root of the word "salt" evokes both the mineral itself and, by extension, preservation and sterility. In the Bible, salt often symbolizes what is enduring and purifying. This geographical name simply reflects the natural characteristic of the site.
H5898.emploi: Ir-Hammélach appears only once in the Bible, in Joshua 15:62, where it is mentioned in the enumeration of desert cities assigned to the tribe of Judah. It is listed between Nibshan and En-Gedi, two other localities in the Judean desert. This list reflects the boundaries and territorial possessions of Judah. The context suggests that it was a minor city in the desert, likely a place of passage or a supply point.

sens: fortified city of Canaan, located in the Jordan Valley east of Jerusalem
H5899.detail: 1. Jericho is designated by the name "City of Palms" due to the lush vegetation that characterizes it, particularly its many date palms. It occupies a strategic position in the Jordan Valley, not far from the river crossing that the Israelites will make upon entering the Promised Land (Deuteronomy 34:3).
H5899.origine: The Hebrew name "Ir Hatmarim" literally means "City of Palms": "ir" means "city" or "town," and "tamrim" refers to palms. This descriptive nickname reflects the geographical environment and agricultural richness of the site, particularly its date palms. The ancient site is known in archaeology as Tell es-Sultan.
H5899.emploi: This name appears four times in the Bible: once in Deuteronomy (at the moment when Moses contemplates the Promised Land from the mountain), and three times in Judges and Chronicles, which recount the beginnings of the conquest and conflicts in Canaan. The references show the persistence of the nickname "City of Palms" throughout the different biblical periods, from the conquest to the time of the kings.
H5899.portee: This poetic nickname reminds us that Jericho was not just a fortress to conquer, but a rich and prosperous city, endowed with fertile agriculture. It invites us to see beyond the account of the miraculous siege: a living city, inhabited, integrated into the land that God promised to His people.

sens: Quitter un lieu en s'en allant
Laisser quelque chose ou quelqu'un sans le prendre ou sans en prendre soin
Renoncer à une alliance, une fidélité, une obéissance
Cesser de suivre ou de servir, notamment en matière religieuse
H5800A.detail:
1. Quitter un lieu physiquement : partir et laisser derrière soi. En Genèse 2:24, l'homme « quittera son père et sa mère » pour former sa propre famille. C'est un départ intentionnel.
2. Laisser sans protection ou sans secours : ne pas s'occuper de quelqu'un qui dépend de vous. Quand on « abandonne » des récoltes dans les champs (Lévitique 19:10), on les laisse sur place sans les ramasser. L'idée est celle du manque d'attention ou de soin.
3. Trahir une relation d'alliance ou de service en la rompant. En Juges 10:6, Israël « abandonne » l'Éternel en se tournant vers d'autres dieux : c'est un acte de désobéissance et d'infidélité qui brise la promesse faite à Dieu.
4. Renier son engagement envers quelqu'un ou quelque chose. En Jérémie 5:19, l'Éternel dit à Israël : « Comme vous m'avez abandonné… » — le peuple a cessé de le suivre et de le servir, donc subit les conséquences.
H5800A.origine: Le verbe hébraïque vient d'une racine qui évoque l'idée de lâcher prise, de ne plus tenir quelque chose. Elle apparaît souvent dans des contextes de rupture — qu'elle soit physique (partir), pratique (cesser de s'occuper) ou relationnelle (renier l'alliance). Le sens premier est très concret : desserrer les mains, laisser tomber.
H5800A.emploi: Ce verbe est extrêmement fréquent dans l'Ancien Testament (188 emplois) et revêt des nuances selon les contextes. Il désigne d'abord des actes concrets : quitter un endroit (Genèse 2:24, Genèse 50:8), laisser quelqu'un seul (Genèse 39:6 où Joseph est laissé aux responsabilités de la maison). Mais surtout, il exprime l'infidélité religieuse : les Israélites « abandonnent » l'Éternel (Juges 10:6, 1 Samuel 12:10, 2 Chroniques 12:1) en adorant d'autres dieux ou en désobéissant. Inversement, l'Éternel promet de ne « pas abandonner » son peuple (Deutéronome 31:6, Josué 1:5), ce qui scelle son engagement éternel. Le mot porte donc le poids de la rupture d'alliance.
H5800A.portee: Pour le lecteur chrétien, ce mot éveille la conscience de la fidélité. Il rappelle que servir Dieu ne consiste pas seulement en actions isolées, mais en une présence constante et fidèle — et que nous avons tous connu l'abandon des promesses faites au Seigneur. Mais il offre aussi la certitude que Dieu ne nous abandonne jamais (Hébreux 13:5 y fait écho), contrairement aux liens humains. C'est un appel à la repentance et une source de réconfort.

sens: descendants du lévite Uzziel
clan familial de la tribu de Lévi
H5817.detail: 1. Les Uziélites sont les descendants d'Uzziel, un homme de la tribu de Lévi qui vivait au temps de l'Égypte et du désert. Uzziel était le fils de Kehath (comme l'étaient aussi Amram, Itsehar et Hébron) et eut cinq fils : Mishael, Élizaphan, Sithri, Micah et Isshiah. 2. Ce nom désigne le clan ou la famille que formaient ces descendants au sein des familles des Kehathites. En Nombres 3:27, Moïse énumère les quatre familles de Kehath : les Amramites, les Jitseharites, les Hébronites et les Uziélites, chacune constituant une branche de l'organisation lévitique.
H5817.origine: Le mot vient du nom propre Uzziel (עֻזִּיאֵל en hébreu), qui signifie « ma force est Dieu ». Le suffixe -élites (ou -ites en français) désigne les descendants d'une personne ou les membres d'un clan qui en descend. C'est une formation courante dans la Bible pour les groupes familiaux issus d'une ancêtre donné.
H5817.emploi: Le mot n'apparaît que deux fois dans la Bible, toutes les deux en relation avec l'organisation des Lévites. En Nombres 3:27, il figure dans la liste des quatre familles de Kehath chargées du transport du tabernacle et de ses accessoires. En 1 Chroniques 26:23, le même énumération revient lors de l'organisation des portiers du temple sous le règne de David. À chaque fois, les Uziélites sont mentionnés comme l'une des quatre branches principales de la descendance lévitique de Kehath.
H5817.portee: Ce nom rappelle que la structure du peuple d'Israël reposait sur des liens de parenté ordonnés : chaque clan avait sa place et sa fonction dans le culte du Seigneur. Les Uziélites, comme les autres familles lévitiques, illustrent comment Dieu organise son peuple en communauté structurée, où chacun a un rôle à remplir dans le service du temple et de Dieu.

sens: Roi de Juda du huitième siècle avant Jésus-Christ, fils d'Amatsia
Monarque qui régna 52 ans et devint très puissant
Prince frappé de lèpre pour avoir voulu faire l'œuvre des prêtres dans le temple
H5818G.detail:
1. Ozias est le nom d'un roi de Juda, fils du roi Amatsia, qui régna longtemps et avec succès au huitième siècle avant Jésus-Christ. Il est aussi appelé Azaria dans certains passages de 2 Rois. Son nom signifie « ma force est l'Éternel ».
2. Durant son règne de 52 ans, Ozias devint extrêmement puissant : il renforça son armée avec des boucliers, des lances et des arcs, et les Ammonites lui payaient tribut, ce qui étendit sa renommée jusqu'aux frontières de l'Égypte (2 Chroniques 26:8, 14).
3. À la fin de sa vie, Ozias commit un acte d'orgueil en entrant dans le temple pour faire l'œuvre des prêtres. L'Éternel le frappa de lèpre en châtiment, et il demeura lépreux jusqu'à sa mort, exclu de la maison de l'Éternel et séparé dans une maison écartée (2 Chroniques 26:21).
H5818G.origine: Le nom Ozias vient de l'hébreu עֻזִּיָּהוּ (Uzziyyahu), composé de « oz » (force) et de « Yah » (l'Éternel). C'est un roi historique bien attesté dans les annales bibliques et extérieures. Dans le Nouveau Testament, le nom prend la forme grecque « Ozias » (Matthieu 1:8-9), où il figure dans la généalogie de Jésus.
H5818G.emploi: Ozias apparaît 22 fois dans la Bible, principalement dans 2 Rois 15 et 2 Chroniques 26-27, ainsi que dans les prophètes Ésaïe, Osée et Amos (au moment de leurs appels prophétiques). Les récits des Rois situent son règne parmi d'autres monarques du nord et du sud : Jotham, son fils, continua après lui en faisant ce qui était droit comme son père (2 Rois 15:34). Ésaïe mentionne l'année de sa mort comme repère pour sa vision du Seigneur (Ésaïe 6:1). Les prophètes Osée et Amos prophétisaient à son époque (Osée 1:1 ; Amos 1:1), révélant les troubles de cette période. Son histoire illustre le destin des rois justes mais tentés par l'orgueil.
H5818G.portee: La vie d'Ozias enseigne au lecteur une leçon grave : la puissance terrestre et la prospérité, si elles viennent de Dieu, ne doivent pas entraîner l'orgueil ni le dépassement de nos limites. Ozias a oublié que chaque charge a ses limites, et que la gloire appartient à Dieu seul. Son châtiment — la lèpre qui isole — montre la sévérité de Dieu envers ceux qui se détournent de son ordre établi, même après des années de fidélité.

sens: Lévite de la tribu de Lévi, fils d'Uriel et père de Saül
H5818H.detail: Ozias est un Lévite mentionné dans la généalogie des descendants de Lévi. Il est le fils d'Uriel et le père de Saül, et il vivait à l'époque de la monarchie divisée en Israël. Son nom signifie « Ma force est l'Éternel ». Il apparaît dans la liste généalogique de 1 Chroniques 6:24, dans la succession des générations de la tribu de Lévi.
H5818H.origine: Le nom Ozias (עֻזִּיָּהוּ) signifie « Ma force est l'Éternel » : uz signifie force ou puissance, et Yah est le nom divin abrégé. C'est un nom théophore, c'est-à-dire un nom qui incorpore le nom de Dieu, courant dans l'Ancien Testament. Le même personnage est aussi appelé Azariah en 1 Chroniques 6:36, indiquant une variante de nom dans la transmission des textes anciens.
H5818H.emploi: Ozias est mentionné une seule fois dans la Segond, en 1 Chroniques 6:24, dans la généalogie des Lévites. Il figure dans la liste des descendants de Lévi qui formaient le clergé d'Israël. Bien que peu documenté, son inclusion dans cette généalogie indique qu'il était un ancêtre reconnu de la lignée sacerdotale lévitique, probablement un personnage de certaine importance dans l'histoire religieuse d'Israël.

sens: Man who lived during the time of the divided monarchy, father of Jonathan
H5818I.detail: Ozias is a character mentioned only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 27:25. He is the father of Jonathan, who served as the royal steward of provisions in the fields, cities, villages, and towers of the kingdom. His name means "my strength is Jehovah," expressing trust in divine power.
H5818I.origine: The name Ozias comes from the Hebrew Uzziyyahu, composed of two elements: "oz" meaning "strength" or "power," and "Yah," which is the abbreviation of the divine name Jehovah. This combination expresses a declaration of faith: "my strength is Jehovah." The name reflects a deep conviction that all power comes from the Lord.
H5818I.emploi: Ozias appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 27:25, in the list of officers of King David. He is presented there as the father of Jonathan, who was in charge of royal provisions. This passage is part of an administrative enumeration showing the organization of David's government and the individuals responsible for various areas: treasury, provisions, fields, cities, villages, and towers.

sens: Priest from the priestly family of Harim who married a foreign woman during the time of Ezra
H5818J.detail: Ozias is a priest belonging to the family of Harim. At the time of the return from exile in Babylon, he made the grave mistake of marrying a foreign woman, a practice that the Law prohibited in order to preserve the religious purity and identity of God's people. His name appears in the list of priests and Levites who had to repudiate their foreign wives, compiled under the direction of Ezra (Ezra 10:21).
H5818J.origine: The name Ozias (עֻזִּיָּהוּ in Hebrew) means "My strength is the Lord" or "My God is my strength." It is composed of two elements: עֻז (oz), meaning "strength," and יָּה (Yah), a short form of the name of God (Yahweh). It is a typical theophoric name in the Old Testament, placing trust in divine power. Several biblical characters bore this name, but here it specifically refers to a priest during the time of Ezra.
H5818J.emploi: Ozias appears only once in the Bible, in Ezra 10:21. He is a priest mentioned in the context of the religious reforms led by Ezra after the return from exile. The Bible reports that the Jewish people, including the priests and Levites, had intermingled with the peoples of the surrounding lands by taking foreign wives. Ezra organized a solemn assembly to rectify this situation. Ozias is among those who agreed to send away their foreign wives, a painful act deemed necessary for faithfulness to the Covenant.
H5818J.portee: The case of Ozias illustrates an important lesson for believers: even spiritual leaders can fail by straying from the Word of God, and repentance sometimes requires difficult sacrifices. His acceptance of separating from his foreign wife shows the priority given to obedience to God over personal ties — a tension that the New Testament will explore in another way. It is a call to separation from what distances one from the Lord.
